[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning. When all sampled rollouts for a prompt share one answer, the method caches them; if a later majority conflicts with that answer, it discards the new pseudo-pairs and uses a cache loss. PC-Dr.DPO sets each prompt’s robust temperature from its observed majority fraction, with weaker majorities receiving sharper within-prompt weighting. The analysis separates population-majority bias, where the policy’s modal answer is wrong, from finite-rollout variation, where sampled majorities differ from that mode. The evaluation adapts on each full evaluation set or official test split using fixed benchmark budgets and reports the final checkpoint rather than the best intermediate checkpoint. Reading boundary: The safeguard preserves earlier self-consistency, which can itself be wrong; it does not correct population-majority bias.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: Process Reinforcement through Implicit Rewards. PRIME can initialize its PRM from the starting SFT/base policy and filters prompts by their sampled accuracy range during training. PRIME updates an implicit PRM online using policy rollouts and outcome supervision and uses token-level dense rewards for policy training. The instantiated advantage estimator computes implicit-process and outcome returns separately before combining them, using leave-one-out baselines. The implicit PRM parameterizes reward with the log likelihood ratio of a reward language model to a reference model, yielding token-level process rewards. Reading boundary: The described filtering aims at intermediate difficulty and PRM data balance; exact selected accuracy bounds are not specified by this claim.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms. On 49 Atari games with metrics averaged over three trials, PPO wins 30 games by average reward across training and 19 by average reward over the final 100 episodes; ACER wins 18 and 28 respectively. PPO proposes a surrogate that takes the minimum of an unclipped probability-ratio advantage term and its clipped counterpart, removing incentive for some excessively large policy updates. The continuous-control surrogate comparison uses seven Gym MuJoCo -v1 tasks, one million timesteps per run, three random seeds per task, and a normalized aggregate over 21 runs. The actor-critic PPO algorithm collects rollout data from parallel actors, computes advantage estimates, then optimizes a surrogate on those samples for multiple minibatch epochs. Reading boundary: Game-win counts depend on the specified metric and compared A2C/ACER implementations.

RAFT selects the batch’s highest-reward fraction for supervised fine-tuning at each stage. For IMDB, the study measures perplexity on 500 test samples and constrains its increase to at most 5%. The IMDB table reports LLaMA 7B-RAFT mean sentiment reward 0.4293 and mean perplexity 9.9375, versus the unaligned row’s 0.0993 and 9.5. The authors identify sparse desirable samples as a failure mode in which RAFT may stall without enough favorable outputs to select. The RAFT algorithm optionally mixes an expert generator with the current generator during data collection. Reading boundary: The reward is a learned sentiment-model score; this result is not a general helpfulness/safety gain.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: REBEL: Reinforcement Learning via Regressing Relative Rewards. REBEL permits its base response distribution to be either a fixed offline dataset or the current policy. The TLDR evaluation compares generated summaries against human references using GPT-4 on a randomly sampled 600-example test subset. In the described experiments, both responses in each REBEL regression pair are generated by the current policy. REBEL regresses response-pair reward differences against policy log-ratio differences, removing the prompt-only partition term. The 6.9B TLDR table reports 78.0% win rate for REBEL and 77.6% for PPO. Reading boundary: The PPO result is imported from Huang et al.; the table is not a jointly rerun paired comparison. GPT-4 is the preference judge, not a human panel.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: REINFORCE++: Stabilizing Critic-Free Policy Optimization with Global Advantage Normalization. REINFORCE++ replaces prompt-local advantage normalization with global normalization and describes a single-response configuration for general RLHF. The baseline variant first subtracts the within-prompt mean reward and then normalizes using global batch statistics. The baseline variant uses a separate KL regularization loss with the k2 estimator. The best-practice discussion distinguishes baseline variants that support binary 0/1 or symmetric −1/1 rewards from plain REINFORCE++, which the authors recommend with symmetric rewards. Reading boundary: Single-response mode means one sampled response per prompt. Selected v9 also evaluates plain REINFORCE++ with k > 1 for reasoning (section 4.2). The baseline variant adds group-mean reshaping and is particularly advised for sample filtering and complex tasks such as multi-turn tool use (sections 3.2 and 5.1); multiple responses alone do not require it.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: RLAIF-V: Aligning MLLMs through Open-Source AI Feedback for Super GPT-4V Trustworthiness. RLAIF-V generates candidate responses with the same model/distribution, decomposes factual response content into atomic claims, queries an open-source multimodal labeler with yes/no questions and constructs preference pairs for iterative DPO training. RefoMB descriptions start with GPT-4V drafts merged by GPT-4, then human additions/corrections and verification by at least two graduate students; GPT-4 uses descriptions to judge response pairs against GPT-4V. The authors acknowledge training costs and remaining hallucination despite improvements, and leave further trustworthiness gains for future methods. For the 146-sample MHumanEval response-level hallucination measure in v1, Table 1 reports 50.7% for OmniLMM 12B, 29.5% after RLAIF-V, and 45.9% for the compared GPT-4V condition. The 7B setting uses LLaVA 1.5 as instruction model and LLaVA-NeXT as labeler; the 12B setting uses OmniLMM as both instruction model and labeler, with four 4k-instruction iterations described for each. Reading boundary: Open-source training feedback does not mean the complete benchmark/evaluation workflow excludes humans or proprietary models. Table 4 defines99 dev and 261 test instructions; the prose’s images wording is inconsistent.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: RLAIF: Scaling Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with AI Feedback. In this v1 summarization study, PaLM2 Large generates preference labels and PaLM2 Extra-Small initializes the models; RL uses modified A2C rather than PPO. Human policy evaluation uses 1,200 ratings: evaluators rank RLAIF, RLHF, SFT and human-reference summaries without ties for held-out TL;DR posts. For each summary pair, the AI labeler is queried twice with reversed candidate order and the resulting preference distributions are averaged to mitigate position bias. Human evaluators prefer RLAIF summaries to SFT 71% of the time and RLHF to SFT 73%; the paper reports the difference as not statistically significant and RLAIF versus RLHF as 50%. Reading boundary: The study is summarization-only v1; longer outputs are a reported confound and comparative monetary costs were not estimated (conclusion p9).

The experiments use the HH preference corpus with the Dahoas/gptj-rm-static proxy reward model. RRHF scores each response with length-normalized conditional log probability. Table 2 reports Alpaca-RRHF with diverse-beam sampling mean proxy reward−1.02 and GPT-2-medium perplexity 14.75 on HH. The pinned RRHF study does not experiment with refreshing the sampling policy at every training step. RRHF adds ranking loss to cross-entropy training on the highest-reward response. Reading boundary: Reward units are model-specific; a high proxy reward is not an independent measure of helpfulness or safety.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: ReMax: A Simple, Effective, and Efficient Method for Aligning Large Language Models. The reported GPT-4 model comparison uses 300 LIMA test samples. ReMax subtracts the reward of a current-model greedy response from the reward of its sampled response when forming the policy-gradient loss. ReMax does not resolve reward bias or reward hacking; the authors identify data collection and reward-learning design as remaining requirements. The authors report no substantial training-speed acceleration for models on the scale of OPT 1.3B after DeepSpeed optimization. The authors report about 2.2× training acceleration for ReMax in a GPT-2-137M IMDB positive-sentiment continuation experiment without DeepSpeed. The rm-static experiments randomly split the public dataset 20% for SFT,40% for reward learning and 40% for reward maximization. Reading boundary: OPT win/tie/loss counts in one displayed comparison sum to 299 rather than 300; that mismatch is retained as an issue and no corrected count is inferred.

The paper uses GPT-4 as judge in AlpacaEval1.0 and MT-Bench, and GPT-4-turbo in AlpacaEval2.0, with text-davinci-003 and GPT-4 references respectively for the two AlpacaEval versions. ORPO combines supervised chosen-response NLL loss with a weighted log-sigmoid odds-ratio loss comparing chosen and rejected responses. ORPO updates the model directly without retaining a separate frozen reference model; the paper compares this computation to its stated RLHF/DPO training setup. The paper leaves scaling beyond 7B parameters, broader preference-method comparisons and more diverse fine-tuning domains to future work. Reading boundary: These are automated evaluation outcomes, distinct from human preference annotation.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: SLiC-HF: Sequence Likelihood Calibration with Human Feedback. The sample-rank experiments generate eight SFT-model decodes per example at temperature 0.7 and top-k 40. SLiC-HF-direct calibrates directly on preferred/rejected human-feedback sequences without training a ranking or reward model. SLiC-HF-direct can face mismatch between the off-policy human-feedback distribution and the SFT model’s decode distribution. In a 100-validation-example four-way human comparison, the sample-rank SLiC-HF model is chosen best 73% of the time. SLiC-HF combines a margin-based sequence ranking calibration loss with cross-entropy regularization. Reading boundary: Three raters per task; choice uses majority vote, with 4% same/no-preference. This is a four-way selection rate, not pairwise win rate against every baseline.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: STAMP Your Content: Proving Dataset Membership via Watermarked Rephrasings. STAMP requires watermarking before online release and access to model token probabilities; it does not retroactively mark previously published content. The method uses a one-sided paired t-test for lower public-version perplexity relative to private versions. STAMP compares a public keyed paraphrase collection with privately held differently keyed paraphrases using paired perplexity differences. STAMP can compare each public paraphrase against the average perplexity over multiple differently keyed private paraphrases to reduce individual-document bias. Reading boundary: The paper also warns about paraphrase errors and evaluates continual pretraining rather than models trained from scratch.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: SelectTTRL: Representation-Guided Data Selection for Efficient Test-Time Reinforcement Learning. Percentile selection is fixed before adaptation without target ground-truth answers, while all target questions remain in the evaluation set. SelectTTRL constructs a frozen correctness-related activation direction from paired correct and incorrect answers in a separate TruthfulQA-derived labeled calibration set. In the reported experiment, subset baselines retain the same question fraction and vary the selection rule while keeping the TTRL procedure, budget and hyperparameters fixed. Initial target responses are scored and ranked, then only a prescribed percentile interval receives standard TTRL multi-response sampling and policy updates. Reading boundary: The selected subset is defined by floor-based percentile ranks and fixed-identifier tie breaking, not post-hoc selection of only correctly answered targets.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: Self-Play Preference Optimization for Language Model Alignment. The authors report that general leaderboard performance for DPO, IPO and SPPO declines after the first or second alignment iteration. SPPO formulates alignment as a two-player constant-sum preference game rather than assuming one transitive scalar reward for all comparisons. The experiment uses three SPPO iterations, advancing a first-epoch model trained on 20,000 prompts each iteration. Table 1 reports 28.53% length-controlled AlpacaEval 2 win rate for SPPO Iter 3 versus 17.11% for Mistral 7B-Instruct-v0.2. The experiment samples five responses per prompt and retains the highest- and lowest-PairRM-scoring responses for preference data. The SPPO convergence theorem assumes realizability of the ideal optimization problem and concerns the mixture policy across iterations. Reading boundary: 805 prompts; GPT-4-Turbo judging/reference protocol. These are ordinary decoding rows, separate from best-of 16 reranking. Table score 28.53 differs from prose 28.52.

The reported blind human A/B evaluation is conducted by the paper authors; Table 6 describes150 examples for each evaluated dataset. The paper limits its main experiments to English and proprietary base models, requires sufficient few-shot/instruction-following ability, and reports that erroneous feedback dominates the analyzed failed refinements. In Table 1, GPT-4 code-optimization performance rises from 27.3% to 36.0%, while math solve rate changes from 92.9% to 93.1%; the paper uses task-specific, human-preference and GPT-4-preference metrics rather than one common accuracy measure. [sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: SimPO: Simple Preference Optimization with a Reference-Free Reward. For Instruct setups, five responses per UltraFeedback prompt are generated from the starting model and PairRM selects the highest/lowest-scoring pair. SimPO introduces a positive target reward margin in the Bradley-Terry preference objective. For Llama 3-8B-Instruct, Table 4 reports AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rate 44.7% for SimPO versus 40.3% for DPO. SimPO uses length-normalized policy log-likelihood as an implicit reward and removes the reference-policy term. The standard RSO experiment generates 64 SFT-policy candidates and rejection-subsamples eight. The CNN/DailyMail experiment assumes no training access to CNN/DailyMail targets or preference texts, testing transfer from TLDR training. [sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: Step-DPO: Step-wise Preference Optimization for Long-chain Reasoning of LLMs. On MATH, the Qwen2-7B-SFT ablation reports 54.8% baseline,55.0% with DPO and 55.8% with Step-DPO. The proposed localization procedure permits humans or GPT-4 to find the first erroneous reasoning step. The described data construction produces 10,000 pairwise preference records for Step-DPO. The authors caution that outputs with correct final answers can still contain erroneous intermediate steps, requiring additional preferred-step filtering. Step-DPO contrasts preferred and rejected next reasoning steps conditioned on the prompt and preceding correct steps. Reading boundary: Both preference methods use 5,000 training records in this ablation; MATH evaluation has 5,000 problems. These values do not describe the full 10,000-record main run.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: TTRL: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning. The example reward function extracts final answers and gives reward one for matching the most frequent sampled answer and zero otherwise. TTRL samples multiple candidate outputs, derives a consensus answer and uses agreement with that answer to construct its reward signal. TTRL is defined as reinforcement-learning adaptation of a pretrained model during test time without ground-truth labels for the target data. The implementation samples 64 responses for voting and downsamples 32 per prompt for policy training. Reading boundary: This exact rule is answer-frequency agreement; it does not validate the intermediate reasoning.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: The Llama 3 Herd of Models. The Llama 3 DPO recipe masks header and termination tokens from both chosen and rejected response losses to stabilize training. Some preference records contain three ranked responses: human-improved edited response, chosen response, and rejected response. The authors report that Llama 3 405B and GPT-4-0125 win rates are within the margin of error on nearly all capabilities in their human evaluation. The human evaluation counts a model win only when an annotator rates its response better or much better, excluding slightly-better ratings from wins. Llama 3 post-training applies six rounds, collecting new preference annotations and SFT data and sampling synthetic data from the latest models each cycle. Rejection sampling typically generates 10 to 30 outputs per human-annotation prompt and uses the reward model to choose one candidate. Reading boundary: About 7,000 prompts across capability sets; pairwise seven-point preference ratings. This is not an across-provider or present-day ranking.

For the paper's 6B verifier, increasing candidate completions helps up to 400 and then reduces performance; the authors attribute this to the risk of finding solutions that fool the verifier. [sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. For RLHF training, the paper combines 137k prompts from the static human-feedback dataset with 369k model-generated prompts; the synthetic prompts are distinct from the human comparison labels used to train preference models. The authors emphasize average-case rather than worst-case behavior, unresolved honesty and subtle-bias issues, and RL stability limitations. A controlled 52B helpfulness experiment uses equal-sized data and identical hyperparameters and finds that a base/rejection-sampling/online mixture is preferred by crowdworkers to all-base data. The study collects helpfulness dialogues by choosing the more helpful response and red-team dialogues by choosing the more harmful response; retained comparisons are treated as equally weighted binary labels without ties. Workers are recruited through US MTurk and Upwork; the authors select workers using writing/dialogue spot checks rather than agreement-based label filtering, and explicitly note that the worker distribution changes over the project. Reading boundary: In this paper, online iterations retrain new models rather than continually updating one model. This is not a guarantee of worst-case safety.

The human generation-evaluation procedure blinds evaluators to the model name and prompt that produced an answer. The paper recruits two external researchers for separate reference-label validation and a human-answer baseline. GPT-judge training includes about 6,900 true/false-labelled author reference answers and about 15,500 human-evaluated model answers. Reading boundary: Section 3.2 (p.6) says the authors carried out all main-generation evaluations. A predefined qualitative rubric maps to scalar truth scores; it does not remove all judgment or disagreement.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective. Dr. GRPO replaces response-dependent loss normalization with a constant and uses a Monte Carlo return baseline in the recovered objective. The authors identify within-question reward-standard-deviation normalization as reweighting questions and introducing difficulty bias. The authors identify response-length normalization as a bias favoring shorter correct responses and longer incorrect responses in their GRPO objective analysis. The optimizer experiment assigns reward one when Math-Verify accepts the final answer and zero otherwise, training on MATH questions and evaluating on AIME2024, AMC, MATH500, Minerva Math and OlympiadBench. Reading boundary: The preceding method also removes group standard-deviation normalization (physical p6 lines150–151); unbiasedness is reported by the paper and not independently proved.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: VAPO: Efficient and Reliable Reinforcement Learning for Advanced Reasoning Tasks. VAPO separates GAE parameters for value targets and policy advantages, using lambda one for the value-network returns. VAPO adjusts policy GAE lambda as a function of output length and a bias-variance control parameter. VAPO combines policy-gradient loss with an additional negative-log-likelihood loss on correctly sampled outcomes. VAPO pretrains the value model on Monte Carlo returns from a fixed policy before saving and loading that value checkpoint for policy training. Reading boundary: Policy lambda is separately length-adaptive in this recipe; no general unbiasedness theorem is asserted by this candidate.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Feedback, rewards and policy optimization: WPO: Enhancing RLHF with Weighted Preference Optimization. The conceptual WPO preference-labeling construction assumes there are no conflicting pairwise preferences for a prompt. The authors state that their preference dataset does not include safety aspects and that they do not study preference optimization for multi-turn conversations. The hybrid experiment labels five SFT-model outputs plus one GPT-4-Turbo output using GPT-4-Turbo additive scoring. In the off-policy Llama 3-8B-Instruct setting, WPO reports AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rate 33.8(1.3)% versus DPO 28.2(0.5)%. WPO weights each preference-pair loss by the product of current-policy response weights, detached from backpropagation; sequence probabilities are length-normalized in practice. Reading boundary: Parentheses are standard deviations across five random-seed runs;805 evaluation instructions. This is the off-policy row, separate from hybrid results.

The StrongREJECT human review uses at least two reviewers per prompt/answer pair, with an expert third reviewer arbitrating disagreements. AppendixA reports mean human assistance grade 1.020 for o1 and 1.335 for GPT-4o on its StrongREJECT review. For SFT filtering, completions are judged repeatedly and assigned the minimum judge score before high-score retention. SFT trains on original prompts with specification text removed, while keeping the generated reasoning/output as targets. During RL, the safety judge sees the policies but not the model’s chain-of-thought; this particular RL reward is used for o1 and o3-mini. Training completions are generated by a specification-agnostic base reasoning model prompted with category-relevant safety specifications. Reading boundary: 2,100 adversarial prompts per model,35 trained reviewers, assistance grades 1/3/5. Gemini API-blocked prompts are scored 1.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Safety, feedback and verification: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms: Methods, Scaling Behaviors, and Lessons Learned. The authors state that they do not know whether crowdworkers have expertise needed to assess some technical harms and that attack coverage is incomplete; the review workflow includes warnings, opt-out previews, support communication and a voluntary well-being survey. Self-reported attack success shows no clear model-size trend, while minimum harmlessness-model scores show RLHF models becoming harder to red-team with scale; harmful outputs still occur. At each dialogue turn, participants see two model responses and select the more harmful; after the conversation they rate attack success on a 0–4 scale, separately from the learned preference-model harmlessness score. A follow-up sample of 500 attacks each on 52B prompted and RLHF models receives three reviewer ratings per transcript; agreement including the attack author is Fleiss kappa0.32 on Likert ratings and 0.49 after binarization. The study’s red team comprises 324 US-based crowdworkers: 307 recruited through MTurk and 17 through Upwork; about 80% of attacks come from roughly 50 workers. Reading boundary: Worker-support descriptions do not establish absence of harm, and reduced average harmfulness does not establish a perfectly safe model.

For the reported 2.6T-token 7B model, the authors augment DCLM-Baseline with StarCoder and ProofPile2, use a math-enriched annealing phase and extend context; Table 9 reports 63.7% MMLU. The human-quality study samples 499 rule-filtered/deduplicated documents and obtains three labels per document from 16 English-speaking AI graduate students/professors; 281 documents have unanimous labels. DCLM’s first evaluation suite omits fairness, multilinguality and safety; compute limits prevent joint exploration of all curation dimensions, sufficient random-seed variation and testing beyond 7B models. The DCLM-Baseline quality filter uses fastText trained with OpenHermes 2.5 plus high-scoring ELI5 positives and RefinedWeb-sampled negatives, retaining the top 10% by classifier score. DCLM provides an unfiltered Common-Crawl-derived pool of 240T GPT-NeoX tokens and five fixed-recipe compute scales; evaluation separates 53-task extended performance, 22-task core performance and five-shot MMLU. Reading boundary: The result is not attributable to raw Common Crawl or the baseline filter alone. The paper’s headline64% is rounded.

DataComp’s filtering track fixes the candidate pool and training compute by total samples seen while allowing the filtered dataset size to vary; it also offers a separate bring-your-own-data track and four compute scales. The paper warns that ImageNet performance is not representative of every task and reports demographic biases in face classification; some tested BYOD sources can increase misclassification risk. At xlarge scale, the image-based/CLIP-score intersection baseline named DataComp-1B contains 1.4B samples and reports 79.2% zero-shot ImageNet accuracy after 12.8B samples seen, versus 72.3% for no filtering under the table’s matched scale. CommonPool generation starts from Common Crawl image URLs with nonempty alt-text, uses unsafe-content filtering and evaluation-image near-duplicate removal to construct the 12.8B xlarge pool, and provides face bounding-box metadata for default blurring during participant image download. Reading boundary: These are described preprocessing steps, not a verified guarantee of absence of unsafe content or personal information.

The paper introduces Dolma as approximately 3T tokens across 5B documents from seven public data sources, alongside an open-source curation toolkit; its design primarily targets English text. Dolma’s general deduplication is within each source subset rather than across sources; its web pipeline uses URL, exact-document and exact-paragraph Bloom-filter stages, while code starts from The Stack’s prior near-deduplicated version. The paper’s Olmo-1b comparison is trained on roughly 3T tokens from preliminary Dolma v1.5; the table explicitly notes unequal training-token budgets for some comparator models and unknown StableLM2 data composition. The web pipeline uses regular-expression PII detection for email addresses, IP addresses and phone numbers; its 1B-model ablation reports no discernible performance difference from the studied masking/removal strategies. The release discussion acknowledges residual incorrect, toxic, hateful, personal and copyrighted content in web-derived corpora despite mitigation, and says the project’s decisions may be revisited. Reading boundary: This is a model-performance observation, not a privacy guarantee or a full PII-recall measurement. The prose and Figure 4 differ on the boundary count, so no exact boundary count is proposed here.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Source curation and demonstrations: WizardLM: Empowering Large Pre-Trained Language Models to Follow Complex Instructions. Evol-Instruct separates instruction evolution, response generation and elimination of failed evolutions; in-depth prompts add difficulty while in-breadth prompts expand instruction diversity. The WizardEval human study uses 218 instructions spanning 29 skills and domains and recruits 10 annotators for source-hidden, shuffled-response comparison using five listed evaluation aspects. The paper acknowledges scalability and reliability limitations of its GPT-4 and human evaluations and warns that its test set may not cover every application scenario or domain. The MMMU study extracts answers using response-processing workflows; if no valid answer is found, it randomly selects an option for multiple-choice questions and marks open-ended responses incorrect. MMMU annotation guidance favors questions whose answers are less directly accessible, such as in separate documents or textbook endings, as a contamination-risk precaution. MMMU flags potential duplicates using lexical overlap and source-URL similarity, has authors review them, checks formatting and typos, and excludes questions classified as very easy. MMMU selects thirty subjects across six disciplines and recruits over fifty university students specializing in those majors to collect multimodal questions and create new questions where needed. Reading boundary: The guidance is a precaution, not an audit establishing absence of training contamination.

MathVista uses heuristic filtering of nineteen VQA datasets followed by three expert annotators and majority voting to identify mathematical-reasoning examples, capping each source at 400 examples. MathVista uses an LLM-based answer extractor such as GPT-4, normalizes the extracted answer into the required format, and computes accuracy against reference answers. Each MathVista testmini question is assigned to five AMT annotators with over 5,000 HITs and acceptance above 0.99; included workers must pass qualification questions and have at least a high-school diploma. The Alaska flight-form experiment ports a web page into the MiniWoB framework, replaces its server backend with a JavaScript surrogate and fixes the environment date to March 1, 2017. The paper introduces MiniWoB++ tasks to test longer horizons, soft natural-language reasoning and stochastically varying layouts. The workflow-guided-exploration study selects forty tasks from the then-public eighty-task MiniWoB distribution and collects ten demonstrations per selected task using Amazon Mechanical Turk. For the paper main MiniWoB experiments, partial rewards are disabled so tasks use sparse end-of-episode success or failure feedback. The method induces workflows from demonstrations using a compositional language that constrains click/type actions and adds shortcut steps for unnecessary or collapsible demonstration actions. Reading boundary: This experiment does not demonstrate successful live flight booking or purchase.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Training systems and orchestration: HybridFlow: A Flexible and Efficient RLHF Framework. The single controller passes data futures between roles, while required output data is transferred directly between GPUs according to parallel ranks. Although ResourcePool supports parallel execution of colocated roles, HybridFlow generally uses sequential execution to avoid contention or out-of-memory failures. HybridFlow’s ResourcePool virtualizes GPU sets; models sharing a pool are colocated, while different pool instances map to distinct GPU sets. HybridFlow attaches collect/distribute transfer protocols to model operations so data can be reshaped between models with different parallelism layouts. Reading boundary: The example is actor generation to critic inference; actual transfer and scheduling behavior depends on the chosen protocols.

[analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — AutoLibra: Agent Metric Induction from Open-Ended Human Feedback. For a buyer, the deliverable is an induced rubric and trajectory judge whose intermediate transformations need their own checks. The demonstrated protocol collects one feedback element per complete text-rendered trajectory. Live or direct step feedback, generated programmatic evaluators and dense-reward RL remain future directions. The validation figures therefore cannot be transferred to those proposed products or read as an end-to-end accuracy guarantee for every induced metric.

[analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — Aya Dataset: An Open-Access Collection for Multilingual Instruction Tuning. Multilingual breadth does not establish equal validation depth in each language. The authors identify contributor concentration in some languages, no dedicated toxic/offensive-speech flags and no language-relabeling component; peer review does not guarantee removal of every unsafe or misclassified example. A proposed purchase should inspect language-specific contributor concentration and error samples. The paper review adds one reviewed work here without independently adding another inspected dataset family or implying a named commercial supplier.

Evidence IDs: [cohort9.claim.crowdagent.fixed-human-ratios](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.crowdagent.fixed-human-ratios)

[analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — CrowdAgent: Multi-Agent Managed Multi-Source Annotation System. A buyer can use this design to ask how uncertain cases reach people and how hidden checks remain hidden. Confidence-threshold convergence is an internal stopping condition, rather than proof of error-free output. The authors acknowledge residual errors and dependence on underlying models. Acceptance should retain independent error inspection after convergence and a separately stated total-cost boundary before any efficiency claim is adopted.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation, feedback and evidence design: CrowdTruth 2.0: Quality Metrics for Crowdsourcing with Disagreement. CrowdTruth 2.0 represents a worker response as a binary annotation vector. Closed tasks share a predefined answer space; an open task instead builds each media unit’s answer space from the workers’ unique keywords. Its worker, media-unit and annotation scores are mutually dependent, start at one and are repeatedly recalculated until total variation falls below a selected threshold, using disagreement-weighted cosine agreement.

Evidence IDs: [cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.vectorization](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.vectorization), [cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.iterative-metrics](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.iterative-metrics)

[sourced_fact] Study result — CrowdTruth 2.0: Quality Metrics for Crowdsourcing with Disagreement. The worker-quality definition multiplies worker–worker agreement by worker–media-unit agreement. Peer consistency and consistency with the aggregate of other workers both affect the score. The inspected paper supplies this operational definition rather than a new controlled accuracy improvement. In open-ended tasks, annotation quality cannot be estimated across multiple media units and is set to one; the model therefore has different information in open and closed settings.

Evidence IDs: [cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.worker-score](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.worker-score), [cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.open-task-limit](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.open-task-limit)

[analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — CrowdTruth 2.0: Quality Metrics for Crowdsourcing with Disagreement. The useful comparison is between assumptions about disagreement. A low consistency score can prompt examination of the worker, the item or the answer space; the formula alone cannot decide which is defective. Further comparative validation across tasks remains future work in this source. Buyers should test whether a proposed weighting rule preserves intended minority interpretations and improves independently checked outcomes before using it to exclude contributors or certify labels.

Evidence IDs: [cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.iterative-metrics](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.iterative-metrics), [cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.worker-score](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.worker-score), [cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.open-task-limit](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.crowdtruth.open-task-limit)

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation, feedback and evidence design: A Data-Driven Analysis of Workers' Earnings on Amazon Mechanical Turk. This earnings study uses plugin logs from September 2014 through January 2017: 3,808,020 HIT records from 2,676 workers before duration-outlier removal, and 3,471,580 HITs from 2,666 workers afterward. Zero-reward qualification tasks remain included. Its accounting compares reward over accept-to-submit intervals with temporal clustering at D=0 and D=1 minute to address overlapping queued work and between-task time; returned HITs contribute zero reward.

Evidence IDs: [cohort9.claim.earnings.sample](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.earnings.sample), [cohort9.claim.earnings.wage-definition](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.earnings.wage-definition)

[sourced_fact] Study result — A Data-Driven Analysis of Workers' Earnings on Amazon Mechanical Turk. For the filtered data, Table 1 reports median work-unit hourly rates of $2.54 per HIT, $3.18 per D=0 cluster and $1.77 per D=1-minute cluster. Their denominators are respectively 3,471,580 HITs, 2,560,066 clusters and 635,198 clusters. These are medians across task or cluster units, not a median across workers. They are historical study figures and do not describe current compensation at any supplier in this report.

Evidence IDs: [cohort9.claim.earnings.work-unit-wages](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.earnings.work-unit-wages), [cohort9.claim.earnings.sample](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.earnings.sample)

[analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — A Data-Driven Analysis of Workers' Earnings on Amazon Mechanical Turk. The operational lesson is to expose the time denominator, including unpaid qualification, returned work and between-task intervals where the project records them. Plugin selection, unknown demographics and script use limit population inference, while elapsed intervals need not equal active effort. Associations between work patterns and earnings are not causal. Neither the historical rates nor a selected plugin sample establishes current worker welfare or a commercial service’s labor cost.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation, feedback and evidence design: Experts Rise Where LLMs Disagree: Using Cross-Model Disagreement to Target Expert Effort in LLM Codebook Revision for Large-Scale Annotation. Experts Rise Where LLMs Disagree prioritizes expert attention using normalized vote entropy from six model predictions and a vote-weighted mean by label across 6,595 unlabeled tutoring utterances. Disagreement is a routing signal, not a determination that any label is wrong. Two experts each supply rationales for 60 selected utterances; GPT 5.6 Sol uses the resulting 120 annotations to revise 24 codebook entries. Mean reported Rationale Labeling time is 169.0 minutes per expert.

Evidence IDs: [cohort9.claim.expertsrise.disagreement-targeting](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.expertsrise.disagreement-targeting), [cohort9.claim.expertsrise.expert-effort](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.expertsrise.expert-effort)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Experts Rise Where LLMs Disagree: Using Cross-Model Disagreement to Target Expert Effort in LLM Codebook Revision for Large-Scale Annotation. On the same 4,032 expert-consensus held-out utterances, Rationale Labeling reaches 64.9% accuracy and 0.658 weighted F1, compared with 57.8% and 0.583 for the final expert-only codebook. The summary averages eight alternative aggregation methods using one temperature-zero run per codebook from each of six models. Aggregators reuse predictions, so they are not independent trials; 6.1% multi-label references are reduced to the first recorded label.

Evidence IDs: [cohort9.claim.expertsrise.heldout-result](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.expertsrise.heldout-result)

[analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — Experts Rise Where LLMs Disagree: Using Cross-Model Disagreement to Target Expert Effort in LLM Codebook Revision for Large-Scale Annotation. The result supports a scoped codebook-revision comparison against the chosen reference label. One longitudinal project, two experts, unequal workflow effort/exposure, differing target-label assignments and possible carryover prevent isolation of input format as the cause. Transcript errors were not systematically measured or corrected. A buyer should preserve selection rules, rationale time and held-out label conventions before expecting similar returns from expert disagreement review in another domain.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation, feedback and evidence design: Garbage In, Garbage Out? Do Machine Learning Application Papers in Social Computing Report Where Human-Labeled Training Data Comes From?. This reporting audit began with five students independently coding the same papers and weekly discussion of disagreements; the team leader decided unresolved cases. After schema changes, at least two team members independently re-examined each of the 164 papers and the team reconciled them again. The repeated examination documents how this audit established its own coded reporting reference rather than assuming an initial extraction was gold.

Evidence IDs: [cohort9.claim.gigo.reconciliation](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.gigo.reconciliation)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Garbage In, Garbage Out? Do Machine Learning Application Papers in Social Computing Report Where Human-Labeled Training Data Comes From?. Within the 74 papers coded for original human annotation, Table 5 finds no original-annotator identity information in 18 (24.32%) and paper-author annotation in 22 (29.73%). Table 7 finds no formal-instruction information in 35 (47.30%), formal definitions/examples in 32 (43.24%), and only question text as instructions in seven (9.46%). These are categories of publication disclosure in the sampled literature.

Evidence IDs: [repair20261111.claim.current-reference045](evidence.html#assertion-repair20261111.claim.current-reference045), [cohort9.claim.gigo.instructions](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.gigo.instructions)

[analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — Garbage In, Garbage Out? Do Machine Learning Application Papers in Social Computing Report Where Human-Labeled Training Data Comes From?. The study audits what publications report, rather than observing the underlying labor process. Its Twitter-classification focus and mostly arXiv sampling limit transfer to other fields; it did not record actual agreement values or adjudication/reconciliation processes in those projects. The procurement implication is a request for missing evidence, not an inference that undocumented instruction, compensation or QA never occurred. Disclosure completeness and delivered label quality require different measurements.

The inspected v2 compares the same codebook wording across trained political-science students, screened US MTurk workers and gpt-3.5-turbo. Model annotations were collected in March–May 2023, using a fresh chat and one tweet per query, with two runs at each temperature of 1 and 0.2. Crowd recruitment required Masters status, over 90% approval, at least 50 approved HITs, two workers per tweet and no worker labeling over 20% of a task’s tweets.

Across the four study datasets, the paper reports ChatGPT accuracy about 25 percentage points above MTurk on average, defining accuracy against trained-human labels only where both trained annotators agreed. The difficult items with trained-rater disagreement are outside that gold denominator. Mean within-group agreement is about 56% for MTurk, 79% for trained annotators, 91% for ChatGPT at temperature 1 and 97% at 0.2.

[analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — ChatGPT Outperforms Crowd-Workers for Text-Annotation Tasks. This is a dated, task-specific model-versus-recruitment comparison, not a universal replacement rule for annotation labor. Repeated model consistency does not establish truth or independence. The source records a relevance-task failure caused by missing prompt examples and leaves other languages and models for future evaluation. A buyer should inspect excluded disagreement cases and prompt sensitivity alongside the retained-set accuracy before deciding how much human review can be removed.

HelpSteer v1 independently rates each response on helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity and verbosity using a 0–4 Likert scale. It collects scalar attributes rather than pairwise preferences. The paper describes approximately 200 US-based annotators engaged through Scale AI, English screening, training ending in 35 sample responses, at least two human QA reviews per annotation, automated checks and later research-team QA. This documents a reported workflow rather than an independent supplier audit.

Within the final 37,120 annotated samples, Table 2 reports Pearson correlation with helpfulness of 0.8525 for correctness and 0.6348 for coherence. These are descriptive associations among the collected 0–4 ratings. They do not estimate how helpfulness would change if a buyer causally changed correctness or coherence, and they should not be substituted for an independently measured improvement from any individual QA stage.

[analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — HelpSteer: Multi-attribute Helpfulness Dataset for SteerLM. A multi-attribute contract can retain distinctions hidden by a single preference label, but its scales still need task and population calibration. All annotations here concern English prompts/responses and all annotators are US-based; the authors state uncertainty about other cultural judgments and non-English gains. The exact recruitment statement can support the scoped role it names, without extending it to every HelpSteer release, sole artifact authorship or current provider performance.

HelpSteer2 v1 initially assigns three raters per response, adding two if the helpfulness range exceeds two points; it reports 3.41 annotators per sample and approximately 1,000 US-based annotators engaged through Scale AI. The pipeline retains the three most-agreeing ratings from up to five, adds QA and removes responses still exceeding the spread rule. About half of collected annotations are excluded overall, leaving 21,362 responses for 10,681 prompts.

The two-epoch regression reward models use batch size 128, validation-loss checkpoint selection and model-specific learning-rate search. Reported RewardBench overall accuracy is 88.8% for Llama 3 70B and 92.0% for Nemotron-4 340B: the mean of four categories over 2,985 tasks, excluding optional Prior Sets. Higher retained-set agreement cannot be read as a randomized estimate of one QA intervention or evidence that excluded preferences were invalid. English-only, exclusively US-based annotation, possible cultural bias, uneven attribute combinations and compute-dependent tuning narrow transfer. Buyers should cost the discarded annotations, preserve disagreement reasons and validate a new target population. Conclusions from the large models do not automatically extend to smaller models.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation, feedback and evidence design: Inherent Disagreements in Human Textual Inferences. This study samples 100 short premise/hypothesis pairs from each of RTE2, SNLI, MNLI, JOCI and DNC, requesting 50 independent AMT ratings per pair on a −50 to 50 likelihood slider. Sentences have at most 20 words. After removing specified sparse/outlier workers, does-not-make-sense responses and pairs with fewer than 15 judgments, it retains 496 pairs averaging 39 labels each. Ratings are z-normalized within worker assignments.

Evidence IDs: [cohort9.claim.inherent.sampling](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.inherent.sampling), [cohort9.claim.inherent.filtering](evidence.html#assertion-cohort9.claim.inherent.filtering)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Inherent Disagreements in Human Textual Inferences. Using ten held-out judgments per pair and averaging ten random splits, the Gaussian-mixture analysis finds a second component with weight above 0.2 for about 20% of pairs; most pairs remain consistent with a single component. That is a model-based description of these collected, normalized judgments. It is not a universal estimate of linguistic ambiguity or an accuracy rate against an independently established single true interpretation.

[analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — Inherent Disagreements in Human Textual Inferences. A buyer can preserve distributions for ambiguous tasks rather than force all cases into a single scale. The authors explicitly warn that normalized scores are not comparable across batches containing different pairs; the meaningful analysis compares raters within the same pair. A data pipeline that merges these normalized numbers across batches without the assignment structure would change the measurement. Recruitment and filtering rules also remain part of the population being described.

LabelAId combines domain-coded labeling functions in a Snorkel probabilistic label model, pretrains an FT-Transformer and fine-tunes on expert-validated city labels to infer image-label correctness. Its proof of concept concerns urban-accessibility imagery. The 34-person university/snowball study obtains consent and pays $30 per hour; two researchers independently validate all 3,574 participant labels, with a third resolving 74 disagreements to define the precision reference.

The between-subjects Project Sidewalk study reports higher overall precision in the intervention group by Mann–Whitney U (p≤0.01). Route-completion time does not differ significantly at p=0.693; reported means are 2,303.3 seconds for control and 2,801.4 for intervention. The nonsignificant test does not establish equal speed. [analysis] Study limitations and buyer implications — LabelAId: Just-in-time AI Interventions for Improving Human Labeling Quality and Domain Knowledge in Crowdsourcing Systems. The useful intervention target is a likely labeling mistake at the moment of work. Its small university/snowball sample may differ from the wider user population. A buyer should separately test precision, time, error categories and participant representativeness rather than infer a general productivity gain from this one proof of concept.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation, feedback and evidence design: Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets Destabilize Machine Learning Benchmarks. The inspected v4 first screens possible benchmark-label errors using confident learning with out-of-sample class probabilities and observed labels. Its noise model assumes class-conditional noise; datasets without test splits use whole-dataset cross-validation. Five MTurk workers then independently choose the given label, predicted label, both or neither. Fewer than three accepting the given label triggers the study’s error rule; QuickDraw and Amazon Reviews use random samples of flagged cases, while the other flagged sets are fully checked.

For ILSVRC 2012, unavailable ImageNet test labels are replaced by the 50,000-image validation set. Table 1 reports 5,440 screened and checked examples, of which 2,916 meet the five-worker rule, or 5.83% of that validation set. These validated issues include ambiguous categories. They are not all cases with a uniquely recoverable replacement label, and they do not give an error estimate for a newly purchased dataset.

The authors caution that even unanimous five-worker corrections can be wrong. Corrected-accuracy experiments remove unknown-label cases and change only the consensus alternative-label set, producing a different denominator from initial validated issues. Buyers should retain the screening candidate, uncertainty, adjudication and final usable correction as separate states rather than present every flagged example as a confirmed, correctable error.

At evaluation time GPT-o4-mini simulates an expert using execution results, canonical code and annotated comments. Its five feedback levels progress from logs through diagnosis and repair guidance to the correct code snippet.

The seven-model study fixes temperature 0 and top-p 1, permits at most ten feedback rounds and three agent actions per turn, and reports correctness and task-solve gains with richer feedback. Those gains are conditional on the added information, including answer-code snippets at the highest level. MRR depends on the first test-correct turn; Recall@n counts tasks solved within n turns; CodeBLEU and CodeBERTScore compare to canonical implementations.

Expert-reviewed task construction and live expert feedback are distinct provenance claims. The evaluated feedback is model-generated, and the conclusion leaves actual human-in-the-loop feedback and broader research stages for future work. Temperature zero is a decoding setting, not proof of deterministic remote responses. A buyer should specify what the feedback provider can see, whether it reveals solution material, and which task-success metric is being purchased before comparing assistance levels.

Across five selected NLP tasks, this study obtains ten independent annotations per item with multiple-choice or fixed-range numeric responses. Its temporal-order experiment deliberately narrows the original noun-and-verb, fourteen-relation problem to verb events and two relations. The cited 0.77 expert agreement comes from the broader task and is not a matched comparator. Separately, a unigram affect predictor trained on 100 headlines and tested on 900 reaches mean Pearson correlation 0.191 with ten-annotator-averaged non-expert training labels versus 0.122 with one expert, using five other experts as reference.

UltraFeedback v2 samples four different models per instruction from a 17-model pool, yielding 255,864 completions for 63,967 instructions. GPT-4 agreement averages 59.7% with individual judges and 68.6% with their majority, including ties. Agreement assesses consistency with these judgments rather than verified factual correctness. On weakness-targeting question–answer evaluations with three completions per prompt at temperature 0.7, the values-targeted models had lower mean toxicity and higher mean human intended-sentiment ratings than base models; the authors report stronger improvements for larger models.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2106.10328.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2106.10328.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Process for Adapting Language Models to Society (PALMS) with Values-Targeted Datasets. The study was limited to U.S. English and selected prompt formats, and the authors warn that underrepresented cultural contexts and other downstream tasks may not generalize; broad training prompts/completions could not be shared under their data policy.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2106.10328.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2106.10328.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Process for Adapting Language Models to Society (PALMS) with Values-Targeted Datasets. The useful deliverable is a documented values specification, writer contribution and revision loop, rather than eighty context-free examples. A pilot should separate adherence to the specified behavior from toxicity proxies and sample cultural cases outside the initial authoring assumptions. Confidence is moderate in this workflow interpretation and unestablished for broad social representativeness. Independent evaluation by affected populations on novel contexts would strengthen or narrow it.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Multilingual and multimodal supervision: CrowdSpeech and VoxDIY: Benchmark Datasets for Crowdsourced Audio Transcription. CrowdSpeech crowdsourced transcriptions of English LibriSpeech audio; VoxDIY synthesized Russian news text with Yandex SpeechKit before human transcription. Each recording was annotated by seven workers. Workers self-reported the task language and took a ten-recording entrance exam requiring WER at most 40%; ongoing controls blocked repeated sub-ten-second tasks and poor recent gold-question WER. Attempted exams and pre-block completed tasks were compensated.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — CrowdSpeech and VoxDIY: Benchmark Datasets for Crowdsourced Audio Transcription. On CrowdSpeech test-clean, Table 4 reports mean WER 7.29 for ROVER versus 4.32 for a gold-aware oracle; on test-other the corresponding WERs are 13.41 and 8.50. The oracle selects the best submitted transcription and does not establish a general upper bound for methods that can edit text.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — CrowdSpeech and VoxDIY: Benchmark Datasets for Crowdsourced Audio Transcription. Speech synthesis can change the distribution of human transcription errors and limit transfer from VoxDIY; the stringent industry QC pipeline also limits coverage of harder or lower-quality annotation settings.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — CrowdSpeech and VoxDIY: Benchmark Datasets for Crowdsourced Audio Transcription. The two corpora distinguish naturally read source speech from synthesized speech before human transcription. A buyer should stratify recording origin and difficulty, compare aggregation with individual transcripts and account for paid entrance attempts. Confidence is high in the provenance distinction and moderate in its procurement relevance. Matched natural and synthetic audio with independently corrected references would change the transfer assessment; an oracle selecting submitted transcripts is not the same comparator as a method allowed to edit them.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.limitation), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.provenance), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.01091.result)

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Curation and provenance: Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better. ExactSubstr uses suffix arrays to remove repeated substrings with a 50-BPE-token threshold; NearDup uses MinHash on 5-grams plus edit similarity greater than 0.8 to identify near-duplicate documents. The duplication analysis uses the English part of Wiki-40B, LM1B, C4 and RealNews; these corpora had differing prior deduplication procedures, so prior cleaning did not ensure equivalent duplication rates.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better. For unprompted top-k sampling with k 50, the authors generated 100,000 sequences up to 512 tokens and marked tokens within 50-token verbatim training matches as memorized; original-C4 models emitted over 1% memorized tokens, about ten times the deduplicated-model rate.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better. The analysis did not distinguish harmful from innocuous or desirable memorization and did not evaluate negative effects of deduplication, including loss of attribution or tasks requiring memorization; deduplication alone cannot remove all privacy-sensitive data.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better. Deduplication is a specified matching procedure with retention tradeoffs. A pilot should retain duplicate-cluster membership, removal reasons and source attribution, and evaluate both memorized-string exposure and task coverage after filtering. Confidence is moderate that this is more informative than a single deduplicated badge; complete privacy protection remains unestablished. An exact-payload audit with sensitivity analyses for thresholds, rare content and attribution loss would change the buyer’s risk estimate.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.limitation), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.provenance), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2107.06499.result)

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation engineering and labor: Learning from Crowds with Crowd-Kit. Crowd-Kit implements crowdsourced-answer aggregation and learning-from-crowds methods in Python, with pandas/scikit-learn-compatible interfaces and PyTorch modules for direct learning from raw crowd labels. Categorical evaluation reused four real-world noisy-label datasets and synthetic datasets from prior work; the direct-learning experiments used IMDB reviews and CIFAR-10, with three annotators per object and 100 gold tasks.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Learning from Crowds with Crowd-Kit. For the D_Product categorical benchmark, Table 3 reports accuracy 0.940 for Dawid–Skene versus 0.897 for majority vote in the authors’ Crowd-Kit implementations.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Learning from Crowds with Crowd-Kit. The library lacks distributed-cluster execution; M-MSR did not process D_Product in reasonable time and no implementation handled the large binary 3/binary 4 datasets. Its categorical aggregation methods assume one objective true label per task.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Learning from Crowds with Crowd-Kit. A common implementation helps compare aggregation under a common interface, but the target assumptions and execution limits still determine fit. Require held-out gold, fixed coverage and resource measurements on the buyer’s own label graph. Confidence is moderate for using the library as a baseline within this setting, without a universal algorithm winner. A representative throughput test and adjudication of systematic disagreements would change both the method and infrastructure choice.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.limitation), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.provenance), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2109.08584.result)

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation engineering and labor: IMDB-WIKI-SbS: An Evaluation Dataset for Crowdsourced Pairwise Comparisons. IMDB-WIKI-SbS sampled 75 photos per age 10–70 and binary gender from IMDB-WIKI, yielding 9,150 photos, and constructed 250,249 comparison edges in a connected random graph. On Toloka, 4,091 workers each chose the older of two cropped faces; each pair had one unique annotator, with three regular and one control task per page. QC used top-half English-speaking workers, timing/skipping checks and 200 gold comparisons with over 20-year age gaps.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — IMDB-WIKI-SbS: An Evaluation Dataset for Crowdsourced Pairwise Comparisons. Whole-dataset NDCG@100 was 0.859 for Bradley–Terry, 0.803 for PageRank and 0.490 for the random baseline; these are age-ranking results on the connected comparison graph, not personal identity or fairness outcomes.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — IMDB-WIKI-SbS: An Evaluation Dataset for Crowdsourced Pairwise Comparisons. The authors noticed incorrect gender metadata in the source and allowed a person to appear in multiple age groups; within-age-group comparisons were harder and graph disconnection prevented meaningful Bradley–Terry ranking in some subgroup evaluations.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — IMDB-WIKI-SbS: An Evaluation Dataset for Crowdsourced Pairwise Comparisons. Pairwise labels do not automatically produce a well-connected or demographically valid ranking problem. For a similar comparison service, inspect graph connectivity within intended subgroups, repeated identities and source-metadata errors before fitting a global rank. Confidence is high that these are separate failure channels and low that the reported age-ranking result transfers to other judgments. Independent subgroup metadata review and a matched connectivity experiment would change the assessment.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.limitation), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.provenance), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2110.14990.result)

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Human and model supervision: WebGPT: Browser-assisted question-answering with human feedback. WebGPT trained GPT-3-family models using human browser demonstrations, comparison-trained reward models, PPO or rejection sampling to generate answers with collected web references. The study collected about 6,000 demonstrations and 21,500 answer comparisons, mostly ELI5; around 25% of data came from 10 Upwork contractors and 75% from 46 Surge AI contractors. Paid trials, manual checks and reference-support annotations were used for QC.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — WebGPT: Browser-assisted question-answering with human feedback. On ELI5 evaluation, the 175B best-of-64 model was preferred to human demonstrator answers 56% of the time and to ELI5 reference answers 69%, counting ties as 50%; the reference-answer comparison stripped citations and used new contractors with minimal instructions.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — WebGPT: Browser-assisted question-answering with human feedback. Reference-answer comparisons have blinding, answer-intent and factual-checking limitations; citation-bearing answers can seem more authoritative and training can incentivize cherry-picked convincing references rather than a fair assessment of evidence.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — WebGPT: Browser-assisted question-answering with human feedback. Citation collection, answer preference and evidence support are separate outputs. A procurement pilot should blind style where possible and independently check whether each material claim is supported, including omitted counterevidence. Confidence is moderate in this separation and unestablished for present-day product accuracy. Matched evidence-grounded evaluations with complete support audits would change the assessment; preference against a dated answer set does not establish a universal factuality advantage.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.limitation), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.provenance), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2112.09332.result)

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Weak supervision and data selection: Shoring Up the Foundations: Fusing Model Embeddings and Weak Supervision. Liger combines weak-source votes with fixed foundation-model embeddings to estimate local source accuracies and extend votes to nearby abstaining points; threshold radii and local smoothness control the extension tradeoff. Evaluation used Spam, Weather, Spouse and three video tasks (Commercial, Tennis, Basketball), with unlabeled train data, smaller hand-labeled development sets and held-out tests; GPT-3 Ada supplied text embeddings and CLIP supplied video-frame embeddings.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Shoring Up the Foundations: Fusing Model Embeddings and Weak Supervision. Across the six tasks, the authors report that Liger improved coverage by 33.2 percentage points on average versus the vanilla weak-supervision label model; hand-labeled development data were used for hyperparameter tuning.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Shoring Up the Foundations: Fusing Model Embeddings and Weak Supervision. The label model assumes conditionally independent weak sources for simplicity, and source extension can lose accuracy when radius is too large or embeddings lack smoothness; embedding-smoothness guarantees therefore do not apply without their stated assumptions.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Shoring Up the Foundations: Fusing Model Embeddings and Weak Supervision. Extending coverage is valuable only if errors introduced by the extension remain acceptable. A buyer should request accuracy-versus-coverage curves, source correlations, abstention behavior and an independently labeled development/evaluation split. Confidence is moderate in the documented local-extension idea under its assumptions, with no universal gain claimed. Shifted-domain tests and correlated-source stress cases would change the decision to automate or escalate labels.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.limitation), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.provenance), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2203.13270.result)

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation engineering and labor: Clustering Without Knowing How To: Application and Evaluation. The system asks three workers per task to group small sets of clothing images by style using palette labels, then aggregates sparse judgments with a reimplemented probabilistic Crowdclustering model whose cluster count is estimated dynamically. Experiments used 2,000 FEIDEGGER dress images and 87 Toloka Shoes images; workers completed progressive five-page training and a qualification test, requiring at least 80 out of 100 to advance.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.10267.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.10267.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.10267.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.10267.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Clustering Without Knowing How To: Application and Evaluation. For an intruder task that inserted an object from another cluster, evaluators selected the intruder with fractions 0.83 for the 2,000-dress experiment and 0.88 for the 87-shoe experiment.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.10267.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.10267.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Clustering Without Knowing How To: Application and Evaluation. Style clustering lacks one uniquely correct gold grouping, so the evaluation measures consistency with other workers’ subjective judgments using intruders rather than recovery of an objective class truth.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.10267.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.10267.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Clustering Without Knowing How To: Application and Evaluation. For subjective style, consistency with a reference panel is the measured construct. An intruder task can identify obvious incoherence without establishing a unique correct taxonomy. Confidence is high in that measurement boundary and moderate in using it for a similar grouping workflow. A buyer should preserve competing clusterings and test downstream retrieval or merchandising outcomes; independently measured improvement on that intended use would change the value assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Human and model supervision: Best Prompts for Text-to-Image Models and How to Find Them. A genetic algorithm proposed keyword sets; Stable Diffusion generated four images per description/set, humans compared image sets blind to keywords, and Bradley–Terry ranks averaged over descriptions supplied the optimization metric. The search pool used 100 popular keywords from Stable Diffusion Discord and 72 manually cleaned descriptions from Reddit/Lexica (60 train, 12 validation); Toloka workers below 80% on controls comparing to DALL-E Mini images were suspended.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.11711.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.11711.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.11711.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.11711.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Best Prompts for Text-to-Image Models and How to Find Them. After 56 search iterations, Table 1 reports the best-training keyword set with mean rank 43.60 on 60 training descriptions and 38.00 on 12 validation descriptions, versus 14.25 and 12.50 for the top 15 popular keywords; higher rank is better among 56 sets.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.11711.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.11711.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Best Prompts for Text-to-Image Models and How to Find Them. The authors cannot conclude the discovered set is optimal because genetic search can converge locally; rank-based metrics are relative and insensitive to convergence, and QC assumed DALL-E Mini images were less appealing.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.11711.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2209.11711.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Best Prompts for Text-to-Image Models and How to Find Them. Human preference can become an optimization signal, but control items can embed the researchers’ own aesthetic premise. A buyer should hold out descriptions, generator versions and rater pools, and inspect whether optimized prompts merely exploit known controls. Confidence is moderate for the demonstrated search workflow and low for global optimality. An independent panel on new image subjects and fixed generation budgets would change the generalization assessment.
