[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Process supervision and reasoning: Learning to Reason With Relational Abstractions. The study added abstract relational plans to arithmetic solutions and contrasted numeric-only, relational-first, interleaved and multitask training formats; in multitask training the model produced relational or numeric sequences on different batches and numeric sequences at test time. GSM8K-R extends GSM8K with human annotations pairing solution steps with short abstract relational explanations; annotators were instructed to keep equation structure while consistently naming the quantities. The published instructions include the actual labeling interface.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Learning to Reason With Relational Abstractions. With GPT-2-XL and greedy decoding on GSM8K-R, multitask relational training achieved 28.05% top-1 test solve accuracy versus 22.97% for equation-only training; the much higher 66.26% ground-truth-relational-prompt result uses privileged test-time auxiliary information.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Learning to Reason With Relational Abstractions. The authors note that human relational annotations can be ambiguous compared with formal variables; sequence length and ordering affect accuracy, and gains from supplying correct relational steps do not show the model can infer those steps unaided.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Learning to Reason With Relational Abstractions. The annotation specification describes relationships, not simply longer reasoning text. A pilot should independently verify relational labels and evaluate the trained model without privileged test-time steps. Confidence is moderate that the reported formats warrant a controlled comparison and high that auxiliary-information conditions must remain separate. Repeated matched-budget training with independently authored test problems would change the estimate of practical gain.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.limitation), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.provenance), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2210.02615.result)

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Human oversight and evaluation: Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models. The experiment compared unaided humans, a 52B helpful RLHF dialog model and human–model teams on MMLU and 5-minute-limit QuALITY questions; human conditions used 100 sampled validation questions per experiment. Surge AI recruited/trained/paid two groups of five participants; one unusually strong unaided participant per task was excluded, leaving four per task in reported results. Participants received answer feedback and at least$20 per active-work hour.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2211.03540.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2211.03540.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2211.03540.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2211.03540.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models. Reported individual accuracy increased from 57.2% unaided to 75.4% with model help on MMLU and from 48.6% to 76.8% on timed QuALITY; assisted confidence-weighted group accuracy was 78.0% and 86.0% respectively.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2211.03540.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2211.03540.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models. The authors say the controlled multiple-choice setting, answer revelation and removal of high-performing participants limit applicability, and the observed confident errors do not validate the protocol for high-stakes oversight of more capable future systems.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2211.03540.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2211.03540.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models. Assistance quality must be tested on human decisions after assistance, including confidently accepted errors. The excluded participants, feedback and time limit materially shape the reported team comparison. Confidence is moderate that this protocol identifies an oversight research question, with no high-stakes validation implied. A larger representative panel, retained exclusions and adversarially misleading assistance would change confidence in operational use.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Human and model supervision: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations. The method samples evaluation inputs conditional on intended labels and ranks/filters them with a discriminator; persona evaluation used a helpful RLHF generator and its preference model to form label-balanced agree/disagree datasets of at most 1,000 statements per behavior. Surge AI workers checked generated inputs and labels; three workers judged each example for 11 full datasets and 100 examples in each of 122 additional datasets, assessing relevance, label correctness and ambiguity.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.09251.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.09251.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.09251.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.09251.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations. In §3.3, the paper reports mean relevance 4.4 ±0.9 on a 1–5 scale, Fleiss κ0.875 between three workers and majority agreement with 95.5% of generated labels; these are validation judgments, not certified correctness of every released example.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.09251.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.09251.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations. Generator/discriminator biases and filtering can narrow diversity, models struggle with unfamiliar concepts or many constraints, and prompt wording or misunderstood instructions can change what an evaluation actually tests.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.09251.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.09251.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations. The human audit checks a sampled generator/discriminator pipeline; it does not convert all generated labels into independent human labels. A buyer should retain selection scores and rejected items, then audit failure clusters and prompt sensitivity outside the generation rubric. Confidence is moderate in sampled validation as a useful control and low in interpreting its agreement as corpus-wide truth. Independently authored held-out behaviors and exhaustive review of a risk-focused subset would change the assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Human and model supervision: DOC: Improving Long Story Coherence With Detailed Outline Control. DOC combines hierarchical detailed outlines with an OPT-350 m FUDGE-style controller trained contrastively on passage summaries; hard negatives splice off-topic continuations into initially relevant passages to maintain outline relevance. Controller training summarized WritingPrompts passages using InstructGPT3-13B; evaluation used 1,000–1,500-word corresponding passages from 20 stories, with three Surge AI annotators comparing each pair on coherence, relevance and interestingness.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.10077.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.10077.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.10077.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.10077.provenance)

[research_gap] Study result boundary — DOC: Improving Long Story Coherence With Detailed Outline Control. No quantitative result assertion is adopted for this work in the approved synthesis input. The report uses its approved method, provenance and limitation observations and does not fill the result gap with a discovery snippet or a superseded candidate.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — DOC: Improving Long Story Coherence With Detailed Outline Control. DOC is specialized for English stories, expensive human evaluation limits detailed ablations, and factual consistency was not a focus; inconsistent names or genders can arise during outlining and cascade into drafting.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.10077.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2212.10077.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — DOC: Improving Long Story Coherence With Detailed Outline Control. Long-form writing quality decomposes into coherence, relevance, interestingness and factual consistency. The inspected approved corpus supplies no adopted quantitative DOC result, so this entry does not invent one from the abstract or reputation. Confidence is moderate in the documented outline-control mechanism and unestablished in a buyer-specific gain. A blinded, complete-story evaluation with factual checks and a matched outline-only baseline would change the purchasing judgment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Curation and provenance: StarCoder: may the source be with you!. StarCoder curation combined extension-level community inspection and source-code filters with a PII detector: human-labeled examples trained StarEncoder token classification for names, emails, keys, passwords, IP addresses and usernames; IDs were excluded because of poor annotation quality. Toloka engaged 1,399 workers from 35 countries to label 12,000 roughly 50-line files in 31 languages; 7,100 files were prefiltered to enrich rare PII and 5,100 were random. Annotators found 22,950 entities, and authors manually inspected 300 files for QC.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.method), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — StarCoder: may the source be with you!. For the 15.5B StarCoder model, Table 12 reports pass@1 of 33.6 on HumanEval and 52.7 on MBPP Python; the evaluation used sampling temperature 0.2 and 200 samples for open-access models. The fine-tuned PII baseline reports F1 above 90% for names, emails and IP addresses, 73.39% for passwords, 56.66% for keys and 59.39% for usernames; the split was 7,878 training and 4,000 test examples, supplemented in training by 400 earlier annotated files.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.main_result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.main_result), [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — StarCoder: may the source be with you!. The authors warn that license detection can misclassify repositories, repository-level opt-out can miss copied code, and PII detection has false positives/negatives; PII annotations are gated to approved individuals and published model evaluations are English-only.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory1.claim.arxiv.2305.06161.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — StarCoder: may the source be with you!. The human annotation contribution concerns PII detector training and review; it does not make every code token human-verified or eliminate personal-data risk. A buyer should separately sample random files and rare-sensitive-type enriched files, retain per-type precision/recall and inspect opt-out propagation. Confidence is high in separating those denominators and moderate in the documented workflow’s relevance. An independently labeled target-code sample and end-to-end removal audit would change the risk assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Evidence-grounded evaluation: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations. ALCE evaluates fluency, dataset-specific correctness, and citation quality separately; citation recall tests whether the concatenated cited passages entail a statement, while citation precision penalizes irrelevant citations. ALCE samples 1,000 development examples from each of ASQA, QAMPARI and ELI 5; its human evaluation samples 100 examples from ASQA and ELI 5, with workers paid an average of $20 per hour.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2305.14627.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2305.14627.method), [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2305.14627.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2305.14627.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations. On ELI 5, Table 6 reports citation recall of 51.1 for ChatGPT VANILLA using five passages and 69.3 with reranking; the corresponding claim-correctness recalls are 12.0 and 11.4.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2305.14627.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2305.14627.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations. The authors acknowledge that NLI errors limit citation evaluation and cannot reliably detect partial support; automatically generated ELI 5 claims may omit valid answers, and the evaluated tasks omit math, coding and multi-hop reasoning.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2305.14627.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2305.14627.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations. Citation recall can rise while claim correctness does not. The appropriate deliverable therefore has separate correctness, support, completeness and irrelevance judgments, with partial-support cases adjudicated. Confidence is high in the metric distinction and moderate in applying this evaluation structure. Independent expert scoring on the buyer’s evidence corpus, including unsupported compound statements and valid alternate answers, would change confidence in an automated citation judge.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Task construction and evaluation: Inverse Scaling: When Bigger Isn't Better. The Inverse Scaling Prize accepted datasets with at least 300 examples, evaluated submitted GPT-3 scaling patterns on held-out model series, and used classification or sequence-completion loss for winning tasks. Task labels were checked by contractors on random samples of at least 50 examples; contractors could use the internet, and multipart tasks were sampled by part or grouped parts rather than treating all labels as exhaustively verified.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2306.09479.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2306.09479.method), [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2306.09479.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2306.09479.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Inverse Scaling: When Bigger Isn't Better. Table 1 reports 11 winning tasks; for example, Sig Figs contains 20,897 examples with 99.5% sampled human agreement, while NeQA contains 300 examples with 98.0% agreement.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2306.09479.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2306.09479.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Inverse Scaling: When Bigger Isn't Better. Inverse scaling can reverse into U-shaped scaling, and some tasks show inverted-U trends or multiple reversals through training; the authors cannot predict the scale needed for improvement on a given task.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2306.09479.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2306.09479.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Inverse Scaling: When Bigger Isn't Better. Sampled label agreement establishes only the inspected task sample under its labeling rule. A buyer should separate task novelty, label validity and behavior across model sizes rather than extrapolate an inverse trend indefinitely. Confidence is high that the observed shapes are conditional and low in predicting future model rankings. Matched versions and repeated evaluations across held-out model families would change the scaling interpretation.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Safety, feedback and verification: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models. The study optimizes one adversarial suffix across multiple training prompts and models, then evaluates whether the resulting suffix transfers to held-out behaviors and models. AdvBench distinguishes 500 target harmful strings from 500 harmful-behavior instructions; exact target-string matches and attempts to comply with a behavior use different success definitions.

[sourced_fact] Study result — Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models. Across 388 harmful behaviors, Table 2 reports ensemble transfer attack success rates of 86.6% for GPT-3.5 and 46.9% for GPT-4, compared with 1.8% and 8.0% for the behavior-only baseline; ensemble success means at least one suffix succeeds.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2307.15043.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2307.15043.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models. Transfer results depend on historical model versions, sampling and interface conditions; the authors discuss shared training/distillation as a potential transfer confound and disclosed findings before publication.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2307.15043.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2307.15043.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models. Transfer attack success is conditional on an attack budget, model version and success rule. A defense pilot should report per-behavior and per-attempt outcomes and include newly authored harmful-intent tests without publishing operational attack recipes in its acceptance report. Confidence is high in the need for those denominators and unestablished for any current defense. Matched contemporary evaluation with independently validated harm and intent preservation would change the risk conclusion.

Beemo uses expert editors to refine machine outputs for factual accuracy, style, coherence and fluency; two lead editors manually validate submissions and annotators may skip already-suitable or substantially unsuitable examples.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.method)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Beemo: Benchmark of Expert-edited Machine-generated Outputs. Table 4 reports Binoculars AUROC of 83.90% for human-written versus machine-generated text and 61.24% for human-written versus expert-edited machine text, on the paper’s out-of-domain benchmark.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Beemo: Benchmark of Expert-edited Machine-generated Outputs. The study has no human detection baseline and does not evaluate commercial/API detectors; results can depend on editing prompts and may not transfer from expert editing to non-expert users. AUROC compares two labeled text populations; it is not accuracy at a chosen operating threshold. Expert-edited model text remains in the machine-origin class. Selection excludes skipped examples, so retained edits are not a random sample of all attempted editing work.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.limitation), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.method), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.provenance), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2411.04032.result)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Beemo: Benchmark of Expert-edited Machine-generated Outputs. Expert editing is a distinct provenance stage that can change detector behavior without making the text wholly human-authored. A buyer evaluating authorship detection should include retained editing histories and task-matched human references, and compare detection errors by editing intensity. Confidence is moderate in this benchmark-specific sensitivity and low for unseen detectors. Independent evaluation of current tools, non-expert editing and different genres would change the assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Weak supervision and data selection: Weak-to-Strong Generalization Through the Data-Centric Lens. The proposed data-source selector treats sources as bandit arms and uses an upper-confidence bound on detected overlap density, targeting points where reliable weak-model signals coexist with patterns learnable by the stronger model. The language-model experiments use Qwen1.5 0.5 B as weak model, Llama 3 8 B as strong model and linear probing on 19 datasets; the weak-supervision experiments separately use nine WRENCH datasets.

[sourced_fact] Study result — Weak-to-Strong Generalization Through the Data-Centric Lens. In the Amazon Polarity and DREAM examples, Figure 3 reports better weak-to-strong accuracy with UCB-based data-source selection than random source sampling, averaged over 20 repeated experiments with 25 selection rounds.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2412.03881.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2412.03881.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Weak-to-Strong Generalization Through the Data-Centric Lens. The authors caution that few overlap points or noisy overlap detection can eliminate the gains; their mechanism assumes a simplified easy/hard feature structure rather than modeling every realistic weak-to-strong setting.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2412.03881.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2412.03881.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Weak-to-Strong Generalization Through the Data-Centric Lens. Source selection is part of the supervision recipe rather than a neutral sampling step. A pilot should record overlap estimates, chosen-source proportions and gains against random selection at the same annotation and compute budget. Confidence is moderate under the modeled feature assumptions and low where overlap detection is noisy. Shifted-domain experiments with independently measured overlap would change whether this approach is preferable to simpler selection.

On the sampled Jordanian image-caption evaluation, Table 3 reports human-rated dialect authenticity of 3.56 for GPT-4o captions and 4.82 for reference human captions on a 1–5 scale; human evaluation uses 50 images per dialect and one blinded rater per caption.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — JEEM: Vision-Language Understanding in Four Arabic Dialects. JEEM covers four dialects with an uneven, relatively small image set; automatic metrics may miss cultural/dialect nuance and human evaluation covers only a subset.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — JEEM: Vision-Language Understanding in Four Arabic Dialects. Dialect authenticity cannot be established by a language code or a machine metric alone. A pilot should obtain native judgments in the target dialect, preserve the question-writing and image-viewing stages and report coverage per dialect. Multiple independent local raters and broader image/domain coverage would change the generalization assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation engineering and labor: Voices of Freelance Professional Writers on AI: Limitations, Expectations, and Fears. The study combines a 64-question questionnaire with a task in which selected multilingual writers prompt an AI chatbot for a local-event advertisement, revise it and submit the interaction and versions; two analysts inductively code free-text responses and resolve disagreements by discussion. The questionnaire includes 301 Toloka freelance writers from 49 countries; the interactive task includes 36 participants selected from 120 invitations using language proficiency, low self-ratings and/or detailed comments.

[sourced_fact] Study result — Voices of Freelance Professional Writers on AI: Limitations, Expectations, and Fears. Among the surveyed professional writers, 73% report using AI chatbots; the paper reports that 75% improve outputs through iterative prompting and audience specification, as a sample-specific self-reported practice.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2504.05008.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2504.05008.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Voices of Freelance Professional Writers on AI: Limitations, Expectations, and Fears. The authors caution that a single-platform, geographically uneven sample and only 36 behavioral participants limit generalization; language ratings with fewer than three respondents are individual observations, and model changes can age these ratings.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2504.05008.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2504.05008.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Voices of Freelance Professional Writers on AI: Limitations, Expectations, and Fears. The source gives writers’ situated reports and observed editing artifacts, rather than an employment forecast. A buyer designing writer-assisted data work should pay for prompting, revision and explanation as well as the final text and test whether feedback improves later tasks. Confidence is moderate in the sampled workflow observations and low outside the platform. A longitudinal, multilingual sample with actual paid-time logs and independently scored outputs would change the labor interpretation.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Weak supervision and data selection: Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers. Weaver uses weak supervision to weight multiple binary verifier signals for response selection; its setup allows a small labeled development subset, roughly 1% of test queries, to estimate global statistics. The main evaluation generates 100 responses per query with Llama 3.3 70 B Instruct and combines a pool of 33 reward models and language-model judges; the paper compares selected-response accuracy with an oracle Pass@100 bound.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2506.18203.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2506.18203.method), [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2506.18203.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2506.18203.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers. Table 1 reports average success rates across four tasks of 87.7% for Weaver, 72.2% for majority voting and 91.9% for oracle Pass@100; these are response-selection results under 100-generation conditions.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2506.18203.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2506.18203.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers. The aggregation model assumes conditional independence of verifier votes, and inference can require 30-plus verifier calls; on harder datasets with few correct candidate responses, selection remains difficult and is bounded by candidate generation.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2506.18203.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2506.18203.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers. The selection gain consumes a large generation and verifier budget, and depends on candidate quality. A buyer should compare total cost per accepted answer with simpler reranking at the same generation budget and preserve a gold holdout outside development calibration. Confidence is moderate for the reported setting and low for a blanket weak-verifier replacement of experts. Correlated-judge stress tests and matched-budget target-task results would change the economic conclusion.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Rubrics and executable evaluation: AdvancedIF: Rubric-Based Benchmarking and Reinforcement Learning for Advancing LLM Instruction Following. AdvancedIF retains prompts that trigger final-turn instruction-following failures; the same human annotator writes the prompt and decomposed rubric, and evaluation requires every applicable final-turn criterion to pass. AdvancedIF contains 1,645 dialogs across complex instructions, carried context and system steerability; RIFL separately uses human rubric/verification data to train a rubric generator and a verifier through supervised and reinforcement learning stages.

Table 5 reports AdvancedIF average scores of 51.4 for Llama 4 Maverick and 58.1 after RIFL, with corresponding MultiChallenge scores 37.4 and 40.3; IFEval changes from 89.9 to 90.0.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2511.10507.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2511.10507.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — AdvancedIF: Rubric-Based Benchmarking and Reinforcement Learning for Advancing LLM Instruction Following. Rubric verifiers can be reward-hacked and can misjudge individual criteria; the authors leave a comprehensive reward-design study to future work, while their ablation compares all-or-nothing, fractional and hybrid rewards on one base model.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2511.10507.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2511.10507.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — AdvancedIF: Rubric-Based Benchmarking and Reinforcement Learning for Advancing LLM Instruction Following. An all-criteria final-turn score differs from a fractional training reward and can depend on the same annotator’s prompt/rubric interpretation. A pilot should introduce independent rubric review and criterion-flipping examples, retaining both strict and fractional outcomes. Confidence is moderate in the method’s relevance to instruction following and unestablished for all instruction classes. Independent prompt/rubric authorship and a no-overlap held-out suite would change the transfer assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Multilingual and multimodal supervision: Multimodal RewardBench 2: Evaluating Omni Reward Models for Interleaved Text and Image. MMRB2 filters near-unanimous model-judge pairs before collecting three blinded human preferences per generative pair; it discards large rater spreads, near-midpoint averages and tied majorities, then evaluates model judges in both response orders. MMRB2 retains 1,000 preference pairs for each of four tasks: text-to-image, image editing, interleaved generation and multimodal reasoning. For reasoning pairs, preferred responses must have correct answers and unanimous human agreement that their reasoning has no major errors.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Multimodal RewardBench 2: Evaluating Omni Reward Models for Interleaved Text and Image. The selected data exclude ambiguous or high-disagreement pairs and prioritize hard comparisons; the benchmark does not yet comprehensively cover multilingual, safety/bias, multi-turn, video or audio preferences.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Multimodal RewardBench 2: Evaluating Omni Reward Models for Interleaved Text and Image. The benchmark measures judge agreement on a selected, low-ambiguity but difficult pair population. Its filter can remove precisely the disagreements relevant to a buyer’s policy. Confidence is high in this selection boundary and moderate in using response-order swaps as a calibration check. A pilot should retain a separate ambiguous-pair stratum; broader modalities, languages and independently validated disagreement distributions would change the recommendation.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional and long-horizon evaluation: APEX-SWE. APEX-SWE uses a persistent ReAct harness with a one-hour timeout; Integration is graded by service-facing pytest tests, Observability by fail-to-pass/pass-to-pass checks, and Pass@1 averages three independent runs. [sourced_fact] Study limitations — APEX-SWE. The leaderboard’s binary test success differs from LM-judged engineering-quality rubrics, which are excluded from leaderboard scoring; the paper reports models that score well on rubrics while still failing task tests.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2601.08806.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2601.08806.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — APEX-SWE. Executable integration success and engineering quality are complementary outputs with different acceptance meanings. A buyer should require both regression-safe function and an independently reviewed maintainability rubric, retaining per-task repeated runs. Confidence is high in separating the two measures and low in extrapolating their scores to an organization’s software backlog. Matched private repositories and prospective deployment results would change the capability assessment.

The hierarchy study evaluates autonomous customer-support tasks in a stateful fictional PC-retail environment using identical system prompts, MCP tools and an LLM judge applying detailed human-written rubrics. [sourced_fact] Study limitations — The Hierarchy of Agentic Capabilities: Evaluating Frontier Models on Realistic RL Environments. The authors identify systematic quantitative failure-distribution analysis, task-category breakdowns, cross-domain evaluation and benchmark-to-production validation as future work; the proposed hierarchy is therefore not a quantified causal model of deployment performance.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — The Hierarchy of Agentic Capabilities: Evaluating Frontier Models on Realistic RL Environments. The hierarchy is a useful vocabulary for inspecting failure traces, with its causal interpretation still untested. A buyer should define reproducible categories and check coding agreement before using the taxonomy to prioritize remediation. Confidence is moderate for descriptive organization and low for predicting production performance. Independently categorized trajectories across different businesses, task mixes and model families would change its explanatory value.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional and long-horizon evaluation: APEX-Agents. APEX-Agents grades each human-authored rubric criterion independently with Gemini 3 Flash and defines task success as satisfying all criteria; Pass@1 averages eight runs per task, while Pass@8 and Pass^8 measure any-attempt success and all-attempt consistency. The benchmark includes 480 tasks split equally among investment banking, law and management consulting across 33 worlds; 256 experts from Mercor’s marketplace create and review worlds, tasks, gold outputs and rubrics, and independent experts baseline 96 tasks.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — APEX-Agents. Worlds are controlled and web search is disabled; the judge is also a leaderboard model, creating a self-preference risk, and aggregate successful-trajectory tool-use associations do not control for task difficulty or agent approach.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2601.14242.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2601.14242.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — APEX-Agents. Repeated attempts expose a reliability question hidden by best-attempt success. The close leading point estimates and corrected paired tests also caution against treating displayed ranks as distinct tiers. Confidence is high in preserving Pass@1, Pass@8 and Pass^8 separately and moderate in the sample’s task relevance. An independent judge, representative held-out work and replicated expert baselines would change the deployment interpretation.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional and long-horizon evaluation: Benchmarking Agents in Insurance Underwriting Environments. UNDERWRITE co-designs fictional insurance rules, data and tasks with Chartered Property Casualty Underwriters; a separate GPT-4.1 user simulator interacts with the agent, and outcome correctness, tool exceptions and uncertain user replies are distinct evaluation criteria. Six seed task types and 3,000 GPT-4.1-generated fictional applicant profiles inform task creation; experts revise and accept tasks, and the reported evaluation uses 300 accepted tasks with up to 50 user-interaction turns.

[sourced_fact] Study result — Benchmarking Agents in Insurance Underwriting Environments. Table 1 reports Claude Sonnet 4.5 answer correctness of 90.30%, with 0.520 tool exceptions and 0.28 uncertain user replies on average per trace; correctness and interaction-error measures have different units.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2602.00456.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2602.00456.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Benchmarking Agents in Insurance Underwriting Environments. The correctness judge is calibrated against one expert’s annotations on held-out 100-trace samples, and hallucination detection conservatively targets nonexistent insurance products; neither metric covers all business-domain reasoning failures.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2602.00456.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2602.00456.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Benchmarking Agents in Insurance Underwriting Environments. A correct final underwriting answer can coexist with interaction errors, and a narrowly defined hallucination check can miss other business mistakes. A buyer should predeclare separate outcome, policy and interaction gates and calibrate judges with multiple experts. Confidence is moderate in the benchmark-specific process lesson and unestablished for regulated production. Prospective domain validation, disagreement adjudication and a broader error taxonomy would change confidence in use.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional and long-horizon evaluation: EnterpriseBench Corecraft: Training Generalizable Agents on High-Fidelity RL Environments. The Corecraft training study fine-tunes GLM 4.6 with GRPO using 16 rollouts per prompt and LM-judged rubric fractions as dense rewards; strict task pass rate separately requires all criteria to be satisfied. [analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — EnterpriseBench Corecraft: Training Generalizable Agents on High-Fidelity RL Environments. [sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Safety, feedback and verification: Intent Laundering: AI Safety Datasets Are Not What They Seem. Intent Laundering tests whether safety refusal depends on overt wording while holding the underlying requested harmful intent as the evaluation target; revised responses receive independent safety and practicality judgments, and success requires both. The study evaluates 207 deduplicated AdvBench cases, 200 standard HarmBench cases and 288 StrongREJECT cases after removing 25 overlaps; judge validation compares 100 sampled responses with majority labels from three human experts.

[sourced_fact] Study result — Intent Laundering: AI Safety Datasets Are Not What They Seem. On the 207-case AdvBench subset across ten evaluated models, Table 1 reports mean attack success rate of 3.86% for original requests and 87.54% for first revisions; the original and revised settings use the paper’s explicitly different success definitions.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2602.16729.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2602.16729.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Intent Laundering: AI Safety Datasets Are Not What They Seem. The revised-request metric requires unsafe and practical content, while original-request ASR uses safety alone; judgments come from GPT-5.1, with human validation limited to100 responses and binary majority agreement rather than exhaustive intent-preservation review. The automated judge is GPT-5.1; the three-expert comparison covers 100 responses and does not establish intent preservation or correct harm judgments for every transformed request. The result retains the explicitly different original and revised outcome definitions.

The two conditions use different success definitions, so their numerical gap cannot be read as a clean causal effect of wording alone. The practical value is a testable concern that safety evaluation can depend on overt cues. Confidence is moderate in that concern and low in a precise deployment-wide incidence. A matched-definition study with independent intent-preservation, practicality and harm adjudication would change the quantitative conclusion.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Evidence-grounded evaluation: $\tau$-Knowledge: Evaluating Conversational Agents over Unstructured Knowledge. Tau-Knowledge builds a structured fictional banking knowledge base, converts it to unstructured documents and co-constructs tasks/tools with human refinement; two reviewers independent of task creation check final states, minimal gold documents and one valid trajectory per task. The tau-Banking domain contains 97 tasks, 698 documents, 51 discoverable tools and 14 permanently available agent tools; its knowledge base spans 21 categories and 194,562 tokens under the stated tokenizer.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.04370.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.04370.method), [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.04370.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.04370.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — $\tau$-Knowledge: Evaluating Conversational Agents over Unstructured Knowledge. Table 2 reports GPT-5.2 High pass^1 of 25.52% with terminal search and 32.73% with gold documents directly in context; Claude 4.5 Opus High reaches 39.69% in the gold setting. Here pass^k requires success in every one of k trials.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.04370.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.04370.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — $\tau$-Knowledge: Evaluating Conversational Agents over Unstructured Knowledge. The user simulator omits many characteristics of real human variation; latency depends on API serving, and unrestricted repeated search may differ from deployments allowing only one or a few searches.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.04370.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.04370.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — $\tau$-Knowledge: Evaluating Conversational Agents over Unstructured Knowledge. Gold documents in context and terminal search change the information-access problem, while all-trials pass^k measures reliability rather than any-attempt discovery. A buyer should freeze search-call budgets, document versions and simulator assumptions and test retrieval failures separately from reasoning errors. Confidence is high in those distinctions and moderate in their buyer relevance. Real-user variation and a private, independently constructed knowledge base would change the transfer assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Process supervision and reasoning: PivotRL: High Accuracy Agentic Post-Training at Low Compute Cost. PivotRL profiles assistant-turn states from demonstration trajectories, retains mixed-outcome difficult turns, and applies short on-policy rollouts with domain-specific functional rewards instead of requiring exact reproduction of a demonstrated string. Same-data SFT comparisons start from Qwen3-30 B-A 3 B-Thinking-2507 in four separately trained agentic domains; demonstration sources include synthetic conversational trajectories and model-generated coding, terminal and browsing traces, rather than an established human-annotator cohort.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.21383.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.21383.method), [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.21383.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.21383.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — PivotRL: High Accuracy Agentic Post-Training at Low Compute Cost. Table 1 reports PivotRL versus same-data SFT scores of 63.81 versus 58.44 on tau2-Bench, 20.00 versus 13.75 on Terminal-Bench and 11.30 versus 1.50 on BrowseComp; on SWE-Bench Verified PivotRL scores 32.67 versus 37.40 for SFT. Table 2 reports average change on eight out-of-domain benchmarks across the four training runs of +0.21 percentage points for PivotRL and −9.83 for SFT, relative to the common base model.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.21383.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.21383.result), [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.21383.result_ood](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.21383.result_ood)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — PivotRL: High Accuracy Agentic Post-Training at Low Compute Cost. The theoretical analysis assumes finite action spaces and positive reference support, and local verifier acceptance does not certify whole-task success; in SWE training the local verifier checks tool-call names without checking arguments or patch quality.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.21383.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2603.21383.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — PivotRL: High Accuracy Agentic Post-Training at Low Compute Cost. Local rewards can improve selected decisions without validating arguments or whole-task patch quality. The SWE result also prevents a claim that the method dominates SFT across every domain. Confidence is moderate in testing short-horizon functional rewards and low for a universal efficiency advantage. A matched-budget study with complete local-check definitions, independent task-success scoring and repeated training runs would change the judgment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Rubrics and executable evaluation: The Hitchhikers Guide to Rubric Quality Understanding and Enrichment. The rubric-quality framework combines content validity, domain mapping, cross-lens judging and weight calibration; its scoring panels are five GPT-5.5-generated expert personas per task, distinct from the human experts who developed the taxonomy. RIFT taxonomy development uses 85 rubrics and 255 expert annotations across five sources with four refinement rounds; the intervention experiment separately uses 60 human-authored rubrics, 30 each from GDPval and Terminal-Bench.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2604.01375.method](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2604.01375.method), [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2604.01375.provenance](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2604.01375.provenance)

[sourced_fact] Study result — The Hitchhikers Guide to Rubric Quality Understanding and Enrichment. Among 48 rubrics with nonconstant panel-rated necessity, 10 have negative weight-necessity rank correlation; Table 1 reports mean ordering correlation+0.195 for human-authored rubrics, scored by the model-persona panel.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2604.01375.result](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2604.01375.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — The Hitchhikers Guide to Rubric Quality Understanding and Enrichment. The controlled experiment injects one failure mode at a time and assesses absolute weight magnitudes; overlapping real-world failures, non-additive scoring/gates and downstream policy-learning consequences remain outside the experiment.

Evidence IDs: [mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2604.01375.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-mandatory2.claim.arxiv.2604.01375.limitation)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — The Hitchhikers Guide to Rubric Quality Understanding and Enrichment. Human involvement in taxonomy design is separate from model-persona scoring of necessity. A buyer should inspect decisive conditions, weight sensitivity and cross-lens disagreement without treating generated personas as independent human experts. Confidence is moderate for this audit framework and low for inferring downstream policy gains. A blinded real-expert panel, overlapping failure cases and an end-to-end acceptance experiment would change its procurement value.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional and long-horizon evaluation: ClawsBench: Evaluating Capability and Safety of LLM Productivity Agents in Simulated Workspaces. ClawsBench uses 44 structured tasks across five stateful SQLite-backed mock services and deterministic before/after state evaluation. Task Success Rate is measured on nonsafety tasks at score≥0.8, while Unsafe Action Rate is measured separately on safety tasks at score<0; domain skills and a meta prompt are varied with an intentionally incomplete factorial design.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.05172.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.05172.method)

[sourced_fact] Study result — ClawsBench: Evaluating Capability and Safety of LLM Productivity Agents in Simulated Workspaces. In the six-model OpenClaw comparison, the paper reports that full skills-plus-meta scaffolding raises Task Success Rate from 0–8% without scaffolding to 39–63%. These are task/condition-level reported results with cluster-bootstrap uncertainty, not current-product safety rankings or proof of transfer to unseen tasks.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.05172.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.05172.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — ClawsBench: Evaluating Capability and Safety of LLM Productivity Agents in Simulated Workspaces. Scaffolding was iteratively refined on the evaluated task set, so the authors treat its measured lift as an upper bound on unseen-task transfer. The mocks omit rate limits, latency and concurrent access; the 44-task study lacks a human baseline and has only five of eleven harness/model pairs with full 2 × 2 coverage. The study separates 20 non-safety tasks from 24 safety tasks. Agents operate the mock REST services through terminal commands, not a browser. Figure 3 reports Flash-Lite Unsafe Action Rate as 22%, whereas Table 4 and adjacent prose report 23%; the discrepancy remains unresolved. Low unsafe-action rate can also reflect over-refusal.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.05172.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.05172.limitation), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.05172.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.05172.method), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.05172.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.05172.result)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — ClawsBench: Evaluating Capability and Safety of LLM Productivity Agents in Simulated Workspaces. Scaffolding tuned on evaluated tasks can be useful diagnosis while overstating unseen-task lift. A pilot should freeze the scaffold before the holdout, complete the intended factorial comparisons and retain safety failures alongside task scores. Confidence is high in this validation requirement and unestablished for current product safety rankings. Prospective tasks with real service constraints and a suitable human baseline would change the generalization assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional and long-horizon evaluation: Riemann-Bench: A Benchmark for Moonshot Mathematics. Riemann-Bench describes 25 expert-authored research-level problems with unique closed-form answers, programmatic answer checking and two independent domain experts solving each from scratch before acceptance. It evaluates agents with code/search over 100 independent runs per problem and reports pass@k estimators.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.method)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Riemann-Bench: A Benchmark for Moonshot Mathematics. Table 1 reports pass@1 between 2% and 6% for the seven listed API models on this private 25-problem evaluation with 100 runs per problem. This is a reported selected-benchmark snapshot, not a measurement of all mathematical reasoning or current model capability.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Riemann-Bench: A Benchmark for Moonshot Mathematics. The problems have known solutions and the benchmark is private. The paper distinguishes this from genuinely open-ended mathematical research, where an answer’s existence can be unknown; benchmark privacy is an anticontamination design choice, not an independent demonstration that leakage or benchmark-selection bias is absent. Active advanced-mathematics researchers author the selected problems; two other domain experts independently solve them from scratch before acceptance. Private problems, credentials, check code and run traces were not independently inspected by this report author.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.limitation), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.method), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.06802.result)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Riemann-Bench: A Benchmark for Moonshot Mathematics. Known-answer private problems isolate a demanding but bounded mathematical task. They do not test whether an agent can decide which open research question has a solution. Confidence is high in that distinction and moderate in the benchmark’s task-specific challenge. Independent reconstruction of answer checks, leakage controls and new expert problems would change confidence in measured capability; broader research usefulness would need a different outcome study.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Process supervision and reasoning: Learning from Less: Measuring the Effectiveness of RLVR in Low Data and Compute Regimes. The study procedurally generates counting, graph and spatial problems, calibrates difficulty using ten models, and compares 100/200/500-example easy versus mixed subsets while fine-tuning Qwen3-4B with LoRA and GRPO under fixed task budgets. Ground-truth checking is programmatic, but graph-answer normalization and spatial fallback parsing use GPT-4o.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.18381.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.18381.method)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Learning from Less: Measuring the Effectiveness of RLVR in Low Data and Compute Regimes. Within Table 2’s counting-problem mean-test-accuracy metric, 100 mixed-difficulty examples and 500 easy examples each report 44.2%. The prose separately reports different solving-accuracy values; this table-specific observation is retained without harmonizing the two presentations or generalizing a fivefold gain to other tasks/models.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.18381.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.18381.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Learning from Less: Measuring the Effectiveness of RLVR in Low Data and Compute Regimes. The authors did not repeat training over multiple seeds, used one 4B model with LoRA and fixed low-compute budgets, and did not test transfer to natural-language benchmarks. They explicitly frame results as empirical observations under interacting composition, size, token and optimization limits, rather than universal scaling laws. Counting reward also contains format and verbosity terms. Difficulty dimensions co-vary, and extraction failures and token limits constrain performance. Counting prose gives Mixed100/200/500 solving accuracies of 50.0/50.5/40.0, while Table 2 labels 44.2/43.4/35.5 as mean test accuracy; the two presentations are not reconciled.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.18381.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.18381.limitation), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.18381.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.18381.method), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.18381.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2604.18381.result)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Learning from Less: Measuring the Effectiveness of RLVR in Low Data and Compute Regimes. The equal table-specific scores are a useful counterexample to counting examples alone, but they do not establish a portable fivefold data-efficiency factor. A buyer should compare composition and compute jointly and preserve parsing-model dependence. Confidence is moderate in the reported low-budget observation and low in a general scaling claim. Multiple seeds, fixed definitions and matched tests across model sizes and task types would change the efficiency estimate.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Multilingual and multimodal supervision: StereoTales: A Multilingual Framework for Open-Ended Stereotype Discovery in LLMs. StereoTales generates stories under one imposed demographic attribute, extracts profiles with a three-LLM ensemble, and identifies overrepresented attribute associations before a separate harmfulness judgment. 247 UK English-language participants recruited through Prolific and the same 23 generating models rate associations, not the original stories.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.10442.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.10442.method)

[sourced_fact] Study result — StereoTales: A Multilingual Framework for Open-Ended Stereotype Discovery in LLMs. For 1580 selected associations, the paper reports Spearman correlation 0.62 between per-association mean human and mean model harmfulness ratings. This is a correlation against one UK normative reference panel, not accuracy against universal moral ground truth or independent validation of all extracted stories.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.10442.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.10442.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — StereoTales: A Multilingual Framework for Open-Ended Stereotype Discovery in LLMs. The human reference is a single-country English-language panel, 89.9% White, while generated stories span ten languages. LLM profile extraction was manually checked only on 30 English/French stories; pairwise co-occurrence does not decompose causal mediation, and both extraction errors and nonuniform abstention can affect associations. There is an unresolved instrument conflict: section 3 and Figure 10 ask harmful-stereotype agreement, while Appendix F.2 describes acceptability with a different direction. Section 3 describes median aggregation, whereas section 4.3 and Figure 4 explicitly compare per-association means over 1,580 associations. The reported correlation is retained at that stated mean-comparison scope, without claiming the instruments are equivalent.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.10442.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.10442.limitation), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.10442.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.10442.method), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.10442.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.10442.result)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — StereoTales: A Multilingual Framework for Open-Ended Stereotype Discovery in LLMs. Multilingual generation and the normative reference panel have different coverage. The measured correlation cannot certify each extracted association or stand in for local harmfulness judgments. Confidence is high in this boundary and moderate in using the framework to generate review candidates. A buyer should commission independent local panels and extraction audits; cross-country agreement and sensitivity to abstention would change the validity assessment. Before using the harmfulness correlation operationally, reconcile the source’s agreement-versus-acceptability instrument wording and mean-versus-median descriptions; a local-panel study cannot repair an unexamined measurement direction.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Human simulation and measurement: AttuneBench: A Conversation-Based Benchmark for LLM Emotional Intelligence. AttuneBench uses 200 multi-turn human/model conversations from 11 US native English participants. Participants supply emotional-state, observed/preferred behavior and response-ranking annotations, with GPT-4o-mini suggesting question subsets and a preference-informed model response helping the reference-editing workflow. Default evaluation predicts annotations without future turns; draft-judge scores are supplementary, not Composite inputs.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.21739.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.21739.method)

[sourced_fact] Study result — AttuneBench: A Conversation-Based Benchmark for LLM Emotional Intelligence. Within the default-mode eleven-model panel, Emotion F1 did not reach omnibus significance(p=0.099), while Pairwise Accuracy differentiated model behavior more strongly. The paper’s conversation-level correlations and model-level correlations are separately defined; these findings do not validate a universal one-dimensional emotional-intelligence ranking.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.21739.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.21739.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — AttuneBench: A Conversation-Based Benchmark for LLM Emotional Intelligence. Only 11 participants contribute 200 imbalanced conversations, with self-reported demographic/diagnostic data and cultural/language restriction. Pooled tests treat conversations as independent despite repeated participants. The authors explicitly exclude clinical mental-health validation and safety-critical deployment decisions from the benchmark’s intended use. The three-rater human baseline covers seven conversations. Golden responses are participant edits after viewing original and preference-informed model outputs. Default, future-informed Omniscient and supplementary draft-judge settings differ; conversation-level Pearson r=-0.097 and model-level Spearman rho=-0.36 have different units.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.21739.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.21739.limitation), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.21739.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.21739.method), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.21739.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2605.21739.result)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — AttuneBench: A Conversation-Based Benchmark for LLM Emotional Intelligence. The eleven participants, repeated conversations and task-specific annotations are the relevant denominators. A buyer should evaluate the intended conversational behavior with participant-level splits and preserve preferred behavior separately from inferred emotion. Confidence is moderate in the benchmark as a bounded research instrument and unestablished for clinical or safety-critical decisions. Larger culturally varied panels and participant-clustered inference would change its external-validity assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional and long-horizon evaluation: Agents’ Last Exam. ALE separates a task workflow from runnable task instances and implements load/start/evaluate interfaces over expert-provided artifacts and references. Expert/engineering QC and code-based checks are the default, but selected visual/free-text workflows still use targeted LLM probes; static grader-type percentages refer to the open reference workflow tree, not all 1490 inventory instances.

The release figure reports 150 public, 1017 private and 323 unverified instances out of 1490; later text describes a 152-task public set while the executed-inventory appendix says 150. This unresolved version/count discrepancy and workflow-versus-instance distinction must remain explicit rather than silently treated as one complete reviewed denominator. The thirteen-domain/fifty-five-subdomain taxonomy is SOC/O*NET-grounded and uses LLM-assisted mapping. Table 1 labels tiers of 67, 55 and 38 instances, which sum to 160, while other passages describe 150 or 152 public tasks. These contexts do not resolve whether the tiers overlap. The conclusion also calls 960 units task workflows, while the figure calls them external-submission variants. No reconciled inventory or implied overlap is supplied.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Rubrics and executable evaluation: ComplexConstraints and Beyond: Expert Rubrics for RLVR. ComplexConstraints describes a three-stage expert prompt/reference/rubric authoring and independent-review workflow, plus iterative LLM-judge calibration and response edits designed to flip verdicts. Qwen3-4B training uses about 900 of the 1000 companion prompts, with GPT5-mini judging required criteria; the 75-prompt public benchmark is separate.

Table 3 reports Qwen3-4B mean per-criterion pass rate increasing from 57.9% to 73.4% on the held-out ComplexConstraints training split. This criterion-average metric differs from the all-criteria task pass rates on the separate 75-prompt public benchmark.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — ComplexConstraints and Beyond: Expert Rubrics for RLVR. The instruction-following result is one training seed, and the authors have not quantified seed-to-seed variance. They describe causal isolation of rubric-design choices and transfer mechanisms as future work; comparisons with other pipelines use different base models/training setups and are suggestive rather than controlled. The second expert reviews and a senior reviewer adjudicates disagreements; GPT-5-mini supplies training judgments. Its two public comparison tables use different-time, different-suite snapshots. Connected CoreCraft results are prior-work reports, not an independently replicated result of this rubric study.

A criterion-average training improvement does not establish all-criteria success on the separate public benchmark. The independent author/reviewer and calibration loop is a concrete service unit worth testing. Confidence is moderate for that design relevance and low for a general RLVR superiority claim. Repeated seeds and a controlled rubric-design ablation on unseen prompts would change the assessment of which human stages produce value.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional and long-horizon evaluation: GDP.pdf: Benchmarking Grounded Multimodal Reasoning over Professional PDF Documents. GDP.pdf retains 100 expert-authored question/PDF tasks across ten professional domains after at least two frontier models make material errors. Experts write atomic rubric criteria; each criterion is judged separately by Gemini 3.5 Flash without the source PDF or reference answer. Strict pass requires every criterion, while mean rubric score gives partial credit.

[sourced_fact] Study result — GDP.pdf: Benchmarking Grounded Multimodal Reasoning over Professional PDF Documents. The July 2026 snapshot reports 2–30.7% strict pass rates across 17 listed models on 100 items, averaging five runs per model with native PDF input and no tools/additional context. These are all-criteria item pass rates on this selected suite, not document-work success rates in general.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — GDP.pdf: Benchmarking Grounded Multimodal Reasoning over Professional PDF Documents. Every retained item was selected because at least two frontier models failed it at collection time. The authors explicitly caution that absolute pass rates therefore describe adversarially selected professional tasks rather than professional document work at large; the live leaderboard also evolves beyond this frozen July 2026 snapshot. The judge does not receive the source PDF or reference answer; the authors report calibration and hand-check discussed failures, but this is not independent calibration by this synthesis. Provider-native PDF processing is part of the measurement. Apache 2.0 benchmark wording does not displace third-party PDF rights.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — GDP.pdf: Benchmarking Grounded Multimodal Reasoning over Professional PDF Documents. Adversarial selection changes the meaning of absolute scores, and judging without the source PDF creates a separate evidence-access boundary. A buyer should retain the selection rule, native document presentation and strict-versus-partial metrics, then validate the judge on source-dependent errors. Confidence is high in these conditions and unestablished for general document-work accuracy. A representative private sample with source-visible expert adjudication would change the deployment estimate.

HANDBOOK.md describes 65 tasks using mutated expert-written 20–124-page policies and 824 programmatic criteria over final workspace/service state. Required outputs and prohibited behavior are checked separately; strict pass@1 requires every criterion and averages four trials per task, while N−1 is a separately labeled relaxed metric.

[sourced_fact] Study result — HANDBOOK.md: A Benchmark for Long-Context Agentic Instruction Following. The frozen July 2026 Table 2 reports a highest strict pass@1 of 36.2% among 30 evaluated model/configuration entries on 65 tasks with four trials each. This is the averaged all-criteria trial metric in one specified harness, not a fraction of unique tasks permanently unsolvable or a current vendor ranking.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.25398.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.25398.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — HANDBOOK.md: A Benchmark for Long-Context Agentic Instruction Following. The study uses fictional company environments, expert-mutated policies, mock services and one common OpenHands harness under explicit call/time caps. Policy mutation is intended to resist memorization; the protocol does not by itself prove uncontaminated pretraining or establish naturalistic corporate compliance and safety outside these tasks. The common harness caps trials at 200 tool calls and one hour; provider/transport errors are excluded and rerun. The July table lists thirty configurations, while the cost section refers to twenty release configurations. Deterministic criteria check the specified state, without proving all possible corporate consequences are covered.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — HANDBOOK.md: A Benchmark for Long-Context Agentic Instruction Following. Required and prohibited actions should be explicit acceptance dimensions. Mutated policies help pose a changing-instruction challenge, but a single relaxed missed criterion could be a decisive control. Confidence is high that strict and N−1 scores must remain separate and moderate in this testing approach. A buyer should add domain-specific critical gates; independently reviewed realistic policies and new harnesses would change the generalization assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional and long-horizon evaluation: APEX-Accounting. The pinned v2 paper describes 160 private tasks across ten synthetic company worlds and a separate 10-task public dev world. Experts author/solve tasks and unweighted binary rubrics, with synthetic world-file population under expert review. The main metric averages rubric criteria met over three selected runs per task; model executions number eight per task before infrastructure exclusions.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.method)

[sourced_fact] Study result — APEX-Accounting. For the pinned nine-model Loop-harness snapshot, the paper reports a highest Mean Criteria@3 of 56.4%, while no model exceeds 2.6% Pass^8. Mean criterion completion and all-eight-attempt complete-task reliability are different metrics and do not measure a fraction of accounting jobs automated.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — APEX-Accounting. World/task difficulty was selected using low scores from three model families; clarification/human-in-the-loop tasks were excluded. The scope omits tax, audit, consolidation, multi-entity/multi-currency work and external reporting. Judge agreement is a calibration/selection-sample result with residual error, not independent proof of general benchmark accuracy. Forty-two experts specify/review worlds and author/solve tasks; most world files are synthetically populated under review, and independent experts re-solve twenty tasks. The GEPA-prompted DeepSeek-v4-Flash judge is selected/calibrated on 1,687 majority-vote labels from 120 trajectories and three human raters; 97.1% agreement is a calibration result. Mean Criteria@3 selects three runs lexicographically by task ID; model-caused failures score zero, while infrastructure exclusions leave 156–160 tasks in paired comparisons. The authors’ 37.1% judge-as-solver stress test does not independently eliminate self-preference. This paper-specific entry uses the v2 160-task count; the separately captured leaderboard conflict is disclosed in the family entry rather than attributed to this paper-only repair.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.limitation](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.limitation), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.method](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.method), [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2607.27189.result)

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — APEX-Accounting. Partial criterion completion is commercially different from repeatedly complete accounting work. Excluded clarification tasks also remove an interaction mode many deployments require. Confidence is high in these measurement distinctions and unestablished for accounting-job automation. A buyer should audit criteria with qualified practitioners, introduce ambiguous cases requiring escalation and retain all execution attempts. Real-world validated tasks and independently calibrated judging would change the use assessment.

The paper post-trains Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on 363 MCP tasks using a selected 3000-trajectory Kimi K2.6 supervised warmup followed by one-epoch RL. Deterministic criterion rewards are combined with a low-score effort floor capped at 0.40; evaluation uses native benchmark scores rather than this shaping reward.

For the updated greedy software-engineering evaluations, Table 2 reports SWE-BenchPro 20.5→26.3% and Terminal-Bench 2 44.9→47.7% after the combined SFT+RL pipeline. The authors report descriptive point estimates from one training run and distinguish these from older four-sample diagnostics and retained tau2 results.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Cross-Benchmark Generalization in Long-Horizon Agents. Toolathlon informed initial base-family/teacher choices and contributed reused MCP surfaces, although no external benchmark tasks/graders entered training according to the authors. Pretraining contamination cannot be audited, the no-effort-floor ablation was not run, and exploratory outcome-conditioned behavior patterns do not establish a causal transfer mechanism. Updated greedy evaluations and older four-sample diagnostics have different provenance. The latter are not identified as standard unweighted any-of-four pass@4. One training run, correlated benchmarks and unavailable paired units limit uncertainty and replication claims.

The combined supervised and reinforcement stages, task selection and shaping reward are a single treatment here. The study describes a combined SFT-plus-GSPO post-training experiment on 363 LHMTA office/general-tool tasks, followed by analysis of 103 base-fail/trained-pass task pairs using Claude Opus 4.8-assisted reports manually checked against raw trajectories. This is an outcome-conditioned analysis, not a random sample of all agent behavior.
