For the same base/trained checkpoints, Table 3 reports greedy SWE-BenchPro pass@1 changing from 20.5% to 26.3%. Over 731 paired SWE tasks, Table 5 separately reports the share containing a formal-test command changing from 37.5% to 73.3%; test invocation is an indirect behavior measure and does not establish semantic correctness.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Post-Training on Office Work Improves Software Engineering: A Behavioral Account of Cross-Domain Transfer. All results come from one model/training run. No task-demand ablation or equal-budget software-training counterfactual was performed; outcome-conditioned examples and analyst-selected explanations cannot establish a causal mechanism, prevalence of capabilities or that office training is the most efficient path to SWE improvement. The paper describes reward as trajectory-level criterion fraction, while companion 2608.00181v1 additionally describes an effort floor and Toolathlon-informed family/teacher choice. Matching checkpoints, recipe and values suggest shared experimental provenance; that is an author inference, not proof of independent replication or permission to equate every protocol description.

The successful-change subset is selected by outcome, so its behavioral themes are hypotheses rather than population frequencies or causal mediators. Test-command invocation is observable but does not establish a correct diagnosis or patch. Confidence is moderate in using the trace analysis to generate follow-up tests and low in a mechanism claim. A randomized task-demand ablation and equal-budget software-training counterfactual would change the explanation. Apparent agreement with the companion paper is not additional independent experimental replication, and the two reward descriptions retain their recorded difference.

Chartography uses 100 professionally authored chart questions verified by three additional experts and screened for at least one meaningful frontier-model failure. Each configuration receives 20 no-tools trials per task; Gemini 3.5 Flash judges the final answer against expert targets/ranges without seeing the chart, and multipart answers require all parts.

[sourced_fact] Study result — Chartography: A Benchmark for Professional Chart Understanding. The frozen July 2026 table reports 45.0% mean pass@1 for the leading configuration across 100 tasks × 20 scored trials, with a reported 95% CI half-width 1.1 percentage points. The metric is the fraction of all graded trials passed; displayed ranks and overlapping intervals should not be interpreted as statistically distinct capability tiers.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2608.10677.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2608.10677.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Chartography: A Benchmark for Professional Chart Understanding. Items are adversarially screened and require specialist standing knowledge under a no-tools single-image protocol. The judge shares identity with an evaluated configuration, and online chart provenance does not establish redistribution rights. Results do not estimate general professional decision accuracy, deployed agent performance or causal superiority of a specific visual mechanism. The 100 tasks use 98 byte-distinct images, including 81 online-sourced and 19 author-created charts. Twenty trials per task produce 2,000 responses per configuration, not independent new tasks. The self-judging configuration and qualitative trajectory explanations do not establish independent judge validity or a controlled perception-versus-reasoning causal ablation.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Chartography: A Benchmark for Professional Chart Understanding. Expert verification, adversarial screening and repeated model trials each answer a different question. The reported uncertainty does not establish distinct capability tiers, and an answer-only judge can miss visual-grounding errors. Confidence is high in retaining those boundaries and moderate in the benchmark’s target relevance. Source-visible independent adjudication, chart-rights review and representative professional-chart sampling would change buyer confidence.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Transfer and generalization: Cross-Benchmark Transfer from RL on Agentic Coding Tasks. The experiment applies one GSPO epoch with a rank 32 LoRA adapter to Kimi K2.7 Code on 1000 expert-built repository tasks and 700 terminal tasks, without a supervised stage. Reward is target-check fraction, but any failed pass-to-pass regression test zeroes repository reward; terminal tasks have no such regression-test gate.

[sourced_fact] Study result — Cross-Benchmark Transfer from RL on Agentic Coding Tasks. For SWE-BenchPro’s 731-task public split under mini-swe-agent, Table 2 reports pass@1 increasing 60.1→64.8%, or 35 additional solved tasks, in matched in-house base/trained runs. This is one trained checkpoint/run and does not establish generalization uncertainty over training seeds.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2610.00890.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2610.00890.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Cross-Benchmark Transfer from RL on Agentic Coding Tasks. Headline DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench 2.1 baselines are public scores, whereas other baselines are in-house; DeepSWE’s in-house base differs from its public baseline. Terminal-Bench 4 revises 3 and is not an independent task family, and eight trained Terminal 3 runs were excluded for harness failures. These provenance/denominator distinctions must accompany cross-benchmark aggregation. Partial credit weights checks/verifier criteria equally, which need not equal one vote per semantic requirement. Eight excluded Terminal-Bench 3 runs leave eight passes among 66 scored runs; Terminal-Bench 4 revises 3 within one family. Terminal-Bench 2.1 has no in-house base run, and its public baseline averages three runs.

Protected regression tests define a meaningful acceptance constraint, but public and in-house baselines cannot be pooled as if all were matched reruns. Confidence is moderate in the matched SWE-BenchPro change and low in a universal transfer advantage. A buyer should require complete harness-failure accounting, an independent task manifest and repeated training seeds; an equal-budget control with stable benchmark versions would change the causal interpretation.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional and long-horizon evaluation: DAYJOB: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Professional Work. DAYJOB describes 130 tasks: 50 healthcare and 80 finance, of which all 50 healthcare and 50 finance are publicly released. A Claude Opus 4.8 agentic judge inspects delivered files against unweighted binary expert criteria. Strict pass@1 requires every criterion, averages scored attempts within each task and weights tasks equally by domain; error attempts are excluded.

[sourced_fact] Study result — DAYJOB: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Professional Work. The frozen September 2026 launch table reports its leading configuration at 24.7% strict pass@1 on healthcare and 23.9% on finance, with at most five scored attempts per task. Relaxed 95%/90% or one-missed-criterion scores are distinct and can accept a missed decisive control.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — DAYJOB: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Professional Work. Healthcare completion-time figures are creator estimates rather than observed completion trials: range midpoints are averaged and more-than-40 hours is capped at 40. The selected task workspaces/rubrics and model judge do not establish population-level professional accuracy, safe autonomous practice or actual labor-time savings. The midpoint/capped-time convention is established for healthcare; the finance mean is separately reported on its dataset card and is not assigned that convention here. Section 5.3 cost covers agent and condenser model calls while excluding the judge. The 50 released finance tasks and the 80 evaluated finance tasks are different denominators.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — DAYJOB: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Professional Work. The buyer’s first question is complete delivery under required controls, followed by its cost and escalation burden. Estimated professional completion time cannot be multiplied by model scores to claim observed labor savings. Confidence is high in that restriction and moderate in the selected-task evaluation design. Prospective practitioner timing, complete execution-error accounting and independent file-level judging would change the economic and deployment interpretation.

[sourced_fact] Study result — PLE: Physical-Engineering’s Last Exam. For the pinned evaluation, Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code reports 50.6% mean task score across 85 tasks and three runs per task. This combines rubric and executable/hybrid scores and is not a strict task pass rate or the percentage of engineering assignments ready for licensed signoff.

Evidence IDs: [repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2610.30537.result](evidence.html#assertion-repair.qualbinding.20261111.v1.mandatory3.claim.arxiv.2610.30537.result)

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — PLE: Physical-Engineering’s Last Exam. The hybrid score is s = 0.4 p + 0.6 G Oprime: a failed hard-constraint gate removes objective credit but does not generally zero the constraint-fraction term. Single-task run variance and model-judge self-preference are reported; benchmark scores therefore cannot certify safety, feasibility or real engineering deployment readiness. Thirty-seven coauthored tasks use the stated constraint/objective formula; four site/MEP tasks have bespoke graders with separately described gates. Fourteen models have restricted harness coverage, rather than every model being crossed with all seven common harnesses; Grok Build is model-specific. The paper plans release of 29 tasks without establishing their present availability. Model regrading is not fresh human engineering validation.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — PLE: Physical-Engineering’s Last Exam. A hybrid mean task score is not the share of engineering deliverables ready for signoff. A failed hard gate can still leave constraint-fraction credit, so buyer acceptance must inspect the gate and each decisive physical requirement directly. Confidence is high in this scoring distinction and unestablished for engineering safety. Independent solver validation, verified physical checks and professional review of new tasks would change the deployment assessment.

[analysis] Cross-study synthesis — aggregation, selection and legitimate disagreement. MACE and Crowd-Kit assume an objective categorical target in their aggregation settings; style clustering evaluates consistency with subjective groupings; MMRB2 discards high-disagreement and near-midpoint pairs. Those procedures can improve a chosen reference fit while changing which cases are represented. The analyst judgment is to predeclare whether disagreement is error, uncertainty or an intended target distribution. Confidence is high in this design distinction. An independently adjudicated target-use study would change which aggregation/filtering choice is appropriate; no cross-paper accuracy winner is inferred.

[analysis] Cross-study synthesis — transfer evidence is a hierarchy of comparisons. Corecraft reports a training-time held-out result and external transfer; the office-to-software papers describe connected checkpoints and an outcome-conditioned behavioral analysis; the coding-task study mixes public and in-house baseline provenance outside its matched SWE-BenchPro comparison. These reports should not be counted as independent replications of one causal mechanism. Confidence is moderate in the documented point-estimate improvements and low in explaining them through a single human-data property. Repeated seeds, equal-budget controls and ablations that isolate task demands, supervised warmup and reward shaping would change the causal assessment.

[analysis] Cross-study synthesis — the verifier is part of the system under test. Weaver’s selection depends on its candidate pool and many verifier calls; PivotRL’s SWE local check can accept a tool-call name without validating arguments or patch quality; ALCE’s NLI support metric can miss partial support; PLE’s failed hard gate does not zero every score component. A technically inspectable acceptance report therefore retains input visibility, check logic, false accepts, false rejects and final-task outcomes. Confidence is high in these distinctions and unmeasured in any buyer deployment. Independent falsification cases and representative, blinded adjudication would change the trust placed in each verifier.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Multilingual and multimodal supervision: CharXiv: Charting Gaps in Realistic Chart Understanding in Multimodal LLMs. The v1 paper reports a four-stage chart selection process: SigLIP similarity filtering of figures extracted from January 2020–September 2023 arXiv preprints, graduate-student selection for visual diversity, removal of near-duplicates, and exclusion of blurry or unclearly labeled charts. The v1 paper acknowledges Microsoft Accelerate Foundation Models Academic Research Initiative support, an Apple Scholars in AIML Fellowship for Mengzhou Xia, and a Gordon Wu Fellowship for Luxi He. The v1 paper uses GPT-4o to extract responses and assign binary correctness grades rather than exact string matching, and acknowledges that automated grading errors or human participant mistakes may affect its measurements. The v1 paper describes graduate-student reasoning-question annotation using ten GPT-4V example question–answer pairs per chart; annotators could choose a suggestion, modify it, or write their own question.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — CharXiv: Charting Gaps in Realistic Chart Understanding in Multimodal LLMs. The useful provenance unit is the chart, question origin and grading path. A broad human-authored label would hide whether a suggestion was accepted, edited or replaced. Confidence is high that those stages should be retained and moderate in the benchmark as an instrument for scientific-chart questions. The v1 paper uses BLEU for RTL/testbench correspondence tasks and an o4-mini model judge for technical question answering, while stating that further investigation is needed into the technical reliability of those question-answer scores. DeepResearch Bench II requires rubrics to check essential, indivisible facts or inferences and encode the target content itself, rather than merely naming a broad topic. [sourced_fact] Study construction and protocol — DeepResearch Bench II: Diagnosing Deep Research Agents via Rubrics from Expert Report. DeepResearch Bench II reports human inspection of all generated tasks and rubrics, followed by more than 400 human-hours of domain-expert review, discussion and iterative refinement. The DeepResearch Bench II pipeline first uses an LLM to extract tasks and rubrics from expert articles, then scores each source article against its generated rubrics and regenerates them if Information Recall or Analysis scores below 90%. The original DeepResearch Bench II experiment uses Gemini 2.5 Pro as judge, evaluates batches of 50 rubrics, and describes task scores as the fraction of rubric requirements passed. The DeepResearch Bench II paper limits its Presentation dimension mainly to report formatting and layout and says adaptation to a user's knowledge and preferences remains unrealized. DeepResearch Bench II adds source-article titles and URLs to a prompt block list and performs a secondary check for generated answers supported by citations to those articles, excluding leaked answers from scoring.

[sourced_fact] Study result — DeepResearch Bench II: Diagnosing Deep Research Agents via Rubrics from Expert Report. The DeepResearch Bench II batch-size ablation uses ten human-labeled model reports in PDF, DOCX, Markdown and HTML formats; with Gemini 2.5 Pro judging 50 rubrics per batch, the paper reports 91.75% accuracy and F1 of 89.57. The captured DeepResearch Bench II README reports a three-way-label comparison on ten reports with 738 matched rubric judgments: GPT-5.5 achieves 91.19% exact-match accuracy, Cohen's kappa of 0.7993 and task-level Pearson correlation of 0.9587. At batch size 50 on the same human-labeled report set, DeepResearch Bench II reports Gemini 2.5 Pro accuracy/F1 of 91.75/89.57, compared with 88.36/78.28 for GPT 5 and 89.45/79.79 for Gemini 2.5 Flash. In DeepResearch Bench II Table 3, OpenAI-GPT-o3 Deep Research has the highest reported total score, 45.40, and Information Recall score, 39.98; Gemini 2.5 Pro Deep Research has the highest Analysis score, 51.91.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Repository engineering and executable verifiers: DeepSWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Original, Long-Horizon Engineering Tasks. DeepSWE contains 113 tasks across 91 active public repositories in TypeScript, Go, Python, JavaScript and Rust; its repository-selection rules require at least 500 GitHub stars and a permissive open-source license. For eight models with publicly reported SWE-Bench Pro results, the DeepSWE paper reports a 69.8-percentage-point pass-rate range on DeepSWE versus 29.7 points on SWE-Bench Pro. DeepSWE evaluates 16 model-and-reasoning-effort configurations under mini-swe-agent with a shared prompt and single bash tool, pinned to commit adfe20233d456104c38c3129161b54f0fd39f2c7. DeepSWE uses binary functional rewards without partial credit and does not score code readability, idiomatic style, maintainability, performance or documentation. Every DeepSWE task includes a prompt, executable functional verifier and reference solution; verifiers exercise public APIs and observable outputs rather than requiring the reference implementation's internal structure. DeepSWE accepts tasks only after LLM-assisted analysis and independent human review of the prompt, verifier, reference solution and diagnostic agent runs.

[sourced_fact] Study construction and protocol — DeepSWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Original, Long-Horizon Engineering Tasks. The pinned DeepSWE README says that since v1.1, grading uses a separate verifier environment and requires Pier newer than 0.3.0: agent commits are collected as a patch and applied in a pristine grading container. DeepSWE's harness pilot compares mini-swe-agent with each model's native harness on the same ten SWE-Bench Pro tasks, for Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro. DeepSWE reference solutions are authored from scratch rather than copied or adapted from public patches, and the paper says the tasks are never merged upstream; task containers contain a shallow clone at the base commit. The DeepSWE paper announces release of the benchmark, executable verifiers and trajectory records while withholding the exact LLM-reviewer prompt; the captured repository contains an Apache 2.0 LICENSE. DeepSWE reports 95% intervals as pass@1 plus or minus 1.96 times the standard deviation of the roughly four benchmark-run scores divided by the square root of the number of runs.

[sourced_fact] Study construction and protocol — DeepSWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Original, Long-Horizon Engineering Tasks. The DeepSWE experiment reports 7,174 scored runs across 16 configurations, with 428-452 scored runs per configuration after starting from approximately four attempts per task. DeepSWE's Figure 2 reports mean prompts of 2,158 characters and reference solutions with 668 lines added and 7.4 files edited. DeepSWE defines pass@1 as the equally weighted average of each task's scored-rollout pass fraction, while pass@4 is the fraction of 113 tasks with at least one success among up to four attempts. In the published DeepSWE comparison, a GPT-5.5 judge disagrees with executable verifier decisions on 10 of 735 DeepSWE runs, 1.4%, versus 256 of 789 SWE-Bench Pro runs, 32.4%.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — DeepSWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Original, Long-Horizon Engineering Tasks. The headline interval measures rerun noise on the same 113 tasks, not task-selection uncertainty. Infrastructure errors are excluded without resampling, while context exhaustion and wall-clock timeout are failures. The pass@4 indicator has a smaller effective budget when fewer than four attempts remain. Judge/verifier disagreement on 735 runs is not an independently measured verifier error rate. The native-harness pilot uses ten SWE-Bench Pro tasks, not the DeepSWE corpus.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — DeepSWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Original, Long-Horizon Engineering Tasks. Original reference patches and implementation-tolerant functional verifiers make the accepted change explicit, while binary reward still omits maintainability and incomplete progress. Confidence is moderate in the fixed-system task result and high in keeping its uncertainty and exclusions visible. A buyer should separately inspect alternative valid patches, regression coverage and production-code review. Representative repository sampling, more reruns and independent adjudication of disagreements would change confidence in comparative capability.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Scientific workflows and recoverable targets: GeneBench-Pro: Evaluating Multistage Statistical Reasoning in Genomics, Quantitative Biology, and Translational Biomedicine. The paper states that AI systems assisted problem design and review and manuscript editing, while the authors reviewed and approved the benchmark design, problem specifications, validation targets, evaluation results and final manuscript. The reported evaluation attempted ten independent runs per model-problem pair for standard evaluations and five for GPT Pro (Extended) and Claude Opus; container, tooling, provider and response-format errors were excluded from per-problem pass-rate estimates. The paper attributes benchmark conception, problem implementation and review, external-review coordination and benchmark testing to Jeremy Li, and model evaluation runs to Andrew Ho; both authors drafted and revised the manuscript. The reported primary metric uses Python binary grading: every prespecified target field must satisfy its exact-match rule or absolute numeric tolerance for the run to pass, and the free-text reasoning field is collected for qualitative analysis but is not graded. The paper reports evaluation of the full 129-problem suite across 60 model configurations, including mainline GPT, GPT Pro and non-GPT baseline rows.

[sourced_fact] Study construction and protocol — GeneBench-Pro: Evaluating Multistage Statistical Reasoning in Genomics, Quantitative Biology, and Translational Biomedicine. The paper defines overall pass rate as the unweighted mean of per-problem pass rates across 129 problems and reports 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals from 20,000 resamples, resampling problems and repeated runs within problems. The authors’ manual review of selected GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol reasoning traces suggests a notice-act gap: failures may identify local diagnostics without sufficiently revising downstream statistical methods or QC. The reported harness used a Linux Docker environment with Python and R scientific and bioinformatics software and no internet access, restricting agents to the prompt, staged files, installed software and model-internal knowledge. The inspected preprint banner states that the preprint was not certified by peer review and is available under CC-BY-NC 4.0. The paper’s construction description and example prompt tell agents that analytical reasoning quality is graded alongside numerical correctness, while its Methods section states that free-text reasoning is not graded. The paper reports no additional uniform wall-clock budget imposed by the evaluation harness, while runs remained subject to provider and platform behavior in the evaluation stack.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — GeneBench-Pro: Evaluating Multistage Statistical Reasoning in Genomics, Quantitative Biology, and Translational Biomedicine. Recoverable target design is central: the correct estimand is what staged observations support, rather than an inaccessible simulation parameter. Binary all-field scoring nevertheless collapses an early failure and a late statistical mistake. Confidence is high in those measurement distinctions and moderate in the curated scientific-workflow relevance. The notice-act explanation is selected-trace interpretation, not a measured chain-length law. Independent review of unreviewed tasks, resolved prompt/grader wording and representative real-data studies would change confidence in generalization.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Health conversations and rubric measurement: HealthBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Towards Improved Human Health. The v1 main text reports that 262 physicians created HealthBench tasks over eleven months, with practice experience in 60 countries and 26 specialties, and that all physician cohort members were compensated. The v1 paper describes most conversations as model-synthetic from physician-designed situation types, with additional physician red-team conversations and transformed HealthSearchQA queries described as released by Google; o1-preview filters for relevance, realism, self-consistency and complete messages. The v1 paper validates model grading against physician grades on the 34 predefined consensus criteria and selects GPT-4.1 as its default grader; it acknowledges that most example-specific criteria were written by individual physicians and were not validated by other physicians. The v1 paper grades each criterion as met or not met, applies its signed nonzero point weight from minus ten to ten, divides the sum by the available positive points per example, and clips the mean example score to zero through one.

It does not supply a numerical benchmark leaderboard for this entry or a measured patient-outcome effect; neither is inferred from physician involvement.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — HealthBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Towards Improved Human Health. The main-text cohort of 262 physicians is distinct from appendix onboarding/rotation/removal counts; no final population is inferred by subtraction. Compensation and credentials are reported rather than independently verified. The 34 predefined consensus criteria receive a validation procedure that does not extend to every individualized rubric. A signed weighted score clipped to 0–1 is not a fraction of tasks fully solved.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — HealthBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Towards Improved Human Health. The source makes an especially consequential distinction between judged response quality and patient outcomes. A system can improve a rubric mean while missing a rare severe requirement. Confidence is high in requiring workflow-specific evaluation and moderate in using the benchmark to expose response dimensions. A buyer should separately gate critical contraindications or missing escalation, calibrate individualized rubrics with independent clinicians, and preserve the full signed criterion vector. Prospective patient-relevant workflow studies would be needed to change the outcome conclusion.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Human-time calibration and composite evaluation: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks. The paper reports approximately eight attempts per agent/task pair and uses general agent scaffolds without task-specific prompting, except that SWAA uses a simple prompting scaffold. The authors state that task-completion horizons depend on the task distribution and on the human reference population’s skill and context. For HCAST, task durations are calculated using the geometric mean time of successful human baseline attempts, with manual estimates for tasks lacking successful baselines; RE-Bench instead receives a fixed eight-hour duration rating. A separate internal-repository study uses five original issues and has maintainers grade submitted solutions manually, rather than requiring every issue to have an automatic checker. The authors label HCAST and RE-Bench tasks for the presence of 16 defined messiness factors and sum those labels into a score from zero to 16. The paper says supplementary material will provide code and data for some core figures, while the full codebase is infeasible to publicize and anonymize; code for additional figures may be provided on reviewer request.

[sourced_fact] Study construction and protocol — Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks. The analysis binarizes task scores using task-specific human-performance thresholds: HCAST uses its target score and RE-Bench uses the average score of human runs lasting seven to nine hours. Section 2.1 describes a composite evaluation suite containing 97 selected HCAST tasks, seven RE-Bench environments and 66 Software Atomic Actions tasks. The method fits an agent-specific logistic model against log human task duration; the fitted horizon is the duration with predicted 50% success, and each task receives weight equal to the inverse square root of its task-group size.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.next8.metr.paper.success-thresholds.v1](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.next8.metr.paper.success-thresholds.v1), [candidate.next8.metr.paper.task-composition.v1](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.next8.metr.paper.task-composition.v1), [candidate.next8.metr.paper.time-horizon-model.v1](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.next8.metr.paper.time-horizon-model.v1)

[sourced_fact] Study result — Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks. The paper extrapolates historical trends toward a one-month horizon defined as approximately 167 human working hours, while treating that result as conditional on continued trends and transfer to real-world software work. The reported 80%-success horizons are four to six times shorter than the 50%-success horizons, while the fitted doubling times are similar at 204 and 207 days respectively. For the reported 2019–2025 model series, the paper estimates a 207-day doubling time with a 95% bootstrapped interval of 166–240 days, using 10,000 resamples over task groups, tasks and runs.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks. The 97 HCAST, seven RE-Bench and 66 SWAA components sum to 170, while the baselining section uses 169; both descriptions remain. Successful-baseline geometric means, missing-baseline forecasts and the fixed eight-hour RE-Bench assignment have different provenance. Humans and agents have different context/qualification conditions. Historical trend intervals do not include future trend changes or most external-validity uncertainty.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks. A fitted 50% horizon is a conditional relationship between this task distribution, a human reference and a system, not a universal duration an agent can safely work. The shorter 80% horizon shows why the reliability target must be chosen before applying the number. Confidence is high in this interpretation and low in unconditional extrapolation to workplace timelines. Measured long-task human baselines, explicit failure costs and new-domain validation would change the deployment inference; a prospective stable-suite trend test would change confidence in extrapolation.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Medical question construction and validation: MedXpertQA: Benchmarking Expert-Level Medical Reasoning and Understanding. The v1 paper assesses leakage risk before and after rewriting with GPT-4o outputs, using perplexity and similarity to collected explanations measured by ROUGE-L and edit distance. The v1 methods describe model rephrasing intended to preserve question information, removal of weak distractors and setting the final choice counts to ten for Text and five for MM, using GPT-4o-2024-11-20 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet-20241022. The v1 paper describes filtering an initial 37,543-question medical exam/textbook bank using model votes, difficulty thresholds based on human-response Brier scores and prior expert difficulty ratings, and semantic-similarity filtering.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — MedXpertQA: Benchmarking Expert-Level Medical Reasoning and Understanding. Approximately 16.78% of source questions lack the human-response/difficulty annotations needed for one filtering stage; that does not imply they skipped final physician review. Methods name two augmentation models despite introduction wording about three. Final MM choice counts do not mean new distractors were generated for every image-dependent question. Leakage proxies are not training-corpus inspection or clinical validation.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — MedXpertQA: Benchmarking Expert-Level Medical Reasoning and Understanding. Reviewing original validity before augmentation is a useful control because rewriting can preserve an invalid premise as easily as a correct one. Text/MM, full-suite and ten-percent model samples need separate denominators. Confidence is moderate in the construction lesson and unestablished for clinical safety. A task-specific pilot would retain the invalid-question log, licensed-physician review roles and extraction scripts, then independently assess a stratified sample. Verified corrections and prospective workflow outcomes would change a deployment assessment.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Knowledge and benchmark construction: MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark. The reported MMLU-Pro evaluation generally uses five-shot chain-of-thought; the model table specifies zero-shot for Gemini-1.5-Pro and Gemini-1.5-Flash. Answer extraction tries two regular expressions and otherwise selects a random answer option. The v1 paper describes filtering out MMLU questions answered correctly by more than four of eight specified models, then using GPT-4-Turbo to extract answers and generate additional distractors, with manual checking of extracted answers. The v1 paper states that its multiple-choice format may fail to capture comprehension depth and creative responses as effectively as open-ended answers, and that its assessment is language-only rather than multimodal.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark. Difficulty filtering partly defines what the benchmark asks: a harder retained set need not be a more representative professional workload. The random fallback also creates a reproducibility requirement for answer extraction. Confidence is high in these design boundaries and unmeasured for workplace validity. A buyer should freeze question and extraction versions, inspect alternative valid answers, and compare failure types on an independently selected target task sample. Replayed extraction under fixed seeds and independent domain review would change confidence in the score.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Program reconstruction and behavioral testing: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?. ProgramBench construction uses mini-SWE-agent with Claude Sonnet 4.5 inside Ubuntu 22.04 containers to build reference executables, generate behavioral tests and remove implementation details for inference. The published construction pipeline flags weak assertions for agent revision, then discards tests that do not pass the reference executable deterministically or that pass a dummy binary. The paper evaluates nine models with a single mini-SWE-agent scaffold, specifying 20 CPUs, 60 GB RAM, a 1,000-step limit and six hours per run. In its internet-access ablation, ProgramBench uses nine model judges from three model families to classify source lookup or binary wrapping, flagging a task when at least five judges identify a violation. Appendix A.3.4 reports manual inspection of test suites for five repositories identified as plausible risks for implementation-dependent output, finding no such numerical-output assertions in those inspected suites.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?. The construction agent can inspect source that the reconstruction worker cannot. Tests combine generated and harvested material, reported as 79.5% and 20.5%. Manual review covers five at-risk repositories and no formal human feasibility study. Finite tests omit some behavior and do not measure speed, memory or disk use. The paper and current card have different difficulty populations; model-panel cheating judgments are not independently established human truth.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?. The acceptance unit is full tested behavior under isolation, not a fraction of a program inferred from partial tests. The dummy-binary filter is useful falsification but can miss subtle weak assertions. Confidence is high in retaining this distinction and moderate in using the benchmark for reconstruction tasks. A buyer should add metamorphic tests, alternative implementations and shortcut attempts while logging excluded tests. Independent black-box behavior checks, human feasibility studies and adversarial isolation tests would change confidence in generality and completeness.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Scientific coding and expert review: SciCode: A Research Coding Benchmark Curated by Scientists. The v1 paper distinguishes numerical input/output tests from domain-specific tests, for which scientists check whether solutions reproduce published results or match analytical solutions from theoretical models. The v1 paper describes SciCode as scientific coding tasks mainly drawn from scientists’ everyday research scripts, organized into main problems with smaller subproblems and explicit input/output docstrings. The v1 paper reports three revision stages: at least two in-domain scientists cross-check the question, solution and domain tests; an out-of-domain scientist reviews clarity and sufficient information; then GPT-4 solutions undergo scientist error analysis and possible test or workflow revision.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — SciCode: A Research Coding Benchmark Curated by Scientists. Cross-domain clarity review complements in-domain correctness review, but neither makes a finite test suite exhaustive. The standard main-problem rule carries generated earlier answers forward, so errors can propagate through the workflow. Confidence is moderate in this construction pattern and low in extrapolating its pass rule to arbitrary research code. A pilot should preserve subproblem dependencies, distinguish supplied from generated code and review scientifically plausible false accepts. Independent reruns and adversarial tests grounded in analytical solutions would change trust in the checks.

The SUPERChem acknowledgments name Center of Mass Educational Tech. Co. Ltd. among educational platforms that contributed original problems used to build the benchmark. The SUPERChem acknowledgments name Chemy Group among educational platforms that contributed original problems used to build the benchmark. The SUPERChem acknowledgments credit Peking University's High-Performance Computing Platform and Computer Center's LLM Working Group with computational resources including LLM access and server support. The SUPERChem manuscript describes creator, reviewer and approver stages: a question enters the bank only after final approval, with return for revision or rejection available at review and approval. The manuscript reports 77 Peking University students contributing to curation, including 3 IChO medalists and 64 CChO medalists. Table 1 labels its reported frontier-model pass@1 figures as means over eight trials, while other model figures use the first trial; input modalities also differ by model. Appendix E defines Reasoning Path Fidelity as weighted recall of expert-authored reasoning checkpoints, with Gemini 2.5 Pro at temperature 1.0 judging semantic matches in the generated reasoning.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Repository engineering and repeated reliability: SWE Atlas: Benchmarking Coding Agents Beyond Issue Resolution. SWE Atlas describes professional software engineers creating tasks and reference solutions, review by an independent quality-control team, and independent audits by three trusted experts of instructions, verification and rubrics. The paper compares human and three model judges on 200 rubric gradings of responses from Opus 4.5 and GPT-5, then reports selecting Opus 4.5 as the judge for its runs. Appendix D states that SWE Atlas task authors and reviewers were compensated under contractual terms, with no unpaid volunteer labor. Appendix J reports Harbor-based experiments in Modal sandboxes with 16 CPUs, 16 GB memory and a six-hour limit, and Fireworks AI API inference for open models. SWE Atlas v1 distinguishes Pass@3, meaning any successful trial, Pass@1, meaning average per-trial success, and Pass3, meaning all three trials succeed.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — SWE Atlas: Benchmarking Coding Agents Beyond Issue Resolution. SWE Atlas makes the completion contract more explicit than a single patch test: Q&A, test writing and refactoring have different decisive conditions. It also exposes a maintenance problem when rubrics and judging change while task identity stays fixed. Confidence is high in keeping any-of-three, average-trial and all-three success separate, and moderate in task-specific procurement relevance. A buyer should pin the grading release and falsify its rubric polarity and no-op tests. Independent same-task reruns under both release protocols would change confidence in longitudinal comparisons.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Professional tasks, judging and economic interpretation: The AI Productivity Index (APEX). APEX-v1.0 grades each rubric criterion with three judges: o3 with thinking Low, Gemini 2.5 Pro with thinking Off, and Sonnet 4 with thinking Off. It uses a two-of-three or unanimous majority for each binary criterion grade. The APEX-v1.0 paper compares its model scores with publicly reported HLE, MMLU Pro, MMMU Val and GPQA scores and reports a mean cross-benchmark correlation of 0.79. The captured APEX-v1.0 paper parses evidence PDFs and CSVs with Reducto and appends the parsed material to each task prompt, using one parsing strategy across models and avoiding the closed models' native file-handling APIs. The APEX-v1.0 paper explicitly cautions that rubric scores need not track real-world value linearly: a response scoring 60% might be effectively useless when value is stage-gated. The APEX-v1.0 judge panel agrees with expert Pass/Fail labels on 89% of 5,818 criterion ratings collected for responses from one model, Gemini 2.5 Pro with thinking On.

[sourced_fact] Study construction and protocol — The AI Productivity Index (APEX). In APEX-v1.0, repeating each judge three times on responses from one arbitrarily selected model, Grok 4, yields reported internal agreement of 99.5% for o3 Low, 99.4% for Gemini 2.5 Pro Off and 99.6% for Sonnet 4 Off. APEX-v1.0 rubrics lack negative criteria that penalize incorrect or irrelevant statements, so passing many positive criteria does not guarantee that a response contains fewer errors. The APEX-v1.0 observational comparison reports mean scores of 55.8% for models offering thinking tokens versus 40.4% for the others, with 16 of 23 models in the thinking group. APEX-v1.0 collects three responses from every model for each prompt and uses the median of their three scored responses for the leaderboard and analysis.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — The AI Productivity Index (APEX). The original 200-case August 2025 experiment uses median-of-three responses and a three-judge criterion majority. Its 89% expert agreement covers 5,818 ratings from one response model, with expert labels not themselves reviewer-validated. Near-99.5% judge repeatability covers another selected model and is not correctness. Cross-benchmark correlations have missing model scores. Thinking-group comparisons confound recency and model type, without a causal ablation.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — The AI Productivity Index (APEX). Providing the needed evidence in context makes this a professional response test rather than a live information-retrieval workflow. Positive rubric completion can coexist with unsupported extra claims because negative criteria are absent. Confidence is high in those restrictions and unestablished for economic value. A buyer should test decisive negative conditions and compare the full response distribution before choosing a best-of or median protocol. Representative prospective work, independent judge calibration and matched thinking on/off experiments would change the operational interpretation.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation methodology and maintenance: Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation. The authors propose keyboard-bound choices and simple annotation tasks, varying option order to reduce priming and showing all alternatives on one screen to avoid scrolling bias. The paper distinguishes intra-annotator stability over time from inter-annotator reproducibility and discusses simple agreement, Kappa variants and Krippendorff alpha as evaluation measures. The authors recommend developing the codebook with annotators and monitoring agreement so that category definitions remain stable as the scheme evolves. For contrastive annotation, the paper describes a common core scheme with language-specific extensions and illustrates this approach with English and Spanish thematic-field annotation in CONTRANOT. The paper discusses reconciliation and adjudication of annotation disagreements, cautioning that reconciliation can raise agreement scores while risking overtraining or drift and recommending it mainly for initial training. The paper emphasizes ownership and distribution licensing when maintaining annotated corpora and describes distributing annotation layers separately when the underlying corpus cannot be distributed directly.

[sourced_fact] Study construction and protocol — Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation. The 2010 paper describes the QDAP annotation center at the University of Pittsburgh as performing annotation for hire for NLP and Political Science clients. The paper proposes an iterative annotation pipeline that selects representative text, instantiates a theory in a codebook, pilots annotation and agreement checks, scales annotation with intermediate checks, and trains and evaluates automation on held-out annotated material. The paper distinguishes corpus representativeness from category balance and describes a tradeoff between preserving natural category frequencies and obtaining enough rare-category examples for learning or theoretical analysis.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation. This 2010 methodological paper proposes procedures and illustrates tradeoffs; it does not supply a current controlled estimate of the best interface or agreement threshold. Its Figure 1 90% gate is illustrative, and later discussion says acceptable agreement depends on use and can be lower for complex tasks. Historical QDAP annotation-for-hire is not evidence of a current qualifying supplier.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation. The strongest connection to modern feedback work is that codebooks, interfaces, training and downstream use jointly define label quality. Agreement can rise through undocumented shared instructions or reconciliation without making the labels more reproducible. Confidence is high in using the paper to pose diligence questions and unmeasured for a universal numeric rule. A pilot should archive each guideline change and compare stability on fresh annotators. Controlled interface studies and downstream validation would change which recommendations merit mandatory acceptance criteria.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Aggregation, transcription and competition measurement: VLDB 2021 Crowd Science Challenge on Aggregating Crowdsourced Audio Transcriptions. ROVER aligns submitted word sequences and votes at each token, allowing an output different from every worker submission; RASA and HRRASA instead choose one submitted transcription. The shared-task dataset was constructed from normalized English Wikipedia and BookCorpus sentences, synthesized as audio with Yandex SpeechKit and transcribed on Toloka by at least five different workers per recording. Table 1 lists 9,700 training recordings with 67,900 transcriptions and 4,502 test recordings with 31,514 transcriptions; the test set is split into 1,500 public and 3,002 private recordings. The competition scores mean per-recording word accuracy, AWAcc = mean(max(0, 1−WER(r))) × 100%, using JiWER for each recording; live competition scores use the public test subset and final standings use the private subset. The authors report releasing the raw texts, baseline methods and scoring program, and link the Toloka/VLDB2021_Crowd_Science_Challenge repository. The report identifies Toloka as the platform used to collect the shared-task transcriptions and thanks the Toloka team for providing the crowdsourcing budget.

[sourced_fact] Study limitations — VLDB 2021 Crowd Science Challenge on Aggregating Crowdsourced Audio Transcriptions. Table 1 separates 9,700 training and 4,502 test recordings; section 2 instead describes 99,414 transcriptions for 9,700 recordings. The mismatch is retained, not repaired by inventing a denominator. Audio is synthesized from normalized texts, so this is not natural recorded conversational speech. AWAcc averages clipped per-recording accuracy rather than computing one corpus WER. Public and private standings use different test subsets.

[analysis] Study assessment and change conditions — VLDB 2021 Crowd Science Challenge on Aggregating Crowdsourced Audio Transcriptions. Choosing an existing transcription and constructing a token-voted transcription are different deliverables. The latter can recover useful fragments while creating an output no worker submitted. Confidence is high in that distinction and moderate in applying the shared-task lesson to similarly synthesized audio. A buyer should compare per-recording errors, rare words and cross-worker dependence, preserving the raw submissions. Natural-speech replications and independently checked reference normalization would change confidence in transfer.

[sourced_fact] Reviewed-work atlas — Visual grounding and crowd collection: WSDM Cup 2023 Challenge on Visual Question Answering. The dataset contains 45,199 question-image instances: 38,990 training, 1,705 public-test and 4,504 private-test instances. The evaluation averages intersection over union between each predicted answer box and its ground-truth box; each item IoU is the boxes intersection area divided by their union area. Toloka workers selected images containing objects they found interesting, composed questions about those objects and then marked the answering objects with bounding boxes to exclude unanswerable questions. The CodaLab competition froze its dataset before the challenge, used public-test prediction submissions during evaluation and then required container-image solutions for organizer execution on the private test set to determine winners. The authors report releasing the complete dataset and ground truth after the competition under the same CC BY license as the selected COCO image subset, with Zenodo, Hugging Face, Kaggle and GitHub release links. The Toloka Visual Question Answering Challenge takes an image and an English question and asks for a bounding box around the object answering that question.

[sourced_fact] Study result — WSDM Cup 2023 Challenge on Visual Question Answering. A separate Toloka annotation round measured non-expert human performance without providing ground truth; the report gives mean IoU of 0.87 ± 0.01 across the three dataset subsets. The winning system used a Uni-Perceiver backbone, ViT-Adapter localization and DINO prediction head with an auxiliary loss and test-time augmentation; Table 3 reports its private-test reproduction score as 76.347 on the displayed IoU ×100 scale. The starter baseline uses YOLOR to propose candidate rectangles, applies CLIP to compare the question with each bounded image region and selects the highest-similarity candidate.

A shared percentage sign is not a shared unit. Confidence is high in these distinctions and unmeasured for a universal best metric. Matched evaluations with independently accepted outputs would change the relative usefulness of each score.

Evidence IDs: [next.claim.mmlu.evaluation](evidence.html#assertion-next.claim.mmlu.evaluation), [next.claim.swebench.collection](evidence.html#assertion-next.claim.swebench.collection)

[analysis] Reasoning-data provenance has at least three separate accounting units: the original question, the generated solution trace and the verification decision. AM distinguishes reused material from its own DeepSeek-R1 responses; s1K-1.1 retains the same questions while changing traces; Light-R1 describes curriculum selection followed by generated correct/incorrect pairs. The implication is to preserve prompt-source, response-source and verification lineage separately. A new teacher response does not establish a new independent question, a human preference or a proved-correct solution. Confidence is high in these documented distinctions and unmeasured in their comparative training benefit. Item-level lineage and matched independent verification would change the uncertainty about actual coverage.

[analysis] A benchmark judge’s information boundary is part of the measured system. Chartography’s final-answer judge does not receive the chart; GDP.pdf’s criterion judge receives neither PDF nor reference answer; Harvey LAB scopes its calls to declared output files. Those observations support an audit question before interpreting scores: can the judge actually observe each fact needed for the criterion, and where is the required evidence encoded? They do not demonstrate that these judges are inaccurate. Confidence is high in treating context visibility as a protocol condition; judge error remains unmeasured here. A blinded expert study with missing-evidence, contradictory-evidence and valid alternative-output cases could validate or revise the proposed acceptance design.

[analysis] Strict task completion, partial-credit quality and repeated-attempt reliability answer different questions even within one release. ComplexConstraints separates all-criteria success from mean criterion satisfaction; Harvey LAB’s two-judge average permits a half score while its strict all_pass requires both judges; APEX-SWE separates pass@1 and pass@3 and keeps supplementary rubric scores outside its leaderboard. This supports reporting a small metric vector rather than converting every percentage to a common success rate. Confidence is high in the mathematical distinction and unknown in any cross-benchmark performance ordering. A common task population with a frozen rubric, judge context, repeat policy and failure denominator would be necessary for a narrower comparison.

[analysis] Environment packaging and completed validation are separate observations. Multi-SWE-bench documents test-transition filtering and a manual review stage; the initial Multi-SWE-RL construction omits that manual stage. Terminal-Bench documents oracle/dummy controls and exploit review while retaining residual flaws; PostTrain Arena explicitly distinguishes static source acceptance from planned dynamic checks that runs do not yet await. The analytical implication is to request evidence for each gate rather than inherit confidence from a Dockerfile or a shared construction pipeline. Confidence is high in the documented stage boundaries and unmeasured for actual task failure rates. Independent replay of the oracle, no-op controls, alternate valid solutions and exploit cases would change the buyer’s operational confidence.

[analysis] Difficulty selection changes what an absolute score represents. BrowseComp screens for difficult retrieval; AdvancedIF retains final-turn instruction failures against a supplied model; GDP.pdf requires meaningful failures by frontier models; µ-MATH intentionally selects text-only problems for judging difficulty rather than representing all U-MATH tasks. These observations support treating each as a stress distribution with an explicit selection rule. They do not yield the frequency of failure in an ordinary buyer workload or the share of a profession that can be automated. Confidence is high in that sampling limit. A prospectively sampled buyer workload, including routine and difficult cases, could establish an appropriately scoped external rate.

## 5. Provider dossiers: offerings, delivery, differentiation and limits

[method] Dossier format: offering and scope; disclosed delivery and operating model; buyer assessment and limits. Every qualifying supplier in the approved input is covered. First-party marketing is evidence of what is offered or reported, not an independently observed delivery. A named case is preserved at its actual attribution, task and date. A dossier with no named customer artifact established here is not evidence that the supplier has never delivered one. Unrecorded language, modality, security or commercial facets are unknown, not negative capabilities. Differentiation means a documented design or responsibility distinction, not a score for provider quality.

[sourced_fact] A.Team — offering and scope. Its RL engineering offer includes graders, rubrics, harnesses and rollout infrastructure. A.Team lists golden trajectories, expert data and RLHF/RFT support within post-training pipeline work. A.Team offers senior engineers to build and validate training environments, tasks and evaluations.

[sourced_fact] Prolific — offering and scope. Prolific’s AI tasker groups cover image, video, audio, comparative reasoning, fact-checking, and structured writing. Prolific offers both researcher-managed participant access and managed complete-dataset collection with multi-stage quality assurance.

Evidence IDs: [repair20261111.claim.current-reference111](evidence.html#assertion-repair20261111.claim.current-reference111), [candidate.supplier.prolific.platform-managed](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.supplier.prolific.platform-managed)

[sourced_fact] Prolific — disclosed delivery and operating model. Prolific’s pricing page reports more than 300,000 active participants and separately over one million on its waitlist. Prolific offers participants selected through verified experience or targeted assessments for AI training and evaluation tasks. The inspected research case establishes recruitment through Prolific into a researcher-owned labeling interface, rather than Prolific authorship of all study data or analysis. Prolific’s captured pricing FAQ states usual platform fees of 42.8% for corporate customers and 33.3% for academic or nonprofit customers. Prolific states minimum permitted participant rates of GBP 6 or USD 8 per hour and recommends GBP 9 or USD 12. Prolific forbids under-18 recruitment and ordinarily disallows collection of directly identifying participant information. Prolific describes identity checks, ongoing pool monitoring, in-study checks, researcher approval history, and human appeals. Prolific states ISO 27001 and Cyber Essentials certification while describing SOC 2 Type 2 as a future plan. The case reports L1 English participants in the UK or US with at least 100 completed experiments and a representative-sample option.

## 6. Dataset and benchmark landscape: provenance, versions and use limits

[method] The atlas below covers the qualifying dataset and benchmark families in the approved graph, retaining exact-release observations beneath each family. A family is an intellectual or curation identity, not a sum of files, splits, formats, subsets or every upstream component. Family roll-up supports coverage only; it does not propagate licenses, supplier roles or quality claims across versions. Construction, supervision origin, review process, task unit, access and rights are read together. A benchmark artifact can also be a dataset in ordinary usage, but this coverage calculation keeps its declared family type consistent.

[analysis] For human preference data, compare the actual judgment unit. HelpSteer3 combines task/language configurations and independent preference judgments; HelpSteer2 uses attribute ratings and a closest-rating aggregation process; HH-RLHF preserves chosen/rejected dialogue structure; WebGPT comparisons carry evidence-bearing response material and a documented label convention. A conversion to one chosen/rejected JSONL schema may be technically convenient while losing rating strength, disagreement, evidence or contributor-level independence. Preserve the source fields before transformation and document each derived training view.

[analysis] For broad text curation, the lineage unit differs from the label unit. FineWeb documents crawl lineage, filtering and per-crawl deduplication; its educational subset uses model-scored supervision. Dolma reports source-specific deduplication and residual-risk limits. Common Pile applies a distinct inclusion definition for public-domain and openly licensed sources and excludes NonCommercial and NoDerivatives material under that definition. These are contrasting curation choices, not evidence that all three corpora have the same rights or that any one eliminates every privacy or copyright risk.

[analysis] For task-rich and composite collections, preserve upstream identity and new contribution separately. DataComp distinguishes a candidate pool, a filtered dataset and training samples seen; FLAN distinguishes datasets, task categories and dataset/category tasks; MathVista combines existing datasets with new sources; MuSiQue’s human-composed questions constitute one family rather than a new family per seed source or answerability serialization. Counting all these units as independent datasets would distort both coverage and an apparent cost-per-example calculation.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — FineWeb: construction, signal and protocol. The paper-described FineWeb release is produced from 96 Common Crawl snapshots and contains about 15 trillion GPT-2-tokenized tokens. The FineWeb datasheet states that the released dataset still includes significant numbers of documents that may be toxic or harmful. The final FineWeb pipeline uses individual per-crawl MinHash deduplication. The FineWeb-Edu classifier is trained on 410,000 model-scored pages, with 50,000 held out for validation against the synthetic scores. Llama-3-70B-Instruct assigns educational-quality scores from zero to five to 460,000 sampled webpages used to develop FineWeb-Edu filtering.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — GSM8K: construction, signal and protocol. The initial thousand GSM8K problems and solutions were collected through freelance contractors on Upwork; the authors then worked with Surge AI to scale data collection. The paper describes GSM8K as math problems and natural-language solutions created by human writers, with optional GPT-3-generated seed questions available to those writers. After collection, workers re-solved GSM8K problems they had not originally written; answer disagreements were repaired or discarded, followed by another agreement check on a smaller subset. Released problems use question and answer fields; calculation annotations occur in answers and the final numeric solution follows ####. The README describes 8.5K grade-school mathematics problems created by human problem writers, segmented into 7.5K training and 1K test problems. The separate Socratic format inserts model-generated subquestions before contractor-provided solution steps; the creators say it was not used in paper experiments.

Human ratings cover helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity and verbosity on a 0-4 scale; dedicated preference labels and justifications complement the ratings. [sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — HelpSteer3: construction, signal and protocol. Each HelpSteer3-Preference sample is assigned to 3 to 5 independent human annotators for preference feedback. Postprocessing retains the three most agreeing preference annotations and excludes samples when their remaining disagreement is greater than two preference-strength points. The pinned collection contains Preference, Feedback, Edit, Edit-Quality and Principle configurations. Preference contains 40,476 samples with pairwise preference scores and individual concise reasons; card specifies a 95%/5% train/validation split.

HotpotQA creators ask MTurk workers to write questions requiring reasoning over introductions of two Wikipedia articles. [sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Human Preference Dataset (HPD/HPS): construction, signal and protocol. HPD v2 reports about 798k pairwise comparisons over 430k images/107k prompts, including 645k training pairs and 153k test pairs. HPD v2 asks human annotators to rank images generated by different models for the same prompt. HPD v2 sources prompts from DiffusionDB and MSCOCO Captions and cleans DiffusionDB prompts with ChatGPT. [analysis] Dataset-family atlas — Magpie: version, rights and buyer interpretation. The Pro-300K-Filtered card revision 523df96eb7474e97bca6f378b3baa372a4735fcc and repository commit b734a36818e4ba7ef7f0f582fc55f7e860407d26 make separate declarations about different materials. This report does not harmonize llama3, a noncommercial data badge and a software license into one governing dataset license. Confidence is high that the inspected labels differ and unestablished for the legal permission governing a buyer’s exact payload. Obtain the applicable dataset instrument and upstream conditions for the intended use; neither a code license nor a top-level badge establishes all corpus rights.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — MuSiQue: construction, signal and protocol. MuSiQue README says its questions are composed from SQuAD, T-REx, Natural Questions, MLQA and Zero Shot RE seed questions. MuSiQue uses MTurk workers to write coherent new multi-hop questions from DAGs of source single-hop questions after checking bridge-entity identity. MuSiQue downloads contain train/dev/test for answerable and full configurations plus dev/test source single-hop IDs. MuSiQue authors selected 17 workers after a 100-worker, 20-example qualification round and sampled 10–20 examples per worker across nine annotation batches. MuSiQue says its model-development raw format differs from official released data only in field names/format, not qualitative content.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Nectar: construction, signal and protocol. The card describes Nectar response rankings as GPT-4-generated seven-way comparisons. The good_natured prompt label is parsed from GPT-4 classification and is described as an approximation. The ranking rubric prioritizes harmlessness and also helpfulness for prompts classified as good natured. The card reports 182,954 prompts with seven responses per prompt.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — NuminaMath: construction, signal and protocol. NuminaMath-CoT collects problems and reference solutions from exam PDFs and mathematics forums before OCR, translation and CoT processing. NuminaMath uses GPT-4o to translate and realign extracted solutions into CoT format with final-answer formatting. Some NuminaMath World Olympiad PDFs were manually segmented before OCR. NuminaMath reports exact-match and embedding decontamination with exceptions for MATH training and synthetic data. NuminaMath acknowledges challenges validating synthetic problem correctness and incomplete CoT detail on hard problems. The NuminaMath-CoT card declares Apache License 2.0.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — OpenAI Summarize from Feedback: construction, signal and protocol. The OpenAI repository reports 64,832 TL;DR summary comparisons plus TL;DR comparison/Likert evaluation and CNN/DM Likert evaluations. The repository reserves valid2 labels for final evaluation because valid1 posts/articles were used for model selection. Summary comparisons are JSONL records of two summaries with choice, worker, batch and split metadata. The comparison note fields contain worker-written naive interpretations before seeing the post, with possible later edits.

[analysis] Dataset-family atlas — OpenAssistant Conversations (OASST1 reviewed release): workflow separation. A separately inspected OpenAssistant project-guidelines document at commit f1e6ed9526f5817531f3ab85441a40b3671ddccb distinguishes writing assistant replies and user prompts/replies, classifying replies and ranking replies, with factual accuracy and helpfulness prioritized in classification/ranking. This is a normative document workflow without a dataset-family, collection-release or parent identity edge. It is not established as the operating protocol of the April 2023 OASST1 snapshot and does not establish annotator compliance. A buyer needing that historical provenance would require a dated release-to-protocol record and collection logs.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — OpenR1-Math: construction, signal and protocol. OpenR1-Math card metadata lists 225,129 all, 93,733 default and 131,396 extended training examples. OpenR1-Math describes prompting R1 on 400k source problems with two solutions per problem, sometimes four, and a 16k token generation limit. [sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Pick-a-Pic: construction, signal and protocol. Pick-a-Pic collects real users’ prompts and preferences over two generated images, allowing a tie. Pick-a-Pic paper identifies Stable Diffusion2.1, Dreamlike Photoreal2.0 and Stable Diffusion XL variants as image generators. Pick-a-Pic reports user authentication, activity monitoring, bans and NSFW phrase filters as data-quality controls. Pick-a-Pic paper forms validation/test data from unique-user prompts and excludes their prompts from training. Pick-a-Pic creator distinguishes original v1 data from v2 with more than one million examples. PickScore repository MIT terms apply to software and associated documentation.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — PKU-SafeRLHF: construction, signal and protocol. The card defines 19 harm categories and labels each question-answer pair with one or more categories. The card describes 83.4K preference entries with two responses per question, safety meta-labels, and separate human-preference dimensions of helpfulness and harmlessness. Helpfulness and harmlessness are ranked separately, with harmless responses always ranked above harmful responses in the harmlessness ranking. The documented responses come from Alpaca-7B, Alpaca2-7B and Alpaca3-8B; the latter two are described as Llama2-7B and Llama3-8B fine-tuned with Alpaca 52K.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — PRISM Alignment Dataset: construction, signal and protocol. PRISM participants complete a demographic/preference survey, then write prompts, rate LLM responses and give fine-grained conversational feedback. PRISM terms prohibit re-identification and warn that raw conversations can be unsafe or offensive. PRISM randomly selects four of 21 backend LLMs for the opening turn and asks participants to score responses from 1 to 100. PRISM utterance JSONL is a long-format presentation of the same conversations and repeats user inputs across candidate responses. PRISM reports 8,011 conversation trees and 68,371 rated human-prompt/model-response/score utterances.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — PRM800K: construction, signal and protocol. The paper describes the full unfiltered PRM800K release as 1,085,590 step-level labels over 101,599 solutions; the filtered training data contains about 800,000 labels over 75,000 solutions. Human labelers provide positive, negative or neutral judgments on steps in model-generated MATH solutions. The repository documents a nonstandard MATH split adding 4,500 original test problems to training and evaluating on the remaining 500 held-out problems. PRM800K is documented as 800,000 step-level correctness labels on model-generated solutions to MATH problems. The README describes human step ratings of -1, 0 or +1 and permits a human-written replacement step in phase 1 when all completions were rated -1. The documented annotation schema reserves common gold-labeled solutions for quality control and 30 initial screening questions for base task performance.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — ProsocialDialog: construction, signal and protocol. ProsocialDialog reports 58K dialogues, 331K utterances, 160K unique rules of thumb and 497K safety labels with free-form rationales. ProsocialDialog creator repo says HF dataframe and direct list-of-dialogues downloads differ only in format and contain the same content. ProsocialDialog creates new dialogues by having GPT-3 generate unsafe utterances and crowdworkers write prosocial responses. ProsocialDialog schema keeps final safety verdicts, three workers raw safety annotations and each workers free-form reasons. ProsocialDialog source field identifies socialchemistry, SBIC, ethics_amt and ethics_reddit seed text origins.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — RichHF-18K: construction, signal and protocol. RichHF-18K reports 17,760 TensorFlow Examples: 15,810 training, 995 development and 955 test. RichHF-18K annotates generated images from Pick-a-Pic v1 and ships filenames rather than original image files. RichHF-18K releases newly collected subjective scores, human-labeled artifact heatmaps and prompt misalignment-token labels. RichHF examples contain filename, four scalar scores, artifact_map, misalignment_map and prompt_misalignment_label. RichHF defines all scores so higher is better; a higher artifact score means fewer artifacts.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Self-Instruct: construction, signal and protocol. The filtered GPT-3 davinci Self-Instruct corpus in this paper contains 52,445 instructions and 82,439 input/output instances. Self-Instruct starts with 175 author-written seed tasks and prompts the language model to generate further instructions and input/output instances. A single expert coauthor evaluates one randomly selected instance for each of 200 randomly sampled instructions; Table2 reports 54% with all fields valid.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Social Bias Inference Corpus (SBIC): construction, signal and protocol. SBIC reports 82.4% pairwise agreement and average Krippendorff alpha of 0.45. SBIC adds structured categorical and free-text bias-implication annotations to social-media posts, with over 150k annotations and over 34k implications in its summary. SBIC splits posts together with their three annotation sets to keep a post from appearing across train/validation/test. SBIC card describes three MTurk annotations per post, with conditional target-group questions and two-to-four written stereotypes per selected group.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Stanford Alpaca: construction, signal and protocol. The Alpaca datasheet reports 52,002 instances and defines instruction, optional input, and text-davinci-003 output fields. Stanford Alpaca modifies Self-Instruct by using text-davinci-003 and generating one instance per instruction. The Alpaca datasheet says all 52K examples were used for its models and recommends no dataset split.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Super-NaturalInstructions: construction, signal and protocol. Natural Instructions documents a community effort to create tasks and natural-language definitions/instructions. The contribution instructions require JSON formatting tests and a maximum of 6.5K instances per task. The official benchmark split trains on a subset of tasks and evaluates remaining unseen tasks for cross-task generalization.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — ToxicChat: construction, signal and protocol. ToxicChat adds toxicity annotations to about 10K user prompts from the Vicuna demo through a human-AI collaborative annotation framework. [sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — UltraInteract: construction, signal and protocol. The pinned pairwise distribution declares 219,522 training examples with trajectory, chosen, rejected, id and parent_id fields. The card reports approximately 86K instructions, 286K correct answers and 219K preference pairs. Correct actions and correct-ending trajectories are described as SFT material; paired correct and incorrect nodes or trajectories support preference learning. UltraInteract is documented as reasoning preference trees combining reasoning chains, environment interaction trajectories, critique and pairwise data.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — WebGPT Comparisons: construction, signal and protocol. WebGPT quotes fields store model-found browsing extracts and source-page titles, while answers are composed using those quotes. WebGPT examples pair model answers to a question with human preference scores. WebGPT score_0 ranges from -1 to 1, sums to zero with score_1, uses zero as a soft 50% label and other scores by sign as hard labels. The WebGPT card describes all comparisons marked suitable for reward modeling by project end, totaling 19,578 comparisons. WebGPT token fields use GPT-2 tokenization of a truncated question-plus-quotes prefix and final answer completion for reward modeling.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — WildChat: construction, signal and protocol. WildChat collects human user conversations by offering free GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 access. The reviewed WildChat-1M variant removes conversations flagged toxic by OpenAI Moderation or Detoxify. WildChat de-identifies data using Microsoft Presidio and author-written rules. WildChat uses ODC-BY, whose license does not cover independent rights in individual database contents. WildChat documents empty user inputs that can cause hallucinated assistant responses.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — WildJailbreak: construction, signal and protocol. WildJailbreak transforms vanilla harmful prompts with 2–7 mined tactics using Mixtral-8×7B/GPT-4, filters low-risk/off-topic results and reuses counterpart vanilla refusals. WildJailbreak separately documents 210 adversarial benign and 2,000 adversarial harmful evaluation examples. WildJailbreak training schema exposes vanilla, adversarial, tactics, completion and four-way data_type fields. WildJailbreak describes 262K synthetic vanilla/adversarial prompt-response pairs with both harmful and superficially harmful-looking benign queries. WildJailbreak uses GPT-4 for vanilla harmful/benign prompts and GPT-3.5 for refusal or complying responses. The 262K figure is rounded card prose; the metadata category 100M<n<1B conflicts and is not used as an observed count. Only the pinned public documentation was inspected, without gated corpus bytes or established payload release identity.
