[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — AgentBench: construction, signal and protocol. For the Mind2Web browsing component, the reported primary metric is step success from element/action matching rather than whole-task success; this paper uses top-10 candidates and CoT few-shot prompts. The initial AgentBench paper defines eight environment families: operating systems, databases, knowledge graphs, digital card games, lateral-thinking puzzles, house-holding, web shopping and web browsing. For OS tasks, about half of instructions are human-created or collected; the other half are mainly GPT-4-generated QA tasks filtered by execution-based checks. Eight programming annotators select and construct human tasks.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — AlpacaEval: construction, signal and protocol. The release documents about 20K human preference annotations, including 2.5K cross-annotations from four annotators over roughly 650 examples. AlpacaEval 2.0 uses weighted_alpaca_eval_gpt4_turbo as annotator with gpt4_turbo reference outputs; the original uses alpaca_eval_gpt4 with text_davinci_003. Length-controlled win rates fit a preference model including output-length difference and average counterfactual preferences at zero length difference.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — GAIA: construction, signal and protocol. The October 2025 GAIA format update replaces former JSONL-backed loading with Parquet splits and per-level views. GAIA describes more than 450 questions divided into three levels, with public validation/dev and tests having private answers and metadata. GAIA preserves task_id, Question, Level, Final answer, file_name, file_path and Annotator Metadata columns, with relative attachment paths. GAIA is documented as evaluating LLMs augmented with tools, prompting and search access. The pinned commit identifies documentation, not a verified corpus-byte release. Private answer values and payload row counts were not accessed or established.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — GPQA: construction, signal and protocol. The creator baseline code instructions distinguish closed-book prompting from Bing-based retrieval modes and expose a seed for shuffling answer choices. GPQA questions are written by domain experts in biology, physics and chemistry, with experts defined as people having or pursuing a PhD in the field. The original study describes 546 Extended questions, 448 main questions and 198 Diamond questions, with the latter two curated subsets. The collection pipeline uses first expert validation, writer revision, second expert validation and three non-expert validators from other domains with web access but no LM assistants.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — HarmBench: construction, signal and protocol. HarmBench evaluates whether each completion instantiates its corresponding behavior using separate text and multimodal classifier models. The HarmBench protocol uses max_new_tokens=512 for target completions and warns other limits can hinder comparisons. HarmBench accepts a behavior-dataset CSV and saves test cases under method/experiment directories with optional behavior-ID selection. HarmBench evaluates attack success rate through test-case generation, target-model completions and completion evaluation.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — HumanEval: construction, signal and protocol. HumanEval computes per-problem pass@k estimates from generated-sample counts and correct counts, then averages only when each problem has at least k samples. HumanEval predictions are JSONL records with task_id and completion-only text excluding the prompt. The pinned HumanEval evaluation function defaults to k=[1,10,100], four workers and a three-second correctness timeout. The OpenAI repository identifies HumanEval as a hand-written evaluation set with a harness for problem solving.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Humanity’s Last Exam: construction, signal and protocol. The documented simple evaluation defaults to temperature zero and advises at least 8,192 completion tokens for reasoning models. The pinned evaluator defaults to o3-mini-2025-01-31 and asks the judge to extract the final answer and compare it with the provided correct answer. [method] Atlas interpretation: a source can document a dataset’s declared license, retained record count or human-checking procedure without this study inspecting every row or reproducing a training run. Unknown or restrictive licensing is a catalogue finding rather than an instruction to retrieve or redistribute the corpus. Empty taxonomy facets remain unknown. A release’s disclosed aggregate count can coexist with a README/example inconsistency; both are retained instead of silently manufacturing a reconciled number.

[analysis] Reference-label provenance should accompany benchmark protocol. The label-error study uses model screening followed by five-worker judgments and distinguishes ambiguous or unknown cases from correctable alternatives. Gilardi evaluates only texts on which two trained annotators agree; HelpSteer2 removes remaining high-spread responses. These are different decisions about which items enter a score. A buyer should retain the original denominator, review-selection rule and accepted reference rather than compare the resulting percentages as if they measured the same difficulty distribution.

[analysis] A paper’s dataset statistics are evidence about its described release, rather than independent confirmation of a current download. Aya separates original annotations from re-annotations and imposes a language inclusion threshold. WildChat v1 contains two unreconciled conversation totals, which this synthesis preserves. These additional paper reviews do not add another dataset family here. A future artifact inspection should bind the exact bytes, reconcile paper/card/repository counts and preserve component lineage before changing family or release accounting.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Polymath Horizon-SWE: construction and protocol. The creator distinguishes Horizon-SWE-PF (pass/fail), requiring complete feature and deployment checks, from Horizon-SWE-PC (partial credit), weighted 60% feature correctness, 30% deployment/DevOps and 10% engineering quality. The creator protocol combines verifiable feature/deployment checks with model-based engineering-quality assessment and describes concrete failure patterns. Horizon-SWE describes 50 tasks in a running containerized application with synthetic traffic and an MCP tool surface.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.mandatory19.cohort4.benchmark.horizon-swe.two-score-views](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.mandatory19.cohort4.benchmark.horizon-swe.two-score-views), [candidate.mandatory19.cohort4.benchmark.horizon-swe.verification-boundary](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.mandatory19.cohort4.benchmark.horizon-swe.verification-boundary), [candidate.mandatory19.revision001.horizon-swe.running-application](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.mandatory19.revision001.horizon-swe.running-application)

[analysis] Benchmark-family atlas — Polymath Horizon-SWE: assessment and access boundaries. Fifty running-application tasks define one family, with strict PF and weighted PC views. A buyer should retain the 60/30/10 component breakdown and inspect feature/deployment checks separately from model-rated engineering quality. Confidence is high in the documented scoring distinction and unestablished for reproducibility of private payloads. Obtain the executed task/harness manifest, judge calibration and project rights before accepting the service as a matched benchmark. Source-code commit history is not a contributor headcount, and synthetic traffic is not naturally observed customer activity.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Toloka Visual Question Answering / WSDMCup2023: construction and protocol. The paper describes crowd workers choosing interesting objects/images, composing English questions and drawing the answer bounding boxes from scratch on a CC-BY COCO image subset. The challenge scores predicted bounding boxes with mean intersection-over-union; its paper separately reports a crowd baseline and annotation agreement using a 1-IoU distance. The paper explicitly checked overlap with COCO boxes and placed overlapping cases in the training set, then released the same complete dataset with ground truth through Zenodo, Hugging Face, Kaggle and GitHub. The paper says the complete question/box dataset was released under the same CC-BY license as its chosen COCO image subset. The creator challenge paper describes 45,199 image-question-box instances: 38,990 train, 1,705 public test and 4,504 private test.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Regulated Advice Bench: construction and protocol. The card reports tax nominal alpha 0.628 on 318 doubly read items including 58 ties excluded from release, and legal alpha 0.714 on 257 doubly judged items including ties. The pinned card states CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 for this release. The full annotation policies are not included. The summarized tax policy follows UK, German and French reserved-advice rules with a protective default elsewhere; native speakers audited sample sets of automated translations. The card describes synthetic dialogue pairs followed by regulatory expert review of English replies: four tax reviewers and five legal reviewers, with two per item where possible, blind to the AI label. Regulated Advice Bench has 338 tax items expanded to 3,042 language rows and 332 legal items expanded to 2,988 rows; each item’s nine translations share a label.

[analysis] Benchmark-family atlas — Regulated Advice Bench: assessment and rights boundaries. The family contains tax/legal configurations and translated manifestations of 670 English-labeled items. Resample by item_id rather than treating 6,030 rows as independent judgments. The alpha denominators include excluded ties and differ from released-item counts. Confidence is high in these units and low in treating the labels as global professional advice standards. A buyer should obtain the full intended policy, qualified local review and translation-specific checks; private policies and inherited English verdicts prevent a universal legal-validity claim. CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 is a release-specific declaration, not blanket upstream permission.

[analysis] Family counting and technical discussion answer different questions. This graph counts 85 dataset families and 87 benchmark families. A named derived collection can be distinct without disjoint source examples: the Flan Collection and xP3 disclose reuse and transformation of upstream tasks, while Chatbot Arena Conversations is defined by paired conversations and human winner votes rather than the single-model LMSYS-Chat-1M schema. Neither the 17 added paper works nor each release/configuration automatically adds a family. HCAST is a benchmark; SWAA is a named dataset task collection; the METR time-horizon lineage is a composite evaluation protocol with overlapping inputs. Versions, translated rows, submixtures, internal groups and public/private subsets remain components, not added families. Current source-backed identity dispositions do not erase earlier holds or establish example-disjointness.

[analysis] Benchmark selection and independent unit. GDP.pdf and Chartography select tasks after model failures; MMRB2 filters model-judge agreement and then human disagreement; Regulated Advice Bench translates one English-labeled item into nine rows. A representative denominator, an adversarial challenge denominator and a repeated-presentation denominator are all useful but answer different questions. Confidence is high that these selection rules must accompany scores and unestablished for their prevalence in a buyer’s workload. Report item-level and participant-level grouping, not only row count, and use an independently drawn target-work sample before estimating operational success.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Chatbot Arena Conversations: construction, signal and protocol. Chatbot Arena Conversations contains cleaned conversations with pairwise human preferences. Chatbot Arena Conversations was collected on Chatbot Arena from April to June 2023. Chatbot Arena Conversations includes toxic tags generated by T5 and RoBERTa taggers trained on manually labeled data. Chatbot Arena Conversations intentionally retains unsafe conversations alongside moderation tags. Chatbot Arena user prompts are CC-BY-4.0, while model outputs are CC-BY-NC-4.0. The card describes terms-based consent and best-effort PII removal while deliberately retaining unsafe conversations with automated moderation and toxicity tags. Arena users converse with two anonymous models, vote their preferences and then see model identities; the platform was free, open without registration and did not pay users. The associated paper documents position, verbosity and reasoning limitations of LLM judging, with mitigation experiments and separate crowd/expert agreement samples. The pinned Chatbot Arena Conversations card describes 33,000 paired conversations from April–June 2023, with 20 model identities and a 13,383-user table.

[analysis] Dataset-family atlas — ELOQUENT Preference Prediction: buyer assessment and change conditions. Preference prediction and explanation generation should be accepted as separate deliverables. Accuracy, lexical similarity, embedding similarity and a judge rank cannot substitute for one another. Confidence is moderate in using the task to compare these outputs and low in treating its labels as universal consensus. A buyer should resolve the field schema, collect repeated independent judgments and verify explanation support. Those records would change the QA assessment.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — SWAA task collection: construction, signal and protocol. Software Atomic Actions (SWAA) consists of 66 short tasks representing software-engineering actions under one minute, using multiple-choice decisions and fill-in-the-blank completion questions. SWAA’s authors wrote an initial 71 tasks without seeing AI attempts or running models on the developing tasks, then retained 66 after excluding tasks that more than one human baseliner failed. SWAA human baselines were collected from internal employees with relevant expertise using a custom web application, with four baselines per decision task and three per fill-in-the-blank task. The time-horizon paper credits Thomas Kwa with leading SWAA task development and Amy Deng with creating most SWAA tasks and collecting their human baselines and AI agent results.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — SWAA task collection: interpretation boundaries. Despite its retained benchmark-prefixed inventory ID, the semantic entity is a dataset task collection. Its five internal groups and 71 preliminary tasks are components; 66 survive the human-failure filter. Internal-employee timing excludes context acquisition, decision tasks permit one choice and fill-in tasks permit repeated attempts. Development was blind to AI task performance, with separate prompt-development tasks.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — The Flan Collection: construction, signal and protocol. FLAN v2 compiles Flan 2021, P3, Super-NaturalInstructions and additional datasets into mixed zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought templates. FLAN downloadable submixtures can be filtered by template_type or task_name and combined at specified mixture rates. FLAN v2 names flan, t0, niv2, cot and dialog submixtures with prompt varieties controlling shots and answer options. The expanded Flan Collection combines prior instruction-task collections with prompt variants, input inversions and mixture weighting; the released example defines five principal submixtures. The paper studies mixed prompt formats, task scaling, input inversion and source balancing using T5-XL and held-in, CoT and held-out MMLU/BBH evaluations. The v2 README explicitly omits several tasks for legal constraints and excludes the Program Synthesis submixture, while the paper’s described recipe includes program-synthesis data.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — xP3: construction, signal and protocol. The xP3 card reports 78,883,588 samples in merged language JSONL files. xP3 defines inputs as the natural-language model input and targets as the natural-language generation target. The xP3mt variant uses prompts in 20 languages machine-translated from English. The xP3 family table identifies xP3 as 13 training tasks in 46 languages with English prompts. The pinned xP3 card distinguishes 13 training task types in 46 languages from the evaluation-inclusive 16-task variant, machine-translated-prompt variant and processed training format. The paper’s rank-classification evaluations use five random prompts and median per-language scores; it notes unintentional exposure to supposedly unseen languages, limited language coverage and shorter-generation bias after multitask fine-tuning. The xP3 card’s language table reports sample and kilobyte totals computed from merged language files. The paper extends P3 with multilingual supervised datasets and uses English prompts for xP3, while xP3mt machine-translates prompts for monolingual datasets.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — APEX-Accounting: construction, signal and protocol. The primary paper describes 42 accounting contributors, median 11 and mean 12.6 years of experience, constructing month-end-close work under U.S. GAAP accrual accounting. The paper grades binary rubric criteria with a DeepSeek-v4-Flash judge calibrated against 1,687 majority-vote expert criterion labels from 120 trajectories. The pinned Harbor edition renders the same ten public APEX-Accounting development tasks in one simulated company world; its card separately describes a closed 160-task, ten-world benchmark. The paper selected eleven difficult worlds from a 599-candidate-task pool using frontier-model scores; the ten hardest worlds became the closed benchmark and the eleventh supplied the public development set. It removed 24 incomplete-information tasks.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — APEX-Accounting: interpretation boundaries. The closed v2 paper has 160 tasks, while the separately captured leaderboard says 100 tasks and 1,475 criteria and calls k=4 canonical. The paper uses Mean Criteria@3. Neither counts nor metrics are harmonized here. The ten-task Harbor dev sample uses static exports and a different default judge/template; its tightened criteria and CC-BY sample terms do not make its scores comparable with the closed leaderboard.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — APEX-Agents: construction, signal and protocol. The original paper describes 256 professional contributors and expert-built workplace worlds; each task has an expert-authored prompt, outcome rubric and golden output. The original paper evaluates criterion judgments against 747 human labels across 60 tasks and reports 98.5% judge agreement on that calibration. The original protocol distinguishes average single-attempt task success, any-of-eight success and all-eight consistency; release 1.1 introduces expert audits and judge changes intended to reduce scattergunning and ambiguity. APEX-Agents 1.1 has 240 tasks across 31 worlds and 955 binary criteria, with 80 tasks in each of investment banking, law and management consulting; the original paper describes 480 tasks across 33 worlds.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — APEX-v1: construction, signal and protocol. For APEX-v1.0, Mercor sourced experienced professionals, interviewed them for 30-45 minutes, and paid selected experts to complete a 1-2 hour prompt-and-rubric assessment before successful applicants were contracted. APEX-v1.0 experts first described 3-5 common daily-work tasks and their required seniority, then used that workflow input to create prompts and find or create supporting evidence sources. The original APEX-v1.0 paper describes a closed heldout evaluation set and publishes four example prompts with rubrics that were created by the same expert group under the same instructions but are outside that heldout set. The paper's original APEX-v1.0 collection has 200 cases, 50 each for investment banking, management consulting, law and medicine, created and reviewed by industry experts. APEX-v1.0 reviews prompts before contributors write the corresponding rubrics, then reviews those rubrics through potentially multiple rounds; 200 of 300 started prompts were approved for the final collection.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — BenchFlow SkillsBench: construction, signal and protocol. The paper acknowledges missing length-matched context controls, limited model/harness coverage, nondeterminism and contamination risks when interpreting skill gains. SkillsBench compares the same agent/model with and without reusable task skills; the original paper averages five binary-reward trials per task over a fixed 84-task denominator. The paper and pinned contributor protocol require outcome verifiers, passing reference solutions, human-written prompts, reusable skills and review for task realism, leakage and environment problems.

[analysis] Benchmark-family atlas — CharXiv: buyer assessment and change conditions. Four descriptive questions plus one reasoning question per chart create nested observations rather than independent new images. Confidence is high that chart grouping and known-label errors must remain visible and moderate in task relevance. A buyer should inspect unanswerable questions and source-chart-dependent mistakes with independent experts. Reconciled counts, corrected answers and a new-chart holdout would change measurement confidence.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — ClawsBench: construction, signal and protocol. The paper evaluates a ragged set of model-harness and skills/meta-prompt conditions with five repeats, reporting 7,224 completed main trials after infrastructure losses. The paper explicitly limits interpretation because services omit latency, rate limits and concurrent access, there is no human baseline, evaluation is single-shot and the design has incomplete factorial coverage. ClawsBench uses 44 tasks across five mock productivity services, with 20 performance tasks and 24 safety tasks; grading compares service state before and after the attempt.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Comprehensive Verilog Design Problems (CVDP): construction, signal and protocol. The v1 paper limits tasks to oracle contexts with minimal relevant information, and describes Docker-based harnesses using open-source EDA tools where possible while some design-verification tasks require Cadence Xcelium. The pinned creator README reports adoption of CVDP by the Silicon Integration Initiative’s LLM Benchmarking Coalition, describing extensions to categories and design domains, refinement of metrics, and maintenance of a leaderboard. The v1 paper reports 783 retained problems across thirteen task categories, partitioned into 617 Non-Agentic and 166 Agentic problems. The v1 paper explicitly thanks Turing for collaboration in developing the benchmark dataset and Cadence for providing EDA tool licenses that enabled collection of digital-verification datapoints.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Comprehensive Verilog Design Problems (CVDP): access and version observations. The pinned dataset license distinguishes non-code material under CC BY 4.0 from original code under Apache 2.0 and says third-party-derived components may carry different upstream terms; its NOTICE lists the VGA-controller and Brent–Kung-adder components with no specified license. The pinned creator README says twenty datapoints were omitted from the initial public release because of harness issues and licensing restrictions, and that reference outputs and agentic patches were excluded from that initial release to mitigate contamination. The pinned dataset changelog describes v1.1.0 as adding context-heavy agentic tasks with public Git bundles, changing simulation tooling and recalibrating three datapoints; it also records earlier harness fixes and a split into commercial and non-commercial variants.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — DAYJOB: construction, signal and protocol. The pinned cross-domain harness README instead documents a 0–1 trial reward, a task mean over five nonerrored attempts, and an unweighted mean across tasks in a domain. The finance and healthcare cards use 100% rubric satisfaction for a task pass, whereas the tax card states a 95% criterion threshold and published pass@1. The finance and tax cards describe professionals authoring assignments and three review layers for correctness, completeness and solvability; tax materials include synthetic documents modeled on practice. DAYJOB explicitly identifies itself as one benchmark family. Its finance card describes 80 full tasks and three samples, healthcare 50 full tasks and three samples, and tax 50 full tasks and two samples. The README specifies Harbor/OpenHands-based execution, an agent-phase allowlist for model API hosts and pinned OpenCode/rewardkit grading dependencies; cards reserve the tasks for held-out evaluation.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — GeneBench-Pro: construction, signal and protocol. The reported task setup gives an agent an isolated workspace, staged files, a minimum viable prompt defining the scientific question and target estimand, and an output schema, while leaving the analysis workflow for the agent to recover. The paper reports 3 to 13 substantive inferential decision points per problem, with a median of 6. The paper’s synthetic DRX1 carrier-screening example requires three linked stages: reportable carrier calling, calibration of assay performance and risk assembly using residual carrier risk and the full partner roster. The paper reports an external scientific reviewer pool of 11 domain experts spanning graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, industry scientists and professors. The paper reports external review of 84 candidate problems: 82 were included in the 129-problem evaluation, and two reviewed candidates were withdrawn for fatal issues. The reported external-review workflow gave reviewers private repositories for assigned problems, containing the prompt and data, a detailed design report, validation materials and an issue thread for feedback.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — GeneBench-Pro: protocol continuation. Table 2 reports that external review identified a genetic-correlation reference implementation presented as LDSC that used incorrect M and OLS rather than WLS, and that the reference implementation was fixed to implement LDSC. The paper describes fully simulated problems and states that prompts tell agents the data came from a real experiment; the pinned public creator card instead quotes task provenance as uncertain and instructs scientific judgement. The pinned creator card states that reference answers and grading tolerances are intentionally public for case studies, reproducibility and model-analysis examples, rather than a hidden-answer leaderboard. The pinned creator card describes problems.csv as the one-row-per-problem inventory, manifest.json as containing per-problem paths, SHA-256 hashes and sizes, and checksums.sha256 as package-wide integrity information. The pinned creator card lists ten public case studies and describes each problem directory as containing an eval configuration, staged agent-visible data files and a public scientific report PDF.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — GeneBench-Pro: protocol continuation. The pinned creator card describes a Python 3.10-or-newer reference grader whose passed boolean is the authoritative grading decision and whose score is only a diagnostic summary of graded fields. The paper defines grading ground truth as the quantity recoverable from agent-visible data, rather than the hidden parameter used to generate those data; it gives the estimate produced by the correct analysis as an example. The paper says the Artificial Analysis subset prioritized relatively difficult tasks and that release-visibility and external-review strata were not randomized. The paper describes a tiered 129-problem release: ten public problem packages, 50 additional held-out problems provided to Artificial Analysis for third-party benchmarking, and 69 retained internally. The paper reports that external-review findings led to prompt clarifications or data-file changes for minor issues, and DGP or ground-truth changes, redesign or withdrawal for more substantive issues; corrected candidates returned through agent pilots and trace examination.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — GeneBench-Pro: protocol continuation. The GeneBench-Pro paper reports 129 evaluations across 10 primary domains and 21 terminal subdomains for multistage analysis in genomics, quantitative biology and translational biomedicine. The paper describes GeneBench-Pro problems as constructively simulated, with the full data-generating process simulated so that graded endpoints are recoverable from staged data. The paper describes checking plausible wrong decisions through ablations, reviewing scientific validity, methodology and target identifiability, and iterating frontier-model pilots and trace analyses to look for leakage, unintended solution paths, prompt-grader mismatch and robustness problems.

[analysis] Benchmark-family atlas — GeneBench-Pro: buyer assessment and change conditions. Target identifiability and wrong-method ablations are strong questions for scientific-task QA. Public case studies are useful for explanation but should not be presented as a hidden-answer leaderboard. Confidence is high in that separation and moderate in the documented validation design. Real-data workflow validation and audited target recovery would change confidence.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — HCAST: construction, signal and protocol. HCAST baseliners commit work to a repository and record screens and spoken work through Loom; the authors manually review most successful baselines, prioritizing unusual times and disagreement among attempts. HCAST recruited technical human baseliners mainly through METR employees’ professional networks and required the large majority to pass domain-specific qualification tasks before main-suite work. Each HCAST task supplies instructions, a container where the agent runs as the agent user, and a scoring function running as root; continuously scored tasks are binarized at heuristically chosen success thresholds. HCAST’s author-assigned contamination categories include 125 tasks with private solutions, 31 with public solutions judged hard to memorize, and 33 with public solutions judged easy to memorize. HCAST’s contribution statement credits Chris Canal and Daniel O’Connell with helping manage task QA/testing and baselining, and its byline identifies both with Equistamp. HCAST v1 contains 189 individually created tasks: METR employees and contractors created 143, while 46 came through its independent-contributor task bounty.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — HCAST: protocol continuation. HCAST combines fresh-human task testing with manually reviewed agent attempts: an unexposed person attempts a task in most task families, and reviewers read all 945 transcripts from five agent attempts on each of the 189 tasks. The HCAST v1 human reference comprises 563 attempts by 140 people, including 341 successful attempts; 110 tasks use the geometric mean of successful baseline times, and 79 use forecasts by a task creator or familiar author. HCAST’s appendix task-family summaries were generated by claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219 from task code, tracked metadata truncated to 10,000 characters, and descriptive information supplied by task authors. HCAST reports paying baseliners $50–100 per hour plus $25–150 per hour in performance bonuses; Appendix E.2.1 defines a successful-completion bonus of (r/2)×t, where r is the baseliner’s hourly rate and t is the average time spent on that task by all baseliners.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — HCAST: interpretation boundaries. The 78 internal setup/scoring groups are components of one 189-task benchmark. Of 563 human attempts by 140 people, 341 succeed; 110 task times use successful geometric means and 79 use forecasts, including 50 with no collected baseline. Humans receive some extra web access and exact thresholds. The public eleven-family subset is marked deprecated; its MIT terms do not expose the withheld whole. Affiliated authors’ QA roles do not establish an organizational supplier contract.

[analysis] Benchmark-family atlas — HCAST: buyer assessment and change conditions. Human calibration is a measurement process with incentives, corrections and missingness. Confidence is high in separating observed successful times from forecasts and moderate in task-specific horizon use. A buyer should retain unsuccessful attempts and the exact human/agent information difference, then measure new long tasks. Independently recorded baselines and representative workload sampling would change confidence.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — HealthBench: construction, signal and protocol. The v1 paper describes HealthBench Consensus as 3,671 base examples with positive consensus criteria, drawn from 34 predefined criteria that are assigned only when more than half of raters and at least two physicians agree that they apply. The v1 paper is authored under OpenAI and releases HealthBench through OpenAI’s simple-evals repository; its acknowledgments name physician collaborators and contributors while explicitly saying their inclusion does not imply endorsement. The v1 paper reports 5,000 single- or multi-turn conversation examples with 48,562 unique rubric criteria, organized into seven conversation themes and five behavior axes. The v1 paper selects HealthBench Hard by scoring base examples across five model providers, excluding examples with no positive score from any model, and taking the 1,000 examples with the lowest average score.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — HealthBench: access and version observations. The immutable simple-evals README lists HealthBench with an MIT license link and states that, from July 2025, the repository will retain reference implementations while no longer updating model or benchmark results; the primary paper asks that benchmark examples not be redistributed online to reduce leakage.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.normal18.healthbench.family.release-terms-and-maintenance](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.normal18.healthbench.family.release-terms-and-maintenance)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — HealthBench: interpretation boundaries. The 5,000 conversations and 48,562 rubric criteria are source-reported units. Consensus and Hard are base-set variations, not new families. Consensus review of 34 predefined criteria does not validate all individualized base rubrics. The captured reference repository stopped updating model/benchmark results in July 2025. Creator MIT declarations coexist with a request against online example redistribution; upstream rights are not independently cleared.

[analysis] Benchmark-family atlas — HealthBench: buyer assessment and change conditions. Theme and behavior coverage is useful for selecting tests, but no rubric mean certifies clinical workflow outcomes. Confidence is high in that restriction and moderate in diagnostic use. A buyer should oversample severe misses and independently calibrate example-specific criteria without conflating them with consensus criteria. Prospective workflow studies and clinician-adjudicated false accepts would change confidence.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — MedXpertQA: construction, signal and protocol. The pinned creator README reports that official model releases from Google DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, ByteDance Seed and Alibaba Qwen include MedXpertQA evaluations. The v1 evaluation generally uses zero-shot chain-of-thought with model-specific exceptions; o1 is evaluated on a ten-percent sample of Reasoning and Understanding questions in each subset with seed 42, rather than the full benchmark. The v1 paper uses GPT-4o to label medical task/subtask and Reasoning versus Understanding, and an LLM to assign a question’s most relevant body system. The v1 paper reports 4,460 questions across Text and MM, including 2,005 multimodal questions and 2,839 images; each subset includes five development questions, with comparison tables reporting 2,450 Text and 2,000 MM test questions.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.normal18.medxpertqa.family.creator-reported-evaluation-adoption](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.normal18.medxpertqa.family.creator-reported-evaluation-adoption), [candidate.normal18.medxpertqa.family.evaluation-comparability.binding-correction-v1](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.normal18.medxpertqa.family.evaluation-comparability.binding-correction-v1), [candidate.normal18.medxpertqa.family.model-derived-attribute-labels](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.normal18.medxpertqa.family.model-derived-attribute-labels), [candidate.normal18.medxpertqa.family.units-and-subsets](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.normal18.medxpertqa.family.units-and-subsets)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — MedXpertQA: access and version observations. The v1 paper states that medical experts holding a physician's license review original and augmented questions and options for missing information, factual errors and contextual validity; its guidelines require reviewers to record and mark an invalid original question and take no further review steps for that question. The immutable creator dataset card declares MIT and exposes Text/MM development and test configurations with question, options, label and image-reference fields; the primary paper withholds per-question source provenance and asks readers not to share benchmark examples online.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — MedXpertQA: interpretation boundaries. Question, image and subset counts differ: 4,460 total questions include development, while 2,450 Text and 2,000 MM are test counts. Most MM tasks already have five options. Physician review does not establish reviewer headcount, independence or perfect labels; model-derived medical attribute labels are not physician annotations. The o1 sample and answer-cleaning exceptions prevent unqualified model-row comparisons. MIT metadata does not establish exam/image rights.

A buyer should use a fixed subset, inspect invalid originals and validate answer cleaning before comparing systems. [sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — METR software-task time-horizon evaluation protocol: construction, signal and protocol. The TH1.1 release reports a post-2023 time-horizon doubling estimate of 130.8 days versus 165.3 days for TH1, using model sets that overlap substantially but are not identical. TH1.1 moves evaluation infrastructure from Vivaria to Inspect and re-estimates horizons for 14 of the 33 models with TH1 estimates. The TH1.1 creator compared Vivaria and Inspect using five models on the old TH1 tasks, and a separate three-model comparison on the new task suite.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — METR software-task time-horizon evaluation protocol: access and version observations. The captured TH1.1 creator release changes the time-horizon suite from 170 to 228 tasks by adding 73 HCAST tasks and removing 15, while updating 53 existing tasks.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.next8.metr.time-horizon.th11-task-version.v1](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.next8.metr.time-horizon.th11-task-version.v1)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — METR software-task time-horizon evaluation protocol: interpretation boundaries. The composite protocol reuses HCAST, RE-Bench and SWAA inputs. TH1.1 changes tasks, estimates and infrastructure, and re-estimates only 14 of 33 model horizons. The all-period fit is hybrid for earlier models; 130.8- versus 165.3-day post-2023 estimates have overlapping but unequal model cohorts. Of 31 tasks estimated at eight hours or more, only five have measured human times. No independent task-origin or replication credit follows.

[analysis] Benchmark-family atlas — METR software-task time-horizon evaluation protocol: buyer assessment and change conditions. A versioned fitted horizon should travel with its task mixture, human-time provenance, scaffold and reliability target. Confidence is high in that requirement and low in interpreting a changed growth fit as pure model progress. A buyer should compare the same systems across old/new tasks and audit estimated long-task times. Prospective stable-suite data and measured long baselines would change trend confidence.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — micro1 MissionReport: construction, signal and protocol. Task reward is positive criterion points minus triggered penalties divided by possible positive points, clamped to 0–1; a missing/corrupt/empty report scores zero. The agentic judge sees the submitted Word document and expert report. MissionReport describes 20 reporting tasks across four report types and five organizational settings; its pinned public release contains five tasks and 42 source files. Each task combines a reporting-expert assignment, reader, working files, template and expert rubric; source files may be assembled, written or adapted by the expert.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Pareto AttuneBench: construction, signal and protocol. The primary scoring composite weights emotion tracking 24%, evaluation quality 49% and holistic comprehension 27%; Kendall tau and draft quality judging are supplementary rather than composite inputs. The paper documents informed consent, withdrawal, topic reassignment and manual PII redaction, while explicitly excluding clinical mental-health validation and safety-critical deployment conclusions. Participants had at least five exchanges with an anonymized original model, completed PANAS/binary labels, compared original and preference-informed model responses, and drafted human-edited golden responses. AttuneBench’s 200 conversations were collected from eleven US-based native-English-speaking adults, with each participant annotating their own emotional states, observed/preferred behavior and response preferences.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — ProgramBench: construction, signal and protocol. The pinned usage guide specifies Linux amd64 containers, task_cleanroom_v6 inference images, task_v6 evaluation images and on-demand retrieval of test archives from Hugging Face. ProgramBench reconstruction tasks supply an executable and usage documentation while withholding original source and evaluation tests; the stated default blocks internet access and permits implementations in any language. ProgramBench defines resolved tasks as passing every associated test without a cheating flag; partial test pass rate records relative progress rather than a percentage of implemented functionality. ProgramBench v1 contains 200 reconstruction tasks sourced from open-source repositories, with a reported 248,853 behavioral test functions and a median of 770 per task.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Proximal FrontierSWE: construction, signal and protocol. The v2 protocol documents separate fresh verifier containers, non-root users and task mutation, while also describing a Modal-daemon bypass that exposed protected reference files. The v2 writeup says v1 wall-clock performance rankings changed on re-scoring, motivating a weighted instruction-count proxy priced to a pinned Intel microarchitecture. The v2 creator protocol reports 0–1 task scores aggregated as mean@5 over 34 tasks, with a 20-hour budget and Proximus as default harness. FrontierSWE v2 adds 21 tasks and retires four from the 17-task v1, producing 34 tasks within the same logical benchmark family.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — SciCode: construction, signal and protocol. In the v1 paper’s standard setup, models receive no supplied scientific background and carry forward generated solutions; a main problem counts as solved only when all subproblems and the integrated main solution are correct. The creator FAQ states that subproblems 13.6, 62.1 and 76.2 receive supplied problem-code context to control evaluation uncertainty, and explains that subproblem overlap is judged in the context of its main problem. The v1 paper explicitly marks a subset of its named authors as data curators and states that problems, solutions and test cases were annotated, revised and verified by senior researchers at PhD-student level or above. The v1 paper reports 80 main problems and 338 subproblems across 16 subfields; development has 15 main problems and 50 subproblems, while test has 65 main problems and 288 subproblems.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — SUPERChem: construction, signal and protocol. SUPERChem pairs multimodal problems with manually prepared text-only counterparts; Appendix C describes general-image descriptions and organic-structure transcription using preliminary DECIMER recognition followed by ChemDraw drawing and revision. SUPERChem's checklist calls for question-source clarity, duplicate checking, plausible distractors, explanations that remain semantically complete and logically coherent after all checkpoints are removed, Chinese/English meaning consistency and correct rendering; its leakage mitigations include masking nonessential entities and discouraging reverse solving. The manuscript describes 633 filtered SUPERChem-All questions, partitioned into a 500-question public release and a 133-question holdout, with a separate 100-question evaluation subset.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — SWE Atlas: construction, signal and protocol. The pinned Artificial Analysis card describes SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA as a modified grading release of Scale AI's same 124-task QnA set, using GPT-6 Luna at xhigh reasoning and five votes per criterion. The pinned SWE Atlas v1.1 README and NOTICE credit Artificial Analysis's SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA release with wording reused for some updated Codebase Q&A rubric criteria. The pinned SWE Atlas v1.1 README credits Inductive ML with reward-hacking feedback used to further harden task environments. SWE Atlas v1 screens passing Refactoring and Test Writing patches against reference patches using added-line Jaccard similarity and raw-diff sequence similarity; the paper explicitly says this does not prove absence of contamination or memorization. SWE Atlas Codebase Q&A asks for codebase exploration and runtime-supported explanations and requires every mandatory rubric item to pass. SWE Atlas Refactoring combines behavior-preservation tests and mandatory rubric checks for code maintainability, artifact cleanup and negative criteria. SWE Atlas Test Writing combines a model-judged test manifest, tests passing on working code and failing or erroring on a no-op mutation, and all mandatory test-comprehensiveness rubric checks.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — AA-LCR: defined object and observation units. The pinned AA-LCR creator card describes 100 text questions over 30 document sets containing 234 documents, with about 100,000 input tokens per document set. Questions require reasoning across documents rather than direct retrieval; questions, document sets and documents are different units of one family.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.third11.aa-lcr.units.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.aa-lcr.units.v2)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — AA-LCR: construction and provenance. AA-LCR’s creator describes undergraduate question writers using non-frontier models to screen difficulty, followed by human testing on the same document sets, revision or removal of failed questions, and at least one correct human solution for every retained question. This is the creator’s reported construction and validation procedure, not an assertion that each question has unanimous human agreement.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.third11.aa-lcr.curation.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.aa-lcr.curation.v2)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — AA-LCR: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The pinned AA-LCR card uses an LLM equality checker with instructions for numerical equivalence, required formats, ordering and a single committed final answer; it identifies GPT-5.6 Luna at medium reasoning as the checker. Mercor’s separately captured AA-LCRv 1.1 implementation specifies Gemini 3.5 Flash, four repeats and pass@1 aggregated across repeats rather than a best-of score. The two judge configurations are preserved separately. AA-LCR version 1.1 corrects sixteen answer keys and adds an equality-checker system prompt while leaving the questions and document sets unchanged; the creator says version 1.0.0 and 1.1 scores are not directly comparable. Four answer-key repairs change the answer itself; the remaining repairs address notation or units. These revisions are manifestations of the retained family.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.third11.aa-lcr.scoring.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.aa-lcr.scoring.v2), [candidate.third11.aa-lcr.version.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.aa-lcr.version.v2)

AA-LCR’s creator card licenses the question set under Apache 2.0 while declining to claim copyright or impose a license over the accompanying text representations of publicly available documents. The question-set license does not establish blanket permission for every underlying document.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — AdvancedIF: defined object and observation units. AdvancedIF’s v2 paper enumerates 402 explicit/complex instruction dialogs, 736 multi-turn carried-context dialogs and 507 system-prompt-steerability dialogs, totaling 1,645; rubrics for multi-turn dialogs are collected only at the final turn. The paper’s dialog/prompt units and final-turn rubric target should be preserved; the three categories are not independent benchmark families.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.third11.advancedif.units.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.advancedif.units.v2)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — AdvancedIF: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The AdvancedIF v2 benchmark evaluation uses o3-mini to check rubric criteria and labels a response correct only if all criteria pass; it reports category percentages and their average. RIFL’s rubric-generator training is a separate process. Mercor’s later implementation uses a different judge and repeat configuration, so that protocol must not be substituted for the paper’s evaluator. The AdvancedIF v2 paper describes manually written prompts focused on instruction following; for multi-turn examples annotators first converse with a supplied model, and the collection retains final-turn prompts that trigger an instruction-following failure. This is adversarial difficulty selection against a provided model, not a random sample of ordinary user instructions.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.third11.advancedif.evaluation.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.advancedif.evaluation.v2), [candidate.third11.advancedif.prompt-collection.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.advancedif.prompt-collection.v2)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — AdvancedIF: evaluation, validation and interpretation. AdvancedIF pairs each prompt with up to twenty final-turn criteria written by the same annotator, and the paper describes subsequent rounds of human review. The benchmark’s human-written evaluation rubrics are distinct from the synthetic rubrics used by the paper’s separate RIFL training pipeline.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.third11.advancedif.rubrics.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.advancedif.rubrics.v2)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — AIME: defined object and observation units. Mercor’s captured AIME 2025 entry describes thirty text problems drawn from the 2025 American Invitational Mathematics Examination, with integer answers from 0 through 999. This identifies the 2025 AI-evaluation manifestation of the retained AIME family; it does not redefine the rules of every human AIME administration.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.third11.aime2025.units.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.aime2025.units.v2)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — AIME: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The captured Mercor AIME 2025 protocol names Gemini 3.5 Flash as an LLM judge for the integer-answer responses. An integer answer format does not by itself establish programmatic exact-match grading in this implementation. Mercor’s AIME 2025 methodology specifies a single-shot agent, four runs and pass@1; its shared rule aggregates repeats rather than reporting a best-of score. Four repeats are evaluation attempts, not four additional question sets.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — AM-DeepSeek-R1-Distilled: construction and provenance. The AM card describes LLM scoring of instructions by difficulty and category, label-based filtering and semantic deduplication; its introduction also claims cleaning against test-set contamination. This creator-described processing is not an independently established uniqueness or contamination-free guarantee for every record. Instruction selection is distinct from model response generation; a dataset-wide human annotation or adjudication process is not established by this card-only read. The AM card describes about 1.4 million Chinese-and-English reasoning entries: about 0.5 million reused from open datasets and about 0.9 million DeepSeek-R1-671B response generations attributed to the AM team. These are creator release-scale descriptions, not independently recounted payload totals; the source tables are non-exhaustive. The reused and AM-generated components have different response provenance, and the limitations warn of inaccurate attribution caused by nested source relationships.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.distill5.am.instruction-selection.v1](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.distill5.am.instruction-selection.v1), [candidate.distill5.am.mixed-response-origins.v1](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.distill5.am.mixed-response-origins.v1)

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — AM-DeepSeek-R1-Distilled: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The AM card declares CC-BY-NC-4.0 and separately restricts project artifacts to research use, disallowing commercial and potentially harmful uses. These are creator declarations, not a legal compatibility decision or blanket permission for all nested upstream data, teacher outputs and linked artifacts. Its factuality and nested-source-attribution warnings remain applicable to reuse and provenance checking. AM processing describes rule- and LLM-based reference-answer checks for part of the data, sandbox verification for code with test cases, and reward-model scoring followed by rejection sampling. The introduction says all responses underwent rigorous verification, but the limitations say the LLM-generated dataset was not strictly verified and retains factuality shortcomings; both statements remain explicit. Reference answers and test cases are documented only for some records; the schema does not establish universal answer-check or executable-test coverage.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — AM-DeepSeek-R1-Distilled: evaluation, validation and interpretation. AM records are documented as user/assistant messages with role, content and info; assistant content separates reasoning and answers, and info can retain source, reference answers, test cases and separate reasoning/answer content. The illustrated user source is natural_reasoning and assistant source am-0309, an example of distinct prompt/response provenance rather than a corpus census. The header represents test_case as a struct but the loading example declares a string; this mismatch is retained without claiming executable parser compatibility. Reference answers and code test cases apply only to some problems, and nested attribution may be inaccurate.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — APEX-SWE: defined object and observation units. The APEX-SWE v3 paper describes two held-out task domains with 100 Integration tasks and 100 Observability tasks, and a public fifty-task development set containing 25 of each. The 200-task leaderboard and 50-task development set are separate evaluation scopes of one retained family.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.third11.apex-swe.units.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.apex-swe.units.v2)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — APEX-SWE: construction and provenance. The APEX-SWE v3 paper says Integration tasks were built by engineers with at least three years of experience and checked for prompt/source alignment, faithful tests without reward hacking, and a human reference solution passing all tests. These are benchmark-author-reported construction checks, not a rerun or independent certification of every task. APEX-SWE Observability tasks are converted from GitHub issue/PR pairs in repositories with at least 350 stars, screening for patches of at least 100 lines across at least three files, and adding synthetic logs plus public developer discussions to reconstruct a production-failure environment. The environment includes normal log lines and bug symptoms; agents receive no failing unit tests and must diagnose the failure from telemetry and context.

Evidence IDs: [candidate.third11.apex-swe.integration-curation.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.apex-swe.integration-curation.v2), [candidate.third11.apex-swe.observability-curation.v2](evidence.html#assertion-candidate.third11.apex-swe.observability-curation.v2)

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — APEX-SWE: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The APEX-SWE v3 paper separates pass@1 task completion from task-specific functional, robustness and style rubrics judged against the final patch and execution logs; it states these rubric scores are not used for its leaderboard. Style criteria apply only to Observability tasks. The paper’s Gemini 3 Pro judge configuration is specific to this supplementary rubric analysis. APEX-SWE v3 uses API-facing pytest suites for Integration and fail-to-pass/pass-to-pass verification for Observability; pass@1 is averaged over three independent runs, while pass@3 records success at least once. The observability README requires all fail-to-pass and all pass-to-pass tests to pass. Code and scorer execution are not implied by this documented protocol.

The APEX-SWE v3 paper describes a released development set under a CC-BY license and an open evaluation harness; the pinned repository declares MIT for its code. The paper’s general CC-BY wording is retained without inventing an unstated license version or transferring the code license to all source repositories.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — BabaIsBench / Baba Is Harbor: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The Baba Is Harbor README warns that oracle move strings are public and the game predates model training cutoffs, and distinguishes hinted and longer-clock variants from the base tasks. The linked memorization audit was not read, so no claim of contamination-free results or validation of that audit is made. Hints, time budgets and additional campaign stages are not counted as new logical benchmark families. The cached BabaIsBench page describes an eight-level Intro arm with three attempts per model per level and a 60-minute limit per attempt, and a fifteen-level Lake arm run once per model with effectively no time limit. The newer creator README lists 55 levels across stages 0–3; this is a different repository scope from the page’s two-arm 23-level evaluation, not an automatically reconciled current count.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — BabaIsBench / Baba Is Harbor: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The Baba Is Harbor creator README describes JSON grid puzzles with an interactive simulator; the agent submits a move string that the real game engine replays, assigning reward 1 when a controlled object reaches a winning object. The task instructions describe mechanics generically and do not name the game. No game was installed, purchased or executed by this author. The creator README describes privilege separation in which a non-root agent can run the game simulator through a gated runner but cannot read or modify the protected engine. This is documented environment design, not an independent security audit or proof against every exploit.

The Baba Is Harbor README declares Apache 2.0 for repository code while excluding copyrighted Baba Is You game content and engine code; running its setup requires a user-owned local game installation. Code licensing does not grant rights to redistribute the game. No paid access or game-asset download occurred in this research.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Bespoke-Stratos: defined object and observation units. Bespoke attributes Stratos-17k to a Sky-T1-style pipeline ported into Curator using DeepSeek-R1, with roughly 5k coding items from APPs/TACO, 10k math items from NuminaMATH subsets and 1k science/puzzle items from STILL-2. DeepSeek-R1 replaces QwQ, and its traces are not passed through Sky-T1's GPT-4o-mini reformatting step. The 17k name and rounded component counts do not establish an exact payload census; the card says rejection sampling can change the exact problems included. Creator/pipeline and teacher-model roles do not establish a paid human annotation workforce or universal human verification.

Bespoke reports generating the synthetic reasoning dataset using Curator and DeepSeek-R1 in about 1.5 hours at a cost of $800. This is a creator description of dataset generation, not a reproduced universal price or the total cost of model fine-tuning and evaluation. The recipe and training/evaluation implementations are linked separately and were not read or executed in this card-only scope.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Bespoke-Stratos: evaluation, validation and interpretation. Bespoke describes rejection sampling of incorrect solutions, Ray-cluster acceleration of code verification, and GPT-4o-mini math filtering in place of Sky-T1 parsing logic. Direct code-execution-verifier integration into Curator is described as work in progress at this card version. The reported increase from 25% to 73% in retained correct math solutions is a creator-reported filtering result, not an independently checked error-rate or adjudication study. The Bespoke card reports AIME2024 values of 63.3 for Stratos-32B and 20.0 for Stratos-7B, identified as fine-tunes of the corresponding Qwen2.5-Instruct models. Tables distinguish creator-measured DeepSeek-distill baselines from reported values: 66.7 versus 72.6 for 32B and 43.3 versus 55.5 for 7B; those columns are not interchangeable. These creator-reported model results are not an independent dataset-quality score, replicated improvement or significance result; linked evaluation code remains unread.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — BinaryAudit: construction and provenance. BinaryAudit’s creator README describes manually inserting artificial backdoors into open-source projects, compiling modified code into stripped binaries and providing agents only the binaries and reverse-engineering tools in Docker. The benchmark does not claim that the upstream projects contain those vulnerabilities in real deployments. No backdoor or exploit was executed here.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — BinaryAudit: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The BinaryAudit page describes binary-analysis pass rate as identifying a backdoor and its location in the binary and reports false-positive rate separately for clean code. No model ranking or creator performance number is endorsed. Test implementation and individual labels were not audited. BinaryAudit includes unmodified clean binaries for which the intended answer is that no backdoor is present, and separate baseline tasks testing operation of Ghidra and Radare 2. These controls separate false alarms and tool-operation ability from successful backdoor localization; their presence is not an independent sensitivity/specificity measurement.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — BrickVision: evaluation, validation and interpretation. BrickVision scores pointing responses by requiring exactly one point per target inside the corresponding segmentation mask, and scores counting responses by exact equality with the reference integer. The card uses the final answer without reasoning because every coordinate pair counts as a point. Coordinate conventions and the optional pixel mode must be kept with the evaluation configuration. No scorer execution or model-performance ranking is proposed.

BrowseComp’s authors caution that its questions are not representative of typical user requests and ask that benchmark examples not be reproduced online to reduce contamination. The BrowseComp paper describes 1,266 human-written browsing questions designed to have stable short factual answers that are difficult to locate online; candidate questions were screened against models with and without browsing and against the first results pages from five Google searches. This describes the original BrowseComp family, not the separate Mercor 130 subset or every browsing benchmark. Difficulty screening is creator-reported and is not a performance ranking.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — BrowseComp: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The BrowseComp paper reports an initial 1,287-question set and removal of 21 questions with answer-format mismatches, ambiguous phrasing or incorrect answers, leaving 1,266 questions. The paper says this review focused on the 118 questions where Deep Research had a zero pass rate; it was not an independent audit of every payload label. BrowseComp uses an AI grader to compare a submitted short answer with the reference answer for semantic equivalence; its appended grading instructions focus on answer matching rather than independently solving the question. The grader prompt is a documented procedure, not an independently validated correctness oracle. No benchmark question, answer or canary string is reproduced in this proposition.

BrowseComp construction uses inverted question design from a chosen answer, reviews plausible answer uniqueness, and revises a question if another valid answer is found; second-trainer attempts were used for a portion of questions. The paper does not guarantee unique answers and does not establish a strict universal 10-minute second-review protocol for every question.

Chartography’s v1 paper describes one hundred task-image records using ninety-eight byte-distinct images; eighty-one records use online-sourced charts and nineteen use expert-created charts. Task records, image files and source categories are different units within one retained benchmark family.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Chartography: construction and provenance. Chartography tasks are authored by working domain professionals with a target answer and a complete walkthrough of the visual readings and calculations; for visually estimated quantities, authors provide a chart-specific acceptable range. Each task is independently checked by three additional domain experts and retained only if screening elicits a meaningful failure in at least one frontier model. Ambiguous or unsupported tasks are revised or rejected; screening yields a deliberately difficult set rather than a random sample of professional chart questions.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Chartography: evaluation, validation and interpretation. Chartography supplies a chart and free-form question without tools, and uses Gemini 3.5 Flash to judge the final answer against expert targets and ranges without showing the judge the chart; multi-part answers are all-or-nothing. The paper reports twenty trials per task; the later README’s leaderboard instructions specify ten. Those trial configurations remain separate dated source scopes.

DecoyCount’s format document discloses 121 potentially stale multi-hop answers in the internal evaluated bank after underlying counts changed, and states that the standalone evaluator does not automatically exclude those items. The DecoyCount format document defines exact-match integer accuracy with API/parsing failures retained in the denominator, a registered-decoy hit rate for neutral/cued counting, and a paired cued-minus-neutral accuracy gap. [sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — FrontierCode: evaluation, validation and interpretation. FrontierCode combines unit tests, build/lint commands, reverse tests on the original broken code, adaptive test alignment, scope checks and LLM quality judgments. Its creator describes adversarial hack reports, four-solution rubric calibration, pod review and final researcher review. These are creator-reported benchmark construction controls, not new independent review receipts or measured false-positive improvements. FrontierCode requires every blocker criterion to pass before awarding a weighted rubric score, otherwise assigning zero; its creator article averages five trials per reasoning effort and reports the best-performing effort. A blocker pass rate and a weighted quality score are different metrics. Best-effort reporting is not a best-of-five success measure.

HANDBOOK.md uses ten expert-written base handbooks adapted from industry practice, changes operative policies for each task, and has expert builders construct the world and hand-written rubric before implementing and iterating programmatic checks. Policy mutation changes rules and thresholds rather than only cosmetic wording; correct behavior can require withholding an action.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — HANDBOOK.md: evaluation, validation and interpretation. HANDBOOK.md reports the fraction of trials satisfying every criterion, averaging four trials per task, and separately reports a metric allowing one missed criterion and mean criterion scores for analysis. Trials are capped at two hundred tool calls and one hour; provider or transport errors are excluded and rerun rather than counted as task failures. HANDBOOK.md’s v3 paper specifies 824 deterministic criteria: 592 required-output checks and 232 prohibited-behavior checks over final files and service states, without LLM judging. Exact-count invariants also check that actions outside the task scope were not performed; counts describe the documented release rather than an independent payload recount.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Harvey LAB: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The pinned Harvey evaluation document scopes each rubric criterion to its declared output files and asks an LLM to judge semantic satisfaction of match_criteria, without a separate golden reference output. The documented scorer fails a criterion without calling the judge when none of that criterion's scoped output files exist, or the run has no output at all. Each judge call uses the criterion-scoped outputs rather than all matter documents or all outputs. The captured Harvey methodology gives each judge a binary all-criteria-pass task score and averages the two default judges’ scores; dual task values can therefore be 0, 0.5 or 1, while strict aggregate all_pass requires both judges to all-pass. The standard pair is Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.5. Pooled and macro criterion pass rates are diagnostics distinct from the headline averaged all-pass rate.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Light-R1 training data family: evaluation, validation and interpretation. Light claims exact- or N-gram-based decontamination and names AIME24/25, MATH-500 and GPQA Diamond as target reasoning benchmarks. The same discussion warns that MATH-500 is compromised by identical or numerically altered questions in public data; this is not silently converted into an exact contamination count for Light's released payload. Creator filtering does not establish an independently contamination-free corpus, particularly for upstream pretraining sources. After SFT stage2, Light describes sampling stage2-model responses, separating correct and incorrect outputs, and constructing DPO pairs using verification results and DeepSeek-R1 responses before model merging. The card describes DPO or NCA with sequence parallelism and a merge of stage2 plus two DPO versions; one DPO-data version skips special tokens in rejected responses. These are creator-described operations, not an inspected payload, executed training recipe or independent human preference-labeling study.

[sourced_fact] Dataset-family atlas — Light-R1 training data family: evaluation, validation and interpretation. Light-R1 describes public math questions with DeepSeek-R1 responses, a 76k first SFT set selected by verification and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview difficulty sampling, and a harder 3k second set mostly filtered from the first. The model starts from Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct; from scratch is explicitly limited to a model without long chain-of-thought capability, not raw-data pretraining. stage1-76k.json and stage2-3k.json are release descriptions, not independently recounted or proven-disjoint corpora, and remain stages of the existing family. Named question sources include OpenR1-Math, OpenThoughts, LIMO, OpenMathInstruct-2, s1K-1.1, Omni-MATH, hendrycks_math and AIME up to 2023. The Light card reports final AIME24/AIME25 values of 76.6 and 64.6, states 64-run score averaging, and estimates training at under six hours on twelve H800s, around $1,000. These are creator-reported scores and cost/time estimates; public-model results may come from existing evaluations, and no experiment, accounting or significance study was reproduced here. A separate stage2-data adaptation statement uses 0.779/0.675 beside 72.6/54.9 for a stated DeepSeek-distill model; its mixed notation is retained rather than substituted for final Light scores. The card describes math-specialized thinking with a forced think marker and some GPQA forgetting; these math results do not independently establish general-domain gains.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Multi-SWE-bench: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The Multi-SWE-bench paper reports 68 outsourced annotators screened for at least two years of target-language experience and a relevant degree, one-hour task training, independent dual labels followed by cross-review, and a 14-engineer internal quality team checking annotations against reference answers and an 80% threshold. No outsourcing supplier is named or inferred. This manual-verification stage belongs to the benchmark; it is explicitly absent from the initial Multi-SWE-RL construction stream. The 80% threshold is the creator’s annotation-quality rule, not a new measured annotation accuracy here. Multi-SWE-bench’s pre-annotation filter runs full test suites at the base commit, after the test patch, and after both test and fix patches; it rejects regressions, requires a failed-to-passed test transition, and tracks skipped or absent tests as well as pass/fail. These test-transition checks establish the paper’s filtering rule, not an independent guarantee that unit tests capture every valid software fix.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Physical Engineering’s Last Exam (PLE): construction and provenance. PLE’s co-authored route starts from engineers’ structured seed briefs, uses Creator and Solver agents to construct and challenge environments and graders, and ends with expert validation and difficulty intensification. The solver is isolated from graders and references; the described loop tests mean performance across typically three attempts rather than assuming a task is hard after one failure. For PLE’s expert-authored route, practising engineers write a realistic work request, construct a multi-format project environment and specify weighted evidence-bound rubric checks on the deliverable; the paper reports 941 rubric items across 44 tasks. These are reported task-construction stages, not an assertion of independent inspection of every environment or engineer’s records.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — Physical Engineering’s Last Exam (PLE): evaluation, validation and interpretation. PLE’s documented evaluation gives an agent the instruction and environment without rubric, grader or reference access, then grades collected deliverables outside the agent container; model/harness pairs run every task three times with a six-hour agent budget. Infrastructure failures are rerun, while runs ending without a gradable deliverable score zero. Results are scoped to the model plus harness and cannot be interpreted as real engineering sign-off. PLE’s v2 paper grades expert-authored tasks by weighted binary rubrics and most co-authored deliverables by 0.4 times constraint compliance plus 0.6 times a hard-constraint-gated normalized objective score. Twelve co-authored graders also use LLM judgments for narrative soft constraints; two site-design and two MEP-coordination tasks retain their own scores. The hybrid formula is not universal to all 85 tasks.

[sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — PostTrain Arena: evaluation, validation and interpretation. The captured PostTrain landing page accepts contributions while challenge runs are paused pending evaluation repairs/base-model measurement. The later README separates public configuration and bounded historical pipeline checks from proof that a full held-out training run completed. Seen-task historical practice and a small same-domain diagnostic are not evidence of broad held-out generalization; illustrative landing-page scoreboards are not measured results. PostTrain Arena’s organizer specification fixes the model, training recipe and held-out suite for a challenge and ranks contributed environment collections by the change in held-out pass@1 after versus before training in the same run. [sourced_fact] Benchmark-family atlas — PostTrain Arena: evaluation, validation and interpretation. PostTrain Arena documents static overlap/leakage checks and planned dynamic reference/no-op/difficulty controls; static acceptance reads source without executing it and is explicitly not proof that the oracle, runtime or verifier works. The planned dynamic checks rerun reference and no-op controls eight times and target one to three base-model successes in four attempts. The specification says runs do not yet wait for these verdicts. PostTrain Arena accepts collections of one to two hundred task packages containing a prompt/limits file, Docker environment, verifier and reference oracle; verifiers run only after the agent finishes and must score substantive output rather than file existence. The documented held-out attempt passes only if its verifier passes, and a time-limit attempt fails. This package contract does not establish that every submitted task’s verifier works.
